title: A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: All that has marks is false and deceptive; take not hold of marks, and abide unmoved in suchness.

inline.s: Course
Teaching Materials
All that has marks is false and deceptive; take not hold of marks, and abide unmoved in suchness.
Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.
Dissolving the inverted thoughts of my myriad kalpas, I attain the Dharma-body without passing through asamkhyeya kalpas.

Why is it that for a thousand years the Diamond Sutra has been on everyone’s lips, known in every household, expounded without number and annotated without number? The reason is not only that the merit and virtue of upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra are immeasurably great, but also that people have come to realize that the Diamond Sutra reveals a truth of boundless power and yet of the utmost profundity—the wish-fulfilling jewel of a king that carries one beyond suffering and death to the Buddha Way. And so everyone earnestly probes and realizes it—what does the Diamond Sutra teach? What is it really teaching?
In the text of the Diamond Sutra, before the sutra proper there stands a verse, “Cloud What Brahma,” which is written exceedingly well:
How may one gain long life and the indestructible vajra body?
And by what causes and conditions may one gain the power of great steadfastness?
How, through this sutra, may one reach the ultimate other shore?
May the Buddha open the subtle and secret and broadly expound it for living beings.

The first line, “How may one gain long life and the indestructible vajra body,” asks how one may end birth and death and realize the Dharma-body. The second line, “And by what causes and conditions may one gain the power of great steadfastness,” asks how, on the path of cultivation, where private desire and false teachings disorder the mind and fork after fork opens before one, one may gain the power of great steadfastness, be undisturbed by the many delusions, and press straight ahead on the path of bodhi. The third line, “How, through this sutra, may one reach the ultimate other shore,” asks how one may rely on this sutra (the Diamond Sutra) to cross the sea of suffering of birth and death and reach the ultimate shore of nirvāṇa. The fourth line, “May the Buddha open the subtle and secret and broadly expound it for living beings,” asks that the World-Honored One broadly reveal and proclaim for living beings the rarest, most subtle and most secret way to Buddhahood: how to gain the indestructible vajra body? How to gain the power of great steadfastness? How to rely on this sutra to reach the ultimate shore of nirvāṇa?
Question: What does “Cloud What Brahma” mean?
Answer: The three words “Cloud What Brahma” carry a double meaning.

First, as to genre: the “Brahma” in “Cloud What Brahma” means a chant of praise, or Brahma chant, and refers to praising the Buddha’s virtues with subtle and wondrous sound. It is used chiefly for lecturing on sutras, for morning and evening recitation, and for repentance rites in the practice hall. In all ceremonies—sutra lectures, ordination, sutra recitation—the Brahma chant is intoned (called “performing the Brahma”) to still clamor and confusion and to gather and settle the mind.
[Pai] An abbreviation of “pai-ni,” meaning the singing of Sanskrit sounds.

As for “cloud what” in “Cloud What Brahma”: the first two words of the verse, “cloud what,” are taken as the name of this chant. Similar chants include, for example, “Brahma of the Tathāgata” and “Brahma of Dwelling in the World”:
Brahma of the Tathāgata
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form and hue, in all the world has no equal;
Beyond compare, inconceivable—therefore I now revere it.
The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and so too is his wisdom;
All dharmas abide forever—therefore I take refuge.
Brahma of Dwelling in the World
Dwelling in the world like empty space, like a lotus that does not touch the water;
With a mind pure, transcending all—I bow my head to the Unsurpassed One.
Second, in a deeper sense, “Cloud What Brahma” means “how to become a Buddha,” and this is the core of the verse. The Kośa says:
“The Buddha corresponds to the supreme Brahma-virtue; therefore the World-Honored One alone should be named Brahma. For it is said in the sutras that the Buddha too is named Brahma.”
[Sutra]
both
according with the capacities of living beings and according with the
scriptures
of truth, that is, the Buddhist sutras.

blocks.text: 2. The Outline of the Great Prajñā Sutra

inline.s: The Diamond Sutra—its full name is the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sutra. In the
years in which the World-Honored One taught the Dharma,

were devoted to the prajñā class of scriptures, in seven hundred and fifty-one fascicles altogether. The largest of these is the Great Prajñā Sutra (its full name the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra), in six hundred fascicles, completed in sixteen assemblies. The Diamond Sutra is the “Section on the Diamond That Cuts Through Illusion” spoken at the ninth assembly of the Great Prajñā Sutra (fascicle 577), just over five thousand characters in all. Prajñā is the outline of the Mahāyāna Dharma, and the Diamond Sutra is in turn the outline of the six-hundred-fascicle Great Prajñā Sutra.

blocks.text: 3. The Essential Message of the Diamond

inline.s: The essential message of this sutra: compassion and emptiness working as one, leaving illusion and waking from the dream.

All dharmas are matters of the dream of ignorance. While one dreams, the myriad things appear in profusion; when one wakes, nothing remains. Hence the mark of all dharmas is this: appearance exists but substance is empty. Therefore with regard to all dharmas one must neither falsely cling to existence (taking them to be real) nor falsely cling to non-existence (denying even their appearance); one should walk the middle way that dwells in neither of the two extremes, letting compassion and emptiness work as one, using illusion to leave illusion until all illusions are gone and the dream of ignorance is ended. In this sutra the World-Honored One reveals this essential message again and again.

[Substance and appearance] Substance means the reality of all dharmas, that is, the true nature of all dharmas. Appearance means the varied forms and marks of all dharmas. We live within the dream of ignorance, and all dharmas are matters of the dream; hence they have their appearance but not their substance (appearance exists but substance is empty). [Appearance exists but substance is empty] While in the dream of ignorance, all dharmas present myriad forms; when the dream of ignorance ends, nothing remains. The Song of Enlightenment says:
“In the dream there plainly are the six destinies
(the six paths)
, but after awakening all is empty and the great thousand worlds are gone
(the great thousand worlds)
For a detailed account of the true nature of all dharmas and the dream of ignorance, see
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
For example:

And thus, though immeasurable, countless, boundless living beings are liberated, in truth no living being obtains liberation.”

Sentences such as these—refuting existence, refuting non-existence, dwelling in neither extreme—are found everywhere in the Diamond Sutra, too many to count. Practitioners should take up the middle way that dwells in neither extreme. If there is a leaning to one side, one should take the remedy suited to the illness: those clinging to existence should cultivate more the contemplation of emptiness; those clinging to non-existence should cultivate more the contemplation of compassion.
The Diamond Sutra has five great characteristics:
1. The Diamond Sutra is the most widely circulated and known in every household.

For more than a thousand years, among those who study the Buddhadharma, whatever their school and whatever practice they cultivate, the Diamond Sutra has been one they must recite; and even for scholars who do not study Buddhism, the Diamond Sutra is one they must read. According to the Oral Instructions on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra by Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, in that era (the time of Empress Wu Zetian) there were more than eight hundred households that composed commentaries and annotations on the Diamond Sutra. The preface to the Oral Instructions says:
“This sutra
(the Diamond Sutra)
has been read and recited by countless people and praised beyond measure, and those who composed commentaries and annotations on it numbered over eight hundred households.”
2. The Diamond Sutra is the mother of all Buddhas—most complete, most direct, most real.
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom,
fascicle 74, says:
“Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas; dwelling in this prajñā, one can fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.”

Thus we know that prajñā is the outline of all Buddhadharma, and that the Diamond Sutra is in turn the outline of the six-hundred-fascicle Great Prajñā Sutra. In this sutra the World-Honored One says:
“All Buddhas and the anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi dharma of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”

This shows that the Diamond Sutra is the mind-dharma of the Tathāgata, the most complete, most direct and most real method of becoming a Buddha. Hence the influence of the Diamond Sutra is exceedingly vast and far-reaching; those who study, annotate, uphold and recite it are countless, and those who thereby awaken to the Way and realize the Way are likewise countless. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records:
“The Master
(Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan)
constantly urged monks and laypeople: simply uphold the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and straightaway realize Buddhahood.”

And the Sixth Patriarch himself, inspired by the Diamond Sutra, went to East Mountain to seek the Way; through the Diamond Sutra he awakened and realized the fruit. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is itself the great practice of the Diamond Sutra.
3. The merit and virtue of upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra are boundless.

The merit and virtue of upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra are exceedingly great, and its karmic reward is inconceivable; the World-Honored One says so again and again in the sutra. For example:

In ages to come, if there are good men and good women who can uphold and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, with Buddha-wisdom, fully knows such people and fully sees such people; all of them accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit and virtue.”

Subhuti, if there are good men and good women who in the first part of the day give their bodies in charity as many times as the sands of the Ganges, who in the middle part of the day again give their bodies in charity as many times as the sands of the Ganges, who in the latter part of the day also give their bodies in charity as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus giving their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; and if again there are people who hear this scripture and their faith is not contrary to it, their merit surpasses that—how much more so if they write it out, uphold and recite it, and explain it to others.”

(Translation: Subhuti, if there are good men and good women who in the morning give their lives in charity as many times as the sands of the Ganges, who at noon again give their lives in charity as many times as the sands of the Ganges, who in the evening again give their lives in charity as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and who thus, three times each day for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, give their lives in charity; and if another person hears this scripture and deeply believes without doubt, the merit he obtains surpasses that of the former. How much more so if he also writes it out, upholds and recites the Diamond Sutra, and explains it to others—the merit he obtains is then beyond all reckoning!)

“If there are people who can uphold and recite it and widely explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows such people and fully sees such people; all of them accomplish merit that is immeasurable, beyond praise, boundless and inconceivable. Such people are fit to bear the Tathāgata’s anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“If in ages to come, in the last five hundred years, there are living beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, uphold and recite it, such people will be foremost and most rare.”

“I recall that in past immeasurable asamkhyeya kalpas, before the Buddha Burning Lamp, I met eight hundred and forty million billion nayutas of Buddhas, and honored and served them all without ever passing one by; yet if there are people in the last age who can uphold and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain—compared with the merit of my honoring all those Buddhas—mine does not come to a hundredth part of theirs, nor to a thousand-myriad-billionth part, nor can it be reached even by reckoning or simile.”

(Translation: I recall that in past countless kalpas, before I met the Buddha Burning Lamp, I encountered eight hundred and forty million billion billion Buddhas, and I honored and served them all without passing one by. If there are people in the last age who can uphold and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain—compared with the merit of my honoring all those Buddhas—my merit does not come to a hundredth part of theirs, nor to a thousand-myriad-billionth part, nor even to the fraction, of a magnitude no reckoning or simile can describe, that is theirs.)

“If good men and good women in the last age uphold and recite this sutra, and I were to set forth in full the merit they obtain, some who heard it would become frantic and bewildered, doubting and unbelieving. Subhuti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is likewise inconceivable.”
Therefore upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra is the joint cultivation of merit and wisdom. The Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra,
preface, says:

“If good people and worthy scholars can diligently and sincerely cultivate, reverently uphold and recite, seeking the Dharma through the sutra and awakening through the Dharma, they will at once extinguish immeasurable offenses and at once obtain the most excellent field of merit.”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“Uphold and recite the Diamond Prajñā Sutra and you will at once see your nature. Know that the merit of this sutra is immeasurable and boundless; the sutra praises it clearly, and it cannot be set forth in full.”
4. Upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra eradicates karmic obstacles.
In the Diamond Sutra the Buddha says:

“If good men and good women uphold and recite this sutra and are despised by others, it is because of offenses committed in former lives, offenses that should bring rebirth in the evil paths. Because in this present life they are despised by others, those former offenses are extinguished, and they shall attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

(Translation: If good men and good women uphold and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because of evil karma created in the past—in this life before upholding this sutra, and in former lives as well—karma that should have brought rebirth in the evil paths immediately after death. Now, because they uphold and recite the Diamond Sutra, though in this life they are despised by others, the evil karma created in the past is thereby extinguished, and they shall certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.) This passage teaches that when one upholds and recites the Diamond Sutra, heavy offenses are lightly requited: the heavy offense is rebirth in the evil paths after death, and the light requital is being despised by others in this present life—while the merit obtained is exceedingly great: one shall certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
5. Upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra requires faith, understanding and practice.

In upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra, faith, understanding and practice stand like the three legs of a tripod, and not one may be missing. Yet the link of “understanding” is very often overlooked. If one does not understand the sutra’s meaning, “faith” has nothing to rest on—one does not know what one believes—and “practice” likewise does not know how to proceed, or may even go the wrong way. Therefore, in upholding the Diamond Sutra, one must put great effort into “understanding”: following the principle one gives rise to faith, relying on the principle one begins to practice, so that faith, understanding and practice correspond.

In reading the scriptures, what matters is to see the text, grasp the meaning, and still the mind; that is, to understand through hearing, to awaken through reflection, and to realize through practice. The place where all this comes to rest is: to practice as taught. The Diamond Sutra is a Socratic dialogue between the World-Honored One and his great disciple Subhuti, going deeper layer by layer, leading Subhuti and the assembly to understand and awaken to the truth of life and the universe, and teaching how to wake from this nightmare of torment by many sufferings, of birth-and-death saṃsāra, of endless affliction, and to realize the great freedom of inexhaustible wondrous powers, moving through all things with great wisdom.
[Stilling the mind] Putting an end to the deluded mind.
Six translations of the Diamond Sutra are extant:
1. The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Kumārajīva in the
Yao Qin dynasty) (“Yao Qin” being the Qin state of the Sixteen Kingdoms of the Five Barbarians.)
2. The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Bodhiruci of the
Yuan Wei) (“Yuan Wei” being the Northern Wei, one of the Northern Dynasties of the Northern and Southern Dynasties period.)
3. The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Paramārtha of the
Chen) (“Chen” being the Chen dynasty, one of the Southern Dynasties of the Northern and Southern Dynasties period.)
4. The Diamond-Cutter Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Dharmagupta of the
Sui)
5. The Diamond-Cutter Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Xuanzang of the
Tang), the same as the “Ninth Section on the Diamond That Cuts Through Illusion” in fascicle 577 of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra.
6. The Buddha-Spoken Diamond-Cutter Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Yijing of the
Tang)
Among them, the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra translated by the great master Kumārajīva is the most widely current, and this book also adopts that translation.
Question: Should students of the Pure Land school uphold and recite the Diamond Sutra?
Answer: They should. The reasons are:

1. Rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss cannot be without roots of merit and blessing (see the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sutra), and the merit and virtue of upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra are exceedingly great; the World-Honored One says so again and again in the sutra.

2. The Pure Land school cultivates a pure mind, for when the mind is pure the land is pure. The Diamond Sutra speaks throughout of how to cultivate a pure mind, and does so by using the most ultimate vajra prajñā to shatter deluded thoughts and afflictions. The Diamond Sutra is precisely the supreme treasure for cultivating a pure mind, shattering deluded thoughts and stilling afflictions—how could a student of the Pure Land school fail to uphold and recite it?

3. Among the six perfections, “the five perfections are like the blind, and prajñā is the eye.” Apart from prajñā, giving, precepts, patience, diligence and meditation cannot be named pāramitā. Hence one should take prajñā as the guide and the Pure Land as the destination.
4. Upholding and reciting the Diamond Sutra is understanding the supreme meaning. The great Pure Land master Layman Wang Longshu says in his Longshu Expanded Pure Land Writings,
fascicle 9:

“The Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations says: one who is born in the highest grade of the highest lot reads and recites the Mahāyāna scriptures and understands the supreme meaning. If one would cultivate the highest grade, then the Buddha’s profound purport must not be left unknown.”
Layman Longshu himself was like this: he mastered birth and death at will, knew in advance the time of his passing, and departed while standing.

[Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations] That is, the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Because this sutra teaches the sixteen contemplations, it is also called the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations. [Supreme meaning] The highest and unsurpassed principle, that is, the true nature of all dharmas. The Buddha says:
“All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is named the real, named the true nature, named the Dharma realm, named ultimate wisdom, named the supreme truth, named the supreme emptiness.”
(Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
fascicle 40,
Chapter on Kaundinya) For a detailed account of the true nature of all dharmas, see
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
Question: The ancients could be born in the Pure Land sitting or standing simply by reciting the Buddha’s name to the very end—why should anything else be needed?

Answer: If one’s skill in Buddha-recitation is effective—like a pearl that clears muddy water, like the great sword Tai’e, like a great wheel of fire—then nothing else is needed, and a single recitation of the Buddha’s name can bring one securely home. But if one’s skill in Buddha-recitation is not effective, then one must do the threefold work: refraining from evil and practicing good, taking the precepts as the foundation, and using prajñā to shatter delusion. Layman Jiang Weiyi says in his Commentary on the Diamond Sutra:

“The Tathāgata’s wisdom and awakened nature is possessed by every living being, lacking in none; but it is obstructed by deluded thoughts and attachments, and so cannot be realized. ... You should know that deluded thoughts and attachments come from beginningless ignorance, while prajñā is the correct wisdom of the principle-essence. When wisdom opens, the ignorant becomes clear; when ignorance is cleared, deluded thoughts and attachments are cut off of themselves. Therefore one who studies Buddhism should first be shown and awakened to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the correct wisdom of prajñā. Whatever practice one cultivates, one must devote effort to this. Hence no dharma can be apart from prajñā, and cultivating the Pure Land and reciting the Buddha’s name is no exception. The sutra says: ‘When the mind is pure, the land is pure.’ If deluded thoughts and attachments are not removed, how can the mind be pure? The ancients said: ‘Where craving is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world.’ Emotional attachment and the view of self are in truth the root of craving. Therefore one who seeks birth in the Pure Land must begin right here. In what is called ‘honest Buddha-recitation,’ the two words ‘honest’ must be attended to: if the world’s defiling conditions and clinging conditions never cease, how can one be honest? From this we know that prajñā and the Pure Land are from the first not two matters. This sutra
(the Diamond Sutra)
is in truth the great outline by which all students leave delusion, the pivotal essential for purifying the mind.”

[Beginningless ignorance] Since the very beginningless outset, the intrinsic nature, by one thought of non-awakening, has been plunged in the long night of confusion, not understanding the truth, and can give rise to all delusions and afflictions: this is beginningless ignorance, also called fundamental ignorance. The ignorance of living beings and the tathāgatagarbha they inherently possess are both beginningless. The Sutra of the Profound Principle of the Mahāyāna Six Pāramitās says:

“A fierce flame blown by the wind can be checked, and the waves of the sea can be stilled, but the deluded mind alone is most difficult to tame. Why? Because beginningless ignorance deludes the mind-nature.”
Question: How should one uphold the Diamond Sutra?

Answer: By prajñā-contemplation. Prajñā-contemplation has two links: clarifying the principle (the middle-way principle of neither existence nor non-existence) and putting it into practice (the form-leaving practice of compassion and emptiness working as one). Clarifying the principle is understanding; putting it into practice is practice.
If prajñā-contemplation is to have real effect, then understanding and practice must correspond: one understands according to the principle, and one practices according to the understanding.
Mr.
Jiang Weiyi
says in his Commentary on the Diamond Sutra
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, what matters is to be deeply and earnestly on guard
(cautious and fearful)
, taking what the Buddha says as a mirror and at all times and in all places using it to reflect on oneself
(using it to check whether one’s body, speech and mind accord with what the Buddha says: accord is awakening, non-accord is delusion)

. If one does not observe and does not reflect, how shall delusion become awakening? This is what is called relying on the words to give rise to contemplation. When the work of contemplation is long sustained, then a vast and solemn sense arises of itself, and the mind of earnest vigilance is born of itself: this is initial awakening. It is also the first opening of the correct wisdom inherent in the principle-essence. Thus, without retreat and without slackening, the work of contemplation grows daily deeper and daily purer. Then what is called initial awakening is at first like the new moon, gradually with more light and less darkness
(the same as “dark”)

until the moon’s disk is full and its radiance shines forth, and the nature-essence appears. This is initial awakening merging with inherent awakening, and then there is no division of initial and inherent. You should know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing else: the awakened nature perfectly luminous. And the opening of the awakened nature cannot come about by any way other than relying on the power of the prajñā of words. Therefore it is said: all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”
[Contemplation] Observing the facts and principles of all dharmas with wisdom, and seeing them clearly.
[Vast and solemn] Grand and magnificent in appearance.
Old Monk Xuyun said:

“Bodhidharma said: ‘To understand the Buddha’s mind-school and have practice and understanding correspond—this is called a patriarch.’ Practice and understanding corresponding means that what one can say, one can do. ... Do not be turned by circumstances.
Like herding an ox: hold the rope steady, and if the ox will not obey, give it a few whacks
If one can constantly subdue one’s mind thus

, then as days pass and the work deepens, there will be news of arriving home.” “When you meet with circumstances, what cannot be let go of must still be let go; at the slightest movement of the eyebrow
(the least deliberation)

, one has broken the patriarchs’ rule. Having heard a good teacher explain it, do not lose your awakened awareness. In all things one should meet the Way: the Way is the principle. The principle is the mind. What is the mind? The mind is the Buddha. The Buddha neither increases nor decreases, is neither blue nor yellow, neither long nor short. As the Diamond Sutra says: ‘If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathāgata.’ Penetrate these principles and you are the same as the Buddha. Govern affairs by principle—what is there that cannot be let go? Shine this principle upon it once, and it is let go—‘all that has marks is false and deceptive.’ From where do afflictions and right and wrong come? If you would cultivate, then what cannot be passed through must still be passed through; grasp the Dharma-nature as suchness.”
(Xuyun’s Upaya Teachings)
The Essentials of the Transmission of Mind says:

“This source, the pure mind, is of itself perfectly luminous and universally illuminating. People of the world do not awaken; they take seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing to be the mind, and are covered by seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, and so do not behold the pure essence. But if one is simply without mind straight away, the essence appears of itself, like the great sun rising in the sky, illuminating the ten directions with no obstruction. Therefore students of the Way, recognizing only seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing and the activities of body and speech, and emptying out seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, find that the mind’s path is cut off and there is no place to enter; one should simply recognize the original mind at the very place of seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing. Yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, nor is it apart from them. Simply do not give rise to views upon seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, do not move thoughts upon them, do not seek the mind apart from them, and do not abandon them to grasp dharmas; neither identical nor separate, not abiding and not attaching, free in all directions—nowhere is not the place of practice.”

Profound meaning” refers to clarifying, before annotating the sutra text, the profound and wondrous principle that this sutra expounds. This is the outline of the whole sutra, so that readers may first grasp the whole and then study the text: once the outline is raised the meshes open, and it is easy to grasp and comprehend.
The main theme of the Diamond Sutra is:
the middle-way principle of neither existence nor non-existence, and the form-leaving practice of compassion and emptiness working as one.
[Leaving marks] Realizing that all marks are false (the sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and deceptive.”
), and being without love and hate, taking and rejecting (the sutra says:
“Take not hold of marks, and abide unmoved in suchness.”
). [Clinging to marks] Taking marks as real, with love and hate, taking and rejecting. (And so one creates karma and receives its retribution, and birth and death continue without end.)
Question: How does one leave marks?

Answer: By leaving marks through contemplation. The cycle of continuing birth and death is: giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution. Therefore, to end birth and death, one must cut off the link of giving rise to delusion, and the method is to leave marks through contemplation. In his book
Commentary on the Diamond Sutra
Mr. Jiang Weiyi sets forth this contemplation method profoundly and in detail. For example:
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, what matters is to be deeply and earnestly on guard
(cautious and fearful)
, taking what the Buddha says as a mirror and at all times and in all places using it to reflect on oneself
(using it to check whether one’s body, speech and mind accord with what the Buddha says: accord is awakening, non-accord is delusion)

. If one does not observe and does not reflect, how shall delusion become awakening? This is what is called relying on the words to give rise to contemplation. When the work of contemplation is long sustained, then a vast and solemn sense arises of itself, and the mind of earnest vigilance is born of itself: this is initial awakening. It is also the first opening of the correct wisdom inherent in the principle-essence. Thus, without retreat and without slackening, the work of contemplation grows daily deeper and daily purer. Then what is called initial awakening is at first like the new moon, gradually with more light and less darkness
(the same as “dark”)

until the moon’s disk is full and its radiance shines forth, and the nature-essence appears. This is initial awakening merging with inherent awakening, and then there is no division of initial and inherent. You should know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing else: the awakened nature perfectly luminous. And the opening of the awakened nature cannot come about by any way other than relying on the power of the prajñā of words. Therefore it is said: all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”
[Contemplation] Observing the facts and principles of all dharmas with wisdom, and seeing them clearly.
[Vast and solemn] Grand and magnificent in appearance.
[The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra]
this is
the title of this sutra.
“Diamond”
means the diamond jewel, whose radiance flashes in all directions and which is supremely hard and supremely sharp. The Buddhist scriptures say:
“Indra has a jewel named the diamond.”
Kumārajīva, the translator of this sutra, says:
“The diamond jewel is an inch square, yet its light can illumine several tens of miles.”

Here the diamond jewel is used to describe prajñā: its radiance flashes in all directions and nothing is too hard for it to destroy; it drives out darkness, cuts off afflictions, shatters delusion and removes attachment.
Prajñā”

is a transliteration of Sanskrit, meaning wisdom; but this wisdom is not the cleverness of the world—it is the wondrous wisdom that penetrates life and the universe, knowing all and capable of all, the correct wisdom of the intrinsic nature. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
“Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas; dwelling in this prajñā, one can fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.”
Pāramitā”

is a transliteration of Sanskrit, also rendered as pāramitā, meaning: to the other shore. We ordinary beings, from beginningless time, have drifted on the sea of karma, our heads bobbing up and down. To cross this sea of birth-and-death suffering, where the winds of circumstance howl and the waves of consciousness surge, and reach the ultimate shore of nirvāṇa, a boat is indispensable—and the diamond prajñā is the great precious Dharma-ship that sails straight to the other shore, breasting wind and cleaving waves.
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
“The prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas. The Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. The Dharma is the prajñāpāramitā.”
The Great Prajñā Sutra says:
“The mahāprajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas; it can give birth to all Buddhas and embraces and upholds the bodhisattvas.”
Sutra”

means the teaching spoken by the Buddha. In Sanskrit it is called sūtra, meaning: threading the Dharma-meanings together so they are not lost, according with the wondrous principle of the Buddhas above and with the capacities of living beings below. It is meant to lead living beings to rely on the words, give rise to contemplation, and realize the true nature.
Section 14 of this sutra says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
This is the meaning of “diamond prajñāpāramitā” in the title of the sutra:
with the wondrous wisdom of the diamond, shattering delusion and removing attachment, leaving all marks and becoming a Buddha.

In upholding this sutra, one must hold firmly to this title, realize how the World-Honored One teaches us to use diamond prajñā to shatter delusion and remove attachment, leave marks and become a Buddha, and put it into practice, practicing as taught.

The so-called essence of the sutra is the main body of a sutra, that is, the principle it clarifies—the purport, core and essential point of a sutra. The essence of this sutra is: clearly penetrating the true nature, shattering delusion and removing attachment, and thereby ending birth and death (delimited birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death).
Clearly penetrating the true nature:

thoroughly awakening to the true nature of all dharmas. What is called the “true nature” is the real situation; the “true nature of all dharmas” is the real situation of all dharmas. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury,
Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, the Buddha says:
“What is named the true nature of all dharmas? All dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.”
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and deceptive.”
For a detailed account of the true nature of all dharmas, see
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
Shattering delusion:

clearly seeing the true nature of all dharmas, awakening to and shattering illusion—“all that has marks is false and deceptive”—no longer confused and inverted, no longer creating karma and receiving retribution. Shattering delusion and returning to the real is the path of bodhi. Master Hanshan says:

“The intrinsic nature of living beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally undefiled, and without any marks of birth and death or coming and going. But because of the first non-awakening, they are confused about their own intrinsic nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance they give rise to deluded thoughts, all kinds of inversion, creating all kinds of karma, falsely grasping the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance
(all this ignorance)

, not understanding one’s own mind, turning with deluded thoughts, like a person deep asleep dreaming all kinds of evil dreams. All kinds of states, all kinds of terror, suffering unbearable; and when they wake, they seek the matters of the dream and cannot find them at all. Therefore living beings fall into the dream of ignorance, follow deluded thoughts and inversion, create all kinds of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could any of those inverted states be found?”
(Dream Roam Collection,
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang)
Removing attachment:
removing attachment to self and attachment to dharmas. This sutra says:
“These living beings no longer have the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being, or the mark of a life-span; no mark of dharma, and likewise no mark of non-dharma.”

[Attachment to self] Also called attachment to person, falsely clinging to the body and mind falsely compounded of the five aggregates as “I.” Because of attachment to self, the affliction-obstacle is formed. [Falsely clinging to the body and mind falsely compounded of the five aggregates as “I”] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All living beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversion, like a person who has lost his way and takes the four directions to be elsewhere, falsely takes the four great elements as the mark of his own body, and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of his own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. The sky in truth has no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is not only confused about the nature of empty space but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence, he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

(Translation: All living beings, from beginningless time, have a confused and inverted intrinsic nature, giving rise to all kinds of inversion, taking the false as real—this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he falsely takes the physical body formed of earth, water, fire and wind as the mark of his own body, and the deliberating mind that is the six sense-roots contacting the six dusts (the shadowy traces of the six dusts) as the mark of his own mind. It is like eyes gone blurry, falsely seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. In fact there are no flowers in the sky; this is an illusion falsely clung to by the diseased eye. Because of this false clinging he not only falsely clings to empty space as real, but further thinks that flowers truly arise from there. Because living beings, through inversion and delusion, falsely take the illusory body and mind as real and cling to them as “I,” birth and death revolve without end; therefore this is called ignorance.)

[Attachment to dharmas] Falsely clinging to the Dharma of the Way as real, thinking that there is a dharma to be obtained, a Way to be cultivated, birth and death to be ended, nirvāṇa to be realized, clinging to cultivating causes and realizing fruits. Because of attachment to dharmas, the obstacle of the known is formed. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
“Though the people of the two vehicles have broken attachment to person
(that is, attachment to self)
, they still have attachment to dharmas.”
The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says:
“From attachment to self and dharmas
(because there is attachment to self and attachment to dharmas)
, the two obstacles are both produced.”

[The two obstacles] The affliction-obstacle and the obstacle of the known. [Affliction-obstacle] The obstacles of greed, anger and delusion and so on that arise from falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as “I”; because of the affliction-obstacle one revolves in the saṃsāra of birth and death. [Obstacle of the known] Giving rise to all kinds of wrong views about the Dharma of the Way; such knowing obstructs perfect enlightenment.
The Heart Sutra says:

“Therefore in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so forth up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, and no ending of ignorance, and so forth up to no old age and death, and no ending of old age and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation or path; no wisdom; and no attainment.”
In this passage of the sutra,

“in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so forth up to no realm of mind-consciousness” speaks of the absence of the five aggregates and the eighteen realms, which shatters the ordinary person’s attachment to self; “no ignorance, and no ending of ignorance, and so forth up to no old age and death, and no ending of old age and death” speaks of the absence of the twelve links of dependent origination, which shatters the pratyekabuddha’s attachment to dharmas; “no suffering, accumulation, cessation or path”
speaks of the absence of the Four Noble Truths, which shatters the śrāvaka’s attachment to dharmas;
“no wisdom”
speaks of the absence of the six perfections, which shatters the bodhisattva’s attachment to dharmas. (For annotations see
“A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra”
And thereby ending birth and death:
ending the two deaths—delimited birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death.

[Delimited birth-and-death] Beings within the three realms and the six paths, whose lifespans are all limited and whose bodies are all of distinct kinds, because of the good and evil karma they have attracted—their birth-and-death is therefore called “delimited birth-and-death.” One who has ended delimited birth-and-death escapes the wheel of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth-and-death] The sages of the Three Vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended delimited birth-and-death, gradually extinguish deluded thought and gradually increase their realization as they cultivate the path. This migration of delusion and awakening differs in every period; the passage from the earlier period into the later is exactly like one round of birth-and-death, and its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable—hence it is called “transformational birth-and-death.” One who has ended transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha fruit.
The true nature of all dharmas is this: all dharmas are illusory, fundamentally not a single thing exists. In
fascicle ten of the Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sutra
, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas are like illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame.”

In the Sutra of Holding the World, the Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusion without reality, without any root.” In the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit on the Royal Law, the Buddha says:

“All dharmas are empty in substance and nature, impermanent, perishing and destroyed. Suppose a man in the night, in a dream, sees fine parks and gardens, mountains and rivers, people and crowds, dense forests and clear springs, halls, houses and pavilions—all delightful. When he wakes up
(to wake from sleep; here the ‘jue’ of ‘shuijue’ means to awaken)
, he sees not one thing.”
(For the true nature of all dharmas, see in detail
The True Nature of All Dharmas
[Dream and awakening] To wake from a dream. Master Taixu said:
“The mind within a dream is the mind of an ordinary being; the mind that knows it dreams within the dream is the mind of a bodhisattva; the mind that has awakened from the dream is the Buddha-mind.”
(An Outline of the Contemplation of Consciousness-Only)
The true nature of all dharmas is the supreme truth. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false. Where they cease—that is called the real, that is called the true nature, that is called the dharma realm, that is called ultimate knowledge, that is called the supreme truth, that is called supreme emptiness.”
(Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
fascicle forty.)
The true nature of all dharmas is the dharma-seal of the Mahāyāna sutras—the seal of true nature. Master Zhiyi says in the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra,
fascicle eight:

“Among the Lesser Vehicle sutras, those sealed by the three seals of impermanence, non-self and nirvāṇa are spoken by the Buddha, and cultivating them one attains the path. Without the three dharma-seals, they are the words of Māra. The Mahāyāna sutras have only one dharma-seal, called the true nature of all dharmas; they are called sutras of definitive meaning and can lead to the great path. Without the seal of true nature, they are the words of Māra.”
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”

This means that all marks are illusions. This includes mountains, rivers and the great earth, the sun, moon and stars, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, living beings and all Buddhas—all are illusions. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Within it, the buddha-worlds of a hundred thousand koṭis of asamkhyeya—inexpressible—Ganges-sands, are like a flower in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion.” “There is fundamentally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa, no attaining Buddhahood and no not attaining Buddhahood, no deluded rebirth and no non-rebirth.” “Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike marks of a flower in the sky.”

[Asamkhyeya] Rendered into Chinese as ‘countless,’ meaning so many that no number can calculate them. [Flower in the sky] In the Buddhadharma this is often used to illustrate illusion. A ‘flower in the sky’ is a flower in empty space. One with diseased eyes sees flowers in empty space, yet empty space originally has no flowers—it is only the illusion of the diseased eye. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Falsely taking the four great elements as one’s own body, and the shadows of the six dusts as the marks of one’s own mind—like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky, and a second moon.”
The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp says:
“With one film over the eye, flowers in the sky fall in confusion.”

is constantly used to demonstrate that all dharmas are illusion. “

” refers to the existence of a mark; “not
A”
refers to the non-existence of its substance; “it is called
A”
means that this thing that has a mark but no substance is

(a mark exists) is not

“The adornment of Buddha-lands
(a mark exists)
, is not adornment
(its substance does not exist)
, therefore it is called adornment
(the adornment of Buddha-lands is illusion)
The Tathāgata speaks of the thirty-two marks
(a mark exists)
, which are not marks
(their substance does not exist)
, therefore they are called the thirty-two marks
(the thirty-two marks are illusion)

In the dream-illusion of “all that has marks is false and illusory” there are two utterly different roads: one is to use illusion to leave illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream is awakened—this is the path of bodhi; the other is to use illusion to enter illusion, turning through birth-and-death—this is the road of rebirth that living beings have walked since beginningless kalpas. The Diamond Sutra arms us with diamond prajñā to awaken to and break through illusion, to be deluded and inverted no more, and to walk the great path of bodhi that is “using illusion to leave illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream is awakened.” This sutra says:

“All that has marks is false and illusory.” “No mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of living beings, no mark of a life-span.” “No mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas.” “Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.” “Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Tathāgata says:
“All Tathāgatas rely on this samādhi to accomplish immeasurable great awesome spiritual power, and even to realize and enter the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are illusions)

, and can therefore manifest all kinds of sovereign matters in all buddha-lands of the ten directions. Suppose a man dreams of all sorts of transformed things, and when he wakes, all he saw is gone. Ordinary beings are likewise:
because of the dream of ignorance
they falsely give rise to the notion of a real substance in regard to all dharmas. The Buddhas, having awakened
(the Buddhas have woken from the dream of ignorance)

, are attached to nothing; therefore in all worlds of the ten directions they can, in a single thought, manifest immeasurable buddha-works, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing to accomplishment all living beings, causing them all to awaken and enter the immeasurable and profound wondrous gate of liberation.”

What does the Diamond Sutra teach? The Diamond Sutra teaches the true nature of all dharmas—that all dharmas are illusory—causing living beings to break delusion and eliminate attachment and thereby attain liberation. But living beings’ two attachments, to self and to dharmas, are deep-rooted and hard to believe; therefore the World-Honored One and Subhūti, in the form of dialogue, break through doubt layer upon layer, causing Subhūti and we living beings to remove doubt and give rise to faith, so that our inherent wisdom may appear. Examined thus, living beings and Buddhas are equal and the two attachments both perish—this is the essential key to leaving illusion and becoming Buddha. (For the true nature of all dharmas, see in detail
The True Nature of All Dharmas

Zong is the essential principle; qu is the direction toward which it tends. Purpose and direction is the method of cultivation that carries the essential principle through—how to practice in accordance with the sutra’s substance, the so-called seeking the principle and returning to its direction. The purpose and direction of this sutra is: leaving marks—leaving the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings, the mark of a life-span, the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas. Relying on the wondrous principle of the true nature of all dharmas, one leaves marks and does not abide, in order to break delusion and eliminate attachment. The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Leaving marks, one is without marks; without marks, one does not abide; not abiding, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Good sons! Those newly learned bodhisattvas and living beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect enlightenment mind should abide in right mindfulness and keep far from all illusions.”

[Mark of self] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as truly existent, and taking them as “I” and giving rise to mind—for example, gain and loss, adversity and favorable conditions, honor and disgrace, and so on. [Mark of person] Falsely clinging to the other party, to other people, as truly existent and giving rise to mind—for example, like and dislike, right and wrong, high and low, and so on. [Mark of living beings] Here “living beings” means groups of people—for example, groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and enemy, age, sex, workplace, region, race, skin color, nation, and so on. The mark of living beings is falsely clinging to these groups as truly existent and giving rise to discriminating mind. [Mark of a life-span] Falsely clinging to lifespan as truly existent and calculating its length. What deluded living beings care about most is nothing other than lifespan; therefore the mark of a life-span is separated out from the mark of self and set up as a separate item. [Mark of dharmas] Falsely clinging to all dharmas (including the dharmas of the path) as truly existent. [Dharmas of the path] The dharmas of cultivating the path, that is, the dharmas for ending birth-and-death and realizing nirvāṇa. [Mark of non-dharmas] Denying all dharmas (including the dharmas of the path), falsely clinging to all dharmas as non-existent and sinking into stubborn emptiness
When the World-Honored One attained the path, his very first words were:
“Wondrous! Wondrous! All living beings on the great earth are fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue-marks, but because of deluded thought and attachment they cannot realize them.”
Therefore, dispelling deluded thought and attachment is the way to Buddhahood. How is it dispelled? By leaving marks! Hence section fourteen of this sutra says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
The so-called leaving of marks is simply not clinging to marks—knowing that marks are illusion, not being deluded by marks, not being turned by marks. This sutra says:
“Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.” “If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.”

[Clinging to marks] Clinging to marks is taking marks as real; then desire arises and thoughts arise, and one runs after desire and thought. Thus one creates karma, and thus one turns through birth-and-death. [Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness] Not clinging to marks as real, and not being moved by them.
In the fifth section, “Truly Seeing Through the Principle,” the Buddha says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”

This means that all marks are illusions; yet living beings, since beginningless time, have taken illusions as real, so deluded thought and attachment never cease, and they are seduced and coerced by them—thus they create karma, thus they receive retribution, thus they turn through birth-and-death and sink into the sea of suffering. Now, to attain liberation and return to the source, one must no longer be deluded by illusions and must not be turned by marks; this requires leaving marks and dispelling deluded thought and attachment.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the preceding thought is deluded
(clinging to marks—being turned by marks)
, one is an ordinary being; when the following thought awakens
(not grasping at marks—leaving marks)
, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves objects, that is bodhi.”
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Seeing illusion, one is immediately free of it, without applying expedients; leaving illusion, one is immediately awakened, with no gradual stages.”
Therefore one should
“not grasp at marks, but be unmoving in suchness.”
(section thirty-two of this sutra)
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“What is called Chan concentration? Externally leaving marks is Chan; inwardly not being confused is concentration. If outwardly one clings to marks, the inner mind is confused; if outwardly one leaves marks, the mind is not confused. The intrinsic nature is itself pure and itself still; it is only because one sees objects and thinks of objects that it is confused. If one sees all objects and the mind is not confused, that is true concentration.”

Aware of the present thought, one enters the state without thought—this is leaving marks; this is doing the work of leaving marks at the very place where thought arises and the mind stirs. Inwardly not turned by thoughts, outwardly not dragged by objects—in the vast wind of circumstances, one is one’s own master.
Section fourteen of this sutra says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
This is the meaning of “Diamond Prajñāpāramitā” in the sutra’s title: by wondrous diamond wisdom, leaving marks and becoming Buddha. In section thirteen, the Buddha says:
“This sutra is named the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā. By this name you should uphold it.”
Diamond prajñā is the great wisdom that, seeing marks, can leave them.
Section eight says:
“All Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra.”
Section fourteen says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
Therefore the way to Buddhahood is what this sutra repeatedly speaks of:
leaving marks

In leaving marks one must cultivate compassion and emptiness together, cultivating the contemplation of compassion while cultivating emptiness, for only thus can one be unattached to both emptiness and existence and leave marks thoroughly and ultimately. If one cultivates emptiness alone, though one may not be attached to existence, one will become attached to emptiness. The sutra says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”

Leaving all marks means not only leaving the marks of existence but also leaving the marks of emptiness; in the end even the mark of leaving marks must be left, until there is nothing left to leave—only then is it ultimate and perfect, only then is the Buddha’s path accomplished. Therefore this sutra says:

“All living beings of whatever kind—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought—I cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without residue and be liberated. And thus immeasurable, countless, boundless living beings are liberated, yet in truth no living being attains liberation. Why? Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings or the mark of a life-span, he is not a bodhisattva.”
This is compassion and emptiness cultivated together, unattached to both emptiness and existence.
In leaving marks, one must first concretely put non-abiding into practice.

Non-abiding is simply not clinging to marks. That is, in regard to the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings, the mark of a life-span, the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas, there is nothing to abide in (not falsely clinging to them as real). The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Leaving marks, one is without marks; without marks, one does not abide; not abiding, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”
In this sutra, passages on leaving marks and non-abiding are found everywhere. For example:
Section three says:
“If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings or the mark of a life-span, he is not a bodhisattva.”
This means a bodhisattva must leave the four marks.
Section four says:
“If a bodhisattva gives without abiding in marks, his merit is inconceivable.”
This means giving must leave marks.
Section six says:

“Hearing these passages, even a single thought of pure faith arises—Subhūti! The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that such living beings attain such immeasurable merit. Why? Because such living beings no longer have the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings or the mark of a life-span; they have no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas.”
Section seven says:
“All sages and saints are distinguished through the unconditioned dharma.”

The unconditioned dharma is leaving marks. This passage says: all sages and saints, because of the differing depth of their leaving of marks, have the distinction of forty-two stages. These forty-two stages are: the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment. Among them, wondrous enlightenment is Buddhahood. Therefore an ancient worthy said:
“Only exhaust the ordinary feelings
(one need only cut off all ordinary feelings)
—there is no other sagely understanding.”

[Wise and noble] A bodhisattva’s cultivation has fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment—wondrous enlightenment being Buddhahood. Among them, the ten abidings, the ten practices and the ten dedications are the wise (called the three stages of the wise), while the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment are the noble.
Section ten says:

“Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind abiding in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; they should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.”
This speaks of leaving the marks of dust-objects: not giving rise to mind abiding in dust-objects, and even when mind arises, not abiding in dust-objects.
Section fourteen says:
“A bodhisattva should leave all marks and give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment.”
This means: on the path of bodhi, from the very beginning, at the moment of giving rise to the mind, one must leave marks.
In section seventeen, Subhūti asks again:
“World-Honored One! When good men and good women give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”
The Buddha answers:

“Good men and good women who give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment should thus give rise to the mind: I should liberate all living beings, and when all living beings have been liberated, in truth not one living being has been liberated.”
Therefore the answer to “How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” is: leaving marks, not abiding, and liberating living beings.
Section twenty-three says:
“With no self, no person, no living beings and no life-span, cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one attains supreme perfect enlightenment.”
This means: leaving the four marks and cultivating any wholesome dharma whatsoever, one realizes the Buddha fruit. From this one sees how important leaving marks is!

(This passage means that the key to realizing supreme perfect enlightenment is being without the four marks, and not what kind of wholesome dharma one cultivates. Wholesome dharmas cultivated without the four marks are the unconditioned dharma. Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the universal principle for realizing supreme perfect enlightenment; from this we also know how pivotal and how important it is to leave the four marks!)
At the end of this sutra, the World-Honored One says:
“Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

This echoes what the World-Honored One displayed at the very beginning of the sutra—putting on his robe, begging for food, washing his feet and spreading his seat—and it runs through the whole sutra. This is leaving marks, not being turned by circumstances, not being dragged by thoughts, unmoving in suchness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“What is called Chan concentration? Externally leaving marks is Chan; inwardly not being confused is concentration. If outwardly one clings to marks, the inner mind is confused; if outwardly one leaves marks, the mind is not confused. The intrinsic nature is itself pure and itself still; it is only because one sees objects and thinks of objects that it is confused. If one sees all objects and the mind is not confused, that is true concentration.”
Therefore the key to Chan concentration is leaving marks.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra,
fascicle one,
the Chapter on Learning the Contemplations, says:
“Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should take non-attachment as their expedient means and perfect prajñāpāramitā, because the nature and marks of all dharmas cannot be grasped.”
“Non-attachment” is not clinging to marks—that is, leaving marks.
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.” “Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

This is the core of upholding the Diamond Sutra—leaving marks. And in the course of learning to leave marks, one should take “stilling deluded thought and breaking the mark of self” as the focus and the point of entry.

Purpose and direction is the cause; benefit is the fruit. This sutra cultivates both merit and wisdom, and its benefits are: breaking delusion and eliminating attachment, producing merit and extinguishing offenses, dissolving karma and escaping suffering, and realizing bodhi. The sutra says a great deal about this, and I shall not enumerate it here; when studying the sutra text, one should match each point one by one.

The character of the teaching” refers to the differing characters of the Buddha’s teaching throughout his life—that is, the features of the various doctrines and their differences. The Buddha taught living beings according to their capacities. Living beings’ faculties are dull or sharp, their obstacles thick or thin; therefore the sutras have teachings that are shallow or deep, gradual or sudden, partial or complete, provisional or ultimate, small or great (Lesser Vehicle, Great Vehicle).

[Partial and complete] Partial and complete. “Partial” means leaning to one side; “complete” means perfectly interfused and unobstructed. [Provisional and ultimate] A teaching suited to a particular time is called “provisional”; a teaching that is ultimate and unchanging is called “ultimate.”

The character of this sutra’s teaching is: the most complete, the most sudden, and the most real of the One Vehicle sutras. “Most complete” means this sutra is the most ultimate and definitive; “most sudden” means this sutra’s teaching does not pass through the various stages but enters directly in a single leap; “most real” means this sutra directly sets forth the true nature of all dharmas; “One Vehicle” means this sutra is the sole teaching that causes people to become Buddha.

[One Vehicle] Also called the Buddha Vehicle—the sole teaching that can cause people to become Buddha. “Vehicle” means a carriage; it is used to illustrate the Buddha’s teaching, because the teaching can carry people to the other shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called a “vehicle.” [Definitive meaning] The principle set forth is utterly complete, thorough and ultimate.
Question: Why is it said that the Diamond Sutra is the most complete, most sudden and most real One Vehicle sutra?
Answer: The sutra says:
“All Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra”
(section eight);
“the Tathāgata speaks it for those who have set out on the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out on the Supreme Vehicle”
(section fifteen)—this shows that this sutra is the most complete One Vehicle teaching. The Buddha says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
This speaks of leaving all marks completely and directly (without passing through the various stages) becoming Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records:
“The Master
(the Fifth Patriarch of Chan, Hongren)
constantly urged monks and laity simply to uphold the Diamond Sutra, and they would thereby see their own nature and directly become Buddha.”
—this shows that this sutra is most sudden. (Section fourteen.) The sutra constantly uses the logical formula “
A
is not
A
, therefore it is called
A”
to demonstrate that all dharmas are illusion, and it also says
“all that has marks is false and illusory”
(section five); both are speaking of the true nature of all dharmas—showing that this sutra is the most real.
[Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin]—
Master Kumārajīva is the translator of this sutra.

Yao Qin”: in history there were three Qin dynasties. One was the state of Qin of the Warring States period, down to the Qin dynasty that unified the realm under the First Emperor. The second Qin dynasty arose in the period of the Five Barbarians and Sixteen Kingdoms, its sovereign being Fu Jian. The third Qin dynasty was founded when Yao Chang, a great general of Fu Jian, killed Fu Jian and set himself up, also calling his state Qin; later generations, to distinguish it from the Qin dynasty of Fu Jian’s time, called it Yao Qin, also known as the Later Qin.

Tripiṭaka”: the sutra-piṭaka, the vinaya-piṭaka and the abhidharma-piṭaka. The sutra-piṭaka is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the vinaya-piṭaka is the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the abhidharma-piṭaka is the treatises composed by the Buddha’s disciples. A “Tripiṭaka Master” is a bhikṣu thoroughly versed in all three piṭakas of sutra, vinaya and abhidharma.
Kumārajīva (343–413
CE

) was rendered into Chinese as Tongshou, “Youthful Longevity.” He was by origin a man of Tianzhu (ancient India) and grew up in Kucha (between present-day Kuqa County and Shaya County in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region). Kumarajiva’s father was a man of Tianzhu whose family had for generations served as ministers of state. He avoided the ministership and left home to become a monk, coming to the kingdom of Kucha; when the king of Kucha heard that he had renounced glory to cultivate the path, he revered him deeply and went out beyond the city walls to welcome him and invite him to be the state preceptor. The king’s younger sister was then just twenty, clear and keen in understanding, able to recite what she had read at a single glance, and when the various kingdoms sought her in marriage she refused them all. Seeing Kumarajiva’s father, she wished in her heart to marry him, and the king forced Kumarajiva’s father to take her as wife; thus Kumarajiva was born. At seven, Kumarajiva followed his mother in leaving home, and traveled throughout the Western Regions (the general name for the states west of Yumen and Yangguan in Gansu). He mastered all the texts and was most skilled in the Mahāyāna. In Kucha, when the kings of neighboring states assembled, each time they invited Kumarajiva to preach they would kneel before his seat and have Kumarajiva step on their shoulders to mount the throne. Later his mother realized the fruit of the anāgāmin (the śrāvaka vehicle has four fruits: srota-āpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin and arhat) and said to Kumarajiva: the Mahāyāna teachings can be transmitted to the Middle Kingdom. Kumarajiva replied: if they can be transmitted, I would sacrifice myself to do it.
In the eighteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin (382
CE
, when Kumarajiva was
years old), the Qin king Fu Jian sent the great general Lü Guang to lead troops against Yanqi, then to destroy Kucha, and to carry Kumarajiva off to Liangzhou.

Three years later Yao Chang killed Fu Jian, destroyed the Former Qin, and proclaimed himself emperor in Chang’an; Lü Guang then carved out Liangzhou for himself and made himself its ruler, so Kumarajiva remained stranded in Liangzhou for
years. It was not until Yao Xing succeeded to the throne that, in the third year of the Hongshi era, troops were sent west against Liangzhou (401
CE
, when Kumarajiva was

years old); the Liang ruler Lü Long was defeated and surrendered, and the Qin king Yao Xing personally welcomed Kumarajiva into Chang’an, where he lodged in the Western Bright Pavilion of Xiaoyao Garden. He was treated with the courtesy due a state preceptor, and a translation hall of great scale was organized in Chang’an, with Kumarajiva invited to preside over the work of translating the scriptures.

Thereafter, for more than ten years, Master Kumarajiva devoted himself wholeheartedly to translating scriptures and preaching the Dharma. When translating at Caotang Temple, with three thousand monks in all, the Master held the old scriptures in his own hands and deliberated and settled them, and none failed to investigate them minutely and penetrate their profound purport. The assistants in the translation hall were rich in talent, with the names of the Four Worthies, the Eight Talents and the Ten Philosophers; the most famous were Sengzhao, Sengrui, Daorong, Tanying and others. The Master once preached at Caotang Temple, and the Qin king, his court ministers and several thousand śramaṇas listened reverently with solemn countenance. Master Kumarajiva was of the same age as Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin, the founding patriarch of the Pure Land school; their kingdoms were not the same (Master Kumarajiva was in the Yao Qin, Master Huiyuan in the Eastern Jin), and they exchanged letters.
Master Kumarajiva translated in all
works,

fascicles. The most important among them are the Large Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, the Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, the Diamond Sutra, the Vimalakīrti Sutra, the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sutra, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sutra, the Treatise on the Stages of the Ten Grounds, the Madhyamaka Treatise, the Hundred Treatise, the Twelve Gate Treatise, the Satyasiddhi Treatise, and the Vinaya in Ten Recitations. The scriptures he translated were extremely broad in scope, faithful in content and fluent in wording; though some were later retranslated, the new versions could hardly replace them, and they hold epoch-making significance in the history of scripture translation in China.
In the eleventh year of the Hongshi era of the Qin (413
CE

) Master Kumarajiva passed away in Chang’an at the age of seventy. At the end he said: if what I have transmitted is without error, then after my body is burned my tongue will not be scorched or rotted. His remains were cremated in Xiaoyao Garden according to foreign custom; when the fire died and the body was consumed, only the tongue remained unspoiled, like a red lotus.

When annotating sutras and treatises, one usually divides the whole text into paragraphs and sections, which is called textual analysis. Here, the divisions into large sections are called major divisions; the divisions of the major divisions into smaller sections are called minor divisions; and the concise, essential wording that marks the content of each division is called division text. On this basis the reader can learn the concise content and the thread of meaning of the annotation, and can determine the annotator’s general view of that sutra or treatise.

The popular editions of the Diamond Sutra divide the whole sutra into thirty-two sections and give each a title; tradition holds that this was done by Prince Zhaoming, Xiao Tong (son of Emperor Wu of Liang). The purport of this analysis is subtle and wondrous, its chapters are detailed yet concise, and it greatly aids the understanding of the text; hence it has been widely handed down without decline (and there are even remains of a “terrace for dividing the sutra”). This book also follows it. Since the titles of these thirty-two sections are textual analysis and not part of the sutra text, one should not read them when chanting the sutra.

[Terrace for Dividing the Sutra] Located in the Shilian Cave National Forest Park south of Susong County seat, Anhui Province. The Terrace for Dividing the Sutra, also called the Stone of Dividing the Sutra, is five meters high and of oval terrace shape. On it are carved the three large characters “Terrace for Dividing the Sutra,” beside which is written “Erected on the eleventh day of the sixth month of the first year of Jiatai of the Imperial Song.” Tradition holds that Prince Zhaoming of Liang divided the Diamond Sutra into thirty-two sections here, hence the name. The stele was erected in the first year of Jiatai (
CE) to commemorate the seven hundredth anniversary of Prince Zhaoming’s birth.

Judging by its content, this sutra can be divided into two parts. Sections one through sixteen are the first part, and sections seventeen through thirty-two are the second part. The first part teaches how to give rise to the mind, how to liberate living beings, how to subdue delusion and how to cut off delusion; this is breaking the self of person in order to end delimited birth-and-death, but the self of dharmas still remains. Therefore the second part teaches how to break the self of dharmas and end transformational birth-and-death. Hence the World-Honored One says at the very beginning of the second part: “In truth there is no dharma by which one gives rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment.” Then he breaks the self of dharmas layer upon layer, until at the end of the part he says: “How should one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness. Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning—thus should they be contemplated.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and all living beings of the final age should keep far from all illusory and false realms. Because of firmly holding the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like illusion is also to be kept far away from; the keeping far away is itself illusion and is also to be kept far away from; the illusion of keeping far away from keeping far away is also to be kept far away from; when there is nothing left to keep far away from, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks rub together, fire comes forth and the sticks are consumed, the ashes fly and the smoke goes out. Cultivating illusion by means of illusion is likewise so; when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation.”

[The two selves] The self of person and the self of dharmas. The self of person is that ordinary beings, not understanding the principle that the five aggregates are falsely compounded, falsely cling to body and mind as “I,” and thereby have the views of self, love of self, pride of self and delusion of self, and so on, forming the affliction obstacle. The self of dharmas is that ordinary beings, not understanding the principle that all dharmas are empty by dependent origination, falsely cling to all dharmas as truly existent, and thereby have discriminating mind, mind of love and hate, mind of becoming Buddha, mind of nirvāṇa, and so on, forming the obstacle of the known.

blocks.text: 3. The Introductory Part, the Main Part and the Circulation Part

inline.s: Traditionally, when annotating a scripture text, one divides it into three great parts: the introductory part, the main part and the circulation part.

The introductory part is the portion that recounts the occasion for the arising of the sutra. Section one of this sutra (Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly) is the introductory part. The introductory part is further divided into two portions: the general introduction and the particular introduction.

The general introduction: this is the introductory account common to all sutras (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was at ...”). For example, the first passage of this sutra (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, together with a great assembly of great bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number.”) is the general introduction. The general introduction is also called the introduction that establishes faith, because it possesses the six matters of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place and assembly, in order to prove that what is said in the sutra is true and credible. These six matters are also called the six accomplishments, the six causes and conditions that accomplish the dharma assembly for preaching the sutra.
