The particular introduction: after the general introduction comes the particular introduction, which is where the introductory portions of the various sutras differ from one another. For example, the second passage of this sutra (“At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged from door to door in order; then he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat and sat down.”) is the particular introduction. The particular introduction is also called the introduction of the arising, because it explains how this dharma assembly came about.
The main part is the portion in which the sutra is properly set forth. Of the whole sutra’s thirty-two sections, from section two through the end of section thirty-one is the main part.

The circulation part is the portion that lists the benefits of upholding this sutra and urges and praises its upholding, recitation and circulation. In this sutra, the last section (Section Thirty-Two: Neither Real nor False) is the circulation part.

blocks.text: Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly

inline.s: The causes and conditions of the dharma assembly” speaks of this sutra, that is, the causes and origin of the Diamond dharma assembly. “Section” corresponds to “chapter.” For example, “Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly” means “Chapter One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly.”

This section (“Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly”) is the introductory part. The introductory part is the portion that recounts the occasion for the arising of the sutra. As said before, it is further divided into two portions: the general introduction and the particular introduction.

[Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, together with a great assembly of great bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number.]

This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. At that time the Buddha was in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden in the country of Śrāvastī, together with twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus.

This passage is the general introduction. The general introduction is also called the introduction that establishes faith, because it possesses the six matters of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place and assembly, in order to prove that what is said in the sutra is true and credible. These six matters are also called the six accomplishments, because a sutra can only be accomplished when these six causes and conditions are present.

Let us now take this passage of the sutra as an example to explain the six accomplishments. First, “Thus” is the accomplishment of faith—the Buddha spoke thus. Second, “have I heard” is the accomplishment of hearing—this sutra was heard by me (Ānanda) with my own ears, and was not heard at second or third hand. Third, “at one time” is the accomplishment of time—that is, the time of the dharma assembly for preaching the sutra, when teacher and disciple were united in the way and capacity and teaching met each other. Fourth, “the Buddha” is the accomplishment of the teacher—the master who speaks the Dharma. Fifth, “was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden” is the accomplishment of place—the place where the Dharma is spoken. Sixth, “together with a great assembly of great bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number” is the accomplishment of the assembly—the great multitude that hears the sutra. Because it clearly points out that this sutra was personally heard by the compiler of the sutra (Ānanda) as the Buddha spoke it thus, and marks the master who speaks the Dharma as well as the time, place and people of the assembly, causing living beings to know that this sutra is indeed without error and thereby to give rise to faith, it is called the introduction that establishes faith.

[Thus have I heard] This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. “Thus have I heard” is the taking up of faith, proving that this sutra was truly spoken by the Buddha and that the text recorded is correct and without error. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, he instructed the Venerable Ānanda: when compiling the sutras in the future, at the head of every sutra place the phrase “Thus have I heard,” to prove that it was truly spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from the scriptures of the outsiders. The “I” in the phrase is the compiler of the sutra, Ānanda, referring to himself. Ānanda was the Buddha’s cousin and was born on the night the Buddha attained the path. Later he left home with the Buddha and became the Buddha’s attendant, and was renowned for “never forgetting what passed his ears, foremost in much hearing.” When Ānanda left home, the Buddha had already been teaching the Dharma for twenty years; therefore he asked the Buddha to repeat for him all that had been spoken before, and Ānanda also attained the samādhi of the sovereign awareness of the nature of dharmas, so that he could comprehend all dharmas in concentration. Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Venerable Mahākāśyapa compiled the sutra-piṭaka in the great stone cave of Magadha, five hundred great arhats gathered in one place and the assembly unanimously urged Ānanda to ascend the seat and recite the sutra text. In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha says: “I and Ānanda and others, at the place of the Buddha King of Emptiness, at the same time gave rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment. Ānanda always delighted in much hearing, while I always strove diligently. Therefore I have already attained supreme perfect enlightenment, while Ānanda protects and upholds my Dharma, and also protects the treasury of the Dharma of the future Buddhas, teaching and bringing to accomplishment the assembly of bodhisattvas.”

[At one time] At that time. This refers to the time when the Buddha spoke this sutra, that is, when teacher and disciple were united in the way and capacity and teaching met each other. The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma applies to gods and humans alike, and the compilation and transmission of it spread throughout the world; since the year, month and day cannot be made the same for all, “at one time” is used to record it. [Teacher and disciple] Teacher and student; master and disciple. [Capacity and teaching meeting each other] “Capacity” is the faculty of the listeners; “teaching” is the Buddha’s bestowal of teaching. Living beings’ faculties differ, and so the Buddha, according to their capacities, bestows teachings shallow or deep. “Capacity and teaching meeting each other” means that the faculties of the listeners at the dharma assembly and the Buddha’s bestowal of teaching resonate and accord. [Buddha] An abbreviation of “buddha,” here meaning Śākyamuni Buddha. “Buddha” is a Sanskrit sound, rendered into Chinese as “the Awakened One.” Inwardly awakened, he is without any deluded thoughts; outwardly awakened, he is unstained by the six dusts. [The country of Śrāvastī] Its location is in the northwest of present-day India, on the south bank of the Rapti River; its king at that time was King Prasenajit.

[Jeta] The grove of Prince Jeta. [Anāthapiṇḍada] the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (“elder” being an honorific for a person of high virtue and great prestige). He was Sudatta, a wealthy merchant of the capital of the country of Śrāvastī. Of charitable disposition, he delighted in giving to the orphaned and the solitary (“orphan” meaning one who has lost his parents; “solitary” meaning one who has lost a spouse; “orphaned and solitary” generally referring to the poor and suffering who have no one to rely on), and so he won the fair name of “Anāthapiṇḍada,” “Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary.” [Garden] A grove or park. [The Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden] A grove in the capital of the country of Śrāvastī, where Śākyamuni Buddha spoke this sutra. The trees of this park belonged to Prince Jeta of the country of Śrāvastī, while the land belonged to the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada; the two of them jointly offered it to the Buddha, hence the name “the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden,” meaning the grove of Prince Jeta and the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Buddha often preached there. The story of their joint offering of the park is this: when the Buddha was preaching in the country of Magadha, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada of the country of Śrāvastī begged the Buddha to come to the city of Śrāvastī and convert its people, and the Buddha consented. After the Elder returned to his country, he searched everywhere for a place, and found that Prince Jeta’s grove was the most suitable for the Buddha to preach in, so he wished to buy it. The prince said in jest: “Cover the ground with gold, spread five inches thick, and it is sold.” The Elder agreed and did so. The prince, moved by the Elder’s sincerity, said: “What people prize most is nothing beyond gold and jewels. He can pour out his whole fortune to buy land and build a monastery—how am I so lacking that I cannot build one?” Thereupon he himself gave rise to the supreme intention to make an offering and asked to retract his earlier promise. The Elder would not agree, and the prince said: “You have promised to take the land for gold, but the trees were not discussed. Let the land be yours, and the grove remain mine; together let us bring the work to completion, each making his own offering.” When the Buddha came to this place, he said to Ānanda: “The park land was bought by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada; the grove was given by Prince Jeta. The two were of one mind in jointly exalting merit. From now on, this place should be called ‘the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden.’”

[Great bhikṣus] “Bhikṣu” is the general name for one who has left home and received full ordination; males are called “bhikṣus,” females “bhikṣuṇīs.” “Great bhikṣus” are bhikṣus of lofty virtue and senior years. [Twelve hundred and fifty in number] These twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus were the Buddha’s constant followers. According to the Sutra of the Causes and Effects of Past and Present,

fascicle four, among these twelve hundred and fifty people were: the small group of fifty headed by Yaśas; five hundred under the teacher-and-disciples Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; two hundred and fifty under Nadī-Kāśyapa; two hundred and fifty under Gayā-Kāśyapa; one hundred under Śāriputra; and one hundred under Mahāmaudgalyāyana. These twelve hundred and fifty people had first served the outsiders, and later, guided by the Buddha’s transformative teaching, attained the fruits; feeling the Buddha’s grace, at every dharma assembly they followed him constantly without leaving, and so were called the constant followers. Hence when the sutras list the assembly at the head of the dharma assembly, they mostly say “together with twelve hundred and fifty in number.” [Together with] In one place.

[At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged from door to door in order; then he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat and sat down.]

At this time the hour for the single meal of the day had come, and so the World-Honored One put on his great robe, took up his alms bowl, led his disciples with dignified and orderly deportment, and with slow steps entered the capital of the country of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city, without distinguishing between poor and lowly or rich and noble households, he received alms in order from door to door. When the begging was finished, he returned to his dwelling. The World-Honored One finished his meal, put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet clean, arranged his seat, and sat cross-legged, solemn and serene, with right mindfulness unmoving.
The translation by Yuan-Wei

Bodhiruci says: “At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged in order; then he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and as usual arranged his seat and sat cross-legged. He settled his body and remained, with right mindfulness unmoving.”

This passage is the particular introduction. The particular introduction is where the introductory portions of the various sutras differ from one another; it comes after the general introduction. It is also called the introduction of the arising, because it explains how that sutra’s dharma assembly came about.

The arising of this sutra’s dharma assembly is that the World-Honored One, through his daily activities (putting on his robe, holding his bowl, entering the city to beg, and even arranging his seat and sitting down), displayed through bodily teaching that prajñā is everywhere—what awakening is, and what the original scenery is.

[At that time] At this time. [World-Honored One] A venerable title of the Buddha. Because the Buddha is endowed with ten thousand virtues, is honored by the world, and is moreover supreme in the world, he is called the World-Honored One. [The hour for the meal] The hour for the single meal of the day had come. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says: “Shaving head and beard and becoming a śramaṇa, one who receives the Dharma of the path renounces worldly goods and takes what he begs as sufficient. One meal a day, one night beneath a tree—be careful never to do more! What makes people foolish and benighted is love and desire.”

[Put on his robe] The three robes and one bowl are the possessions a bhikṣu carries with him. The three robes are the antarvāsa, the uttarāsaṅga and the saṃghāṭī; in Sanskrit all three are called kaṣāya (“kaṣāya” originally meaning a dyed, faded-color robe, because the Dharma robes worn by monks who have left home must all be dyed muddy colors). The antarvāsa is rendered into Chinese as the “body robe”; it is made of five strips (that is, five squares of cloth sewn and joined like a field, hence “field robe”), and is worn for work and for sitting and lying down. The uttarāsaṅga is worn over the antarvāsa, hence its name “upper robe”; it is made of seven strips, and is donned when performing Dharma matters and entering the assembly. The saṃghāṭī is rendered into Chinese as the “robe for the assembled multitude,” also called the great robe; it is made of nine to twenty-five strips, and is worn on solemn occasions. Now, since he was about to enter the city to beg, he deliberately put on the great robe.

[Bowl] An abbreviation of the Sanskrit pātra, the eating vessel of a bhikṣu. [The great city of Śrāvastī] The capital of the country of Śrāvastī; the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden was five or six li southeast of the city. [Begging for food] A bhikṣu, free of all greed and seeking, subduing his pride, constantly practices begging for food to sustain his physical body and assist his work on the path. [Begging in order] In begging for food, a bhikṣu is not attached to flavor, does not slight living beings, and does not choose between rich and poor; with an equal mind he begs from house to house in order, not exceeding seven households or the prescribed time; even if his bowl is not filled, he must return. [His original place] The Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, where he lived. [Finished] Completed.

When the Buddha spoke other sutras, he often arose to the occasion by emitting light and displaying auspicious signs. This sutra is the Tathāgata’s mind-dharma of attaining Buddhahood, yet it arises to the occasion through daily activities—there is indeed deep meaning in this, for it shows that prajñā is nowhere else but in daily activities. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Ordinary beings are Buddhas; affliction is bodhi. When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the following thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves objects, that is bodhi.” This sutra says: “Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.” The World-Honored One’s display is awareness in every thought, leaving objects in every thought; in putting on his robe and holding his bowl, entering the city to beg, and even arranging his seat and sitting down, he everywhere displays the wondrous flavor of prajñā—“not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness”—to proclaim the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā, so that the whole assembly may learn and realize within daily life what the original scenery is.

[Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness] Not clinging to marks as real, and therefore not being moved by them. That is, not clinging to marks and not stirring the mind. [Original scenery] Also called the original face; it is a Chan expression describing the intrinsic state of the self-nature (the state of complete awakening).

There is a story about this. A woman went to ask the Buddha: how can I attain awakening? The Buddha said: what is your work? She said: I make my living by drawing water. The Buddha then told her: when you draw water, your mind should be perfectly clear and aware in every movement (do not let any unaware, habitual movement occur). The woman earnestly did as the Buddha taught, and attained awakening.

The mind should be perfectly clear and aware in every movement”—this is the wondrous method of bringing cultivation into daily life by being aware and illuminating in the present. If one can do this, one will no longer worry about having no time to cultivate, and will never again be anxious and uneasy, fearing that cultivation is being delayed. How can cultivation be brought into daily life? By never losing awareness and illumination! At all times and in all places, never losing awareness and illumination, being perfectly clear and aware of one’s own mental activity, and not being turned by circumstances.

Buddha means awakened. The Buddha is the awakened one who has already woken from the dream of ignorance; though in daily life he is the same as ordinary people, his realm is utterly different—at every moment awareness is shining forth.

The World-Honored One displayed how to cultivate within daily life: when conditions come, one gives; when conditions cease, one is still. In giving, awareness and illumination are not lost, and one is always serene and at ease—the so-called “not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

In this way the World-Honored One, through daily activities such as putting on his robe, holding his bowl, begging for food, returning to his original place, eating, putting away his robe and bowl, washing his feet, and arranging his seat and sitting down, taught us that there is no time and no place where cultivation is impossible, and pointed out the point of entry for us who are people of dust and toil. Therefore in the text below, the Elder Subhūti exclaims that this is rare, and says: in doing this, the Tathāgata truly protects and cares for the bodhisattvas well, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas well!

Cultivation is divided into work on the seat and work off the seat. On the seat is training; off the seat is real combat. If one uses it well, there is no time and no place that is not cultivation. The Sixth Patriarch said: “What is called sitting in Chan? In this Dharma gate there is no obstruction and no hindrance (one is not constrained by circumstances and conditions). Externally, in regard to all good and evil circumstances, not giving rise to thought is called sitting; inwardly seeing the intrinsic nature as unmoving is called Chan.” A verse says: A day of practice earns a day of merit; a day without practice leaves a day empty. True cultivation lies in daily life; the Buddha’s path is itself within living.

There was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, after a long journey, arrived dust-covered in the city of Śrāvastī to seek the Dharma from the Buddha, and saw the Buddha in the city begging for alms from house to house, his every gesture and movement graceful and beautiful, his six faculties fully tamed and guarded, serene and still. Bāhiya came forward, bowed, and asked the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to teach him the Dharma of endless benefit and peace. The Buddha said that he was now going from door to door for alms and it was not suitable to teach the Dharma. But Bāhiya begged again and again, and so the Buddha taught him on the spot: Bāhiya! You should train thus: in the seen there is only the seen; in the heard there is only the heard; in the known there is only the known; in the cognized there is only the cognized. Bāhiya! When you can make it so that in the seen there is only the seen, in the heard there is only the heard, in the known there is only the known, and in the cognized there is only the cognized, then you have reached the state of no clinging and no obstruction. If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no present world, and no future world either. Since you have neither this present world nor the future world, all sorrow, lamentation, pain and grief are utterly dispersed. (The original text is found in the Pali Udāna, chapter one, section ten.)

[The three times] The past world, the present world and the future world. Dharmas that have already arisen and ceased are called “the past world”; dharmas that have arisen and not yet ceased are called “the present world”; dharmas not yet arisen and not yet produced are called “the future world.”

Note: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no present world, and no future world either. Since you have neither this present world nor the future world, all sorrow, lamentation, pain and grief are utterly dispersed.” It would seem it should be: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no past world, and no future world either. Since you have neither the past world nor the future world, all sorrow, lamentation, pain and grief are utterly dispersed.” This may be a mistake in the copying of the text.
Subhūti” is the Chinese rendering of the name of Subhūti. Subhūti rose from his seat and requested the World-Honored One to teach the Dharma. From this section on, the sutra enters the main part.

[At that time the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata truly protects and cares for the bodhisattvas well, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas well. World-Honored One! When good men and good women give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?]

At this time the Elder Subhūti, in the midst of the great assembly, rose from his seat. Baring his right shoulder, placing his right knee on the ground, joining his palms in reverence, he said to the Buddha: Incomparably wondrous, World-Honored One! Taking your own person as the model, you teach thus by bodily example at all times and in all places—this is truly the best protection and care and the best instructive guidance for all bodhisattvas! World-Honored One! When good men and good women who have given rise to the great mind of becoming Buddha and liberating living beings—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”—this is the main theme of this sutra. The first part of the sutra answers these two questions; at the beginning of the second part (Section Seventeen: Ultimately No Self), Subhūti raises these two questions again, and the World-Honored One answers them further.
For whom was the Diamond Sutra spoken? From this passage it can be known that the Buddha spoke this sutra for ordinary beings who have given rise to the great mind.

[At that time] At this time, that is, when the World-Honored One had finished sitting at ease. [Elder] A bhikṣu of advanced years, virtue and prestige. [Subhūti] One of the Buddha’s ten great disciples; rendered into Chinese as Kongsheng, Shanjian and Shanji, and renowned among the ten great disciples as “foremost in understanding emptiness.” [Baring his right shoulder] When wearing the kaṣāya robe, to bare the right shoulder and cover the left. This was originally a ceremony of respect in ancient India, and Buddhism followed it: when a bhikṣu paid respects to the Buddha or inquired of his teacher or the saṃgha, he had to bare the right shoulder, meaning that he was ready to serve and to receive orders and be sent on errands. [Said] To state something to a superior. [Rare indeed] Incomparably wondrous! An expression of praise. [Tathāgata] One of the ten titles of the Buddha. Usually “World-Honored One” is the general title, used in addressing him; “Buddha” indicates the virtue of fruition; “Tathāgata” indicates the virtue of nature.
[The Buddha’s ten titles]

The Buddha has ten venerable titles: 1. Tathāgata—the Buddha rides the way of suchness, comes to accomplish perfect enlightenment, and comes to the three realms to bestow transformation. 2. Arhat (worthy of offerings)—the Buddha is worthy of the offerings of gods and humans. 3. Fully Enlightened—the Buddha truly and universally knows all dharmas. 4. Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct—the Buddha is complete in the three knowledges of the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye and the extinction of taints, and in the five practices of the noble practice, the brahma practice, the divine practice, the infant practice and the sick practice. 5. Well-Gone—the Buddha freely and well departs into nirvāṇa. 6. Knower of the World—the Buddha can understand the affairs and principles of all worlds. 7. Unsurpassed One—the Buddha is the being supreme beyond all. 8. Tamer of Beings—the Buddha is the great being who tames and governs all living beings, causing them to leave defilement and attain nirvāṇa. 9. Teacher of Gods and Humans—the Buddha is the guide of all gods and humans. 10. World-Honored One—the Buddha is the one honored in common by all the world.

[The Tathāgata truly protects and cares for the bodhisattvas well, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas well.] “Protects and cares” means to tend, protect and compassionately remember. “Entrusts and instructs” means to entrust, charge and admonish, which also means to teach. This passage is Subhūti’s incomparable praise of the World-Honored One for taking his own person as the model and tending, protecting, guiding and teaching the bodhisattvas at all times and in all places. [Good men and good women] Men and women who observe the five precepts and the ten good deeds. [Supreme perfect enlightenment] Perfect and supreme wisdom—the wisdom of the Buddha. Rendered into Chinese as “supreme, correct and universal enlightenment,” also called “supreme universal knowledge.” [Giving rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment] Giving rise to the great mind of becoming Buddha. “Giving rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment” is also abbreviated as “giving rise to the bodhi mind.” Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna says in the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom,

fascicle forty-one: “When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind, taking the supreme way as his condition—‘I shall become Buddha’—this is called the bodhi mind.” [How] In what way. “How” has the following several meanings: for what reason, why; in what way, what to do, how it is. [How should they abide?] “How should they abide” means “how should one abide”; this uses inverted sentence order, placing “should” after “how” in order to strengthen the tone. (The answer to “How should they abide?” is in section four: “giving without abiding in marks.” Not abiding in marks is emptiness, and giving is compassion; compassion and emptiness cultivated together—this is the bodhisattva path.) [How should they subdue their minds?] How should they subdue their minds? (The answer is in section three: single-mindedly liberating all living beings while being without the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings and the mark of a life-span. This is the wondrous remedy for affliction: as it is said, to stop water from boiling by ladling it out is not as good as withdrawing the firewood from beneath the cauldron. To single-mindedly liberate all living beings while being without the four marks—this too is compassion and emptiness cultivated together.) [Inversion] A rhetorical figure that inverts word order to strengthen the tone, harmonize rhythm or interweave sentence patterns; it was constantly used in ancient Chinese, so one should be attentive to this when reading Buddhist sutras.

Day after day the World-Honored One displayed thus (not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness), yet the great assembly did not notice; today it was at last seen through by Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness (who saw the signs), personally perceiving the Tathāgata’s painstaking care, and he praised him without cease. When the World-Honored One had sat at ease, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha: Incomparably wondrous, World-Honored One! Taking your own person as the model, not grasping at marks and unmoving in suchness, you teach thus by bodily example at all times and in all places—this is truly the best protection and care and the best instructive guidance for all bodhisattvas!

But why are the bodhisattvas unable to achieve “not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness”? For this reason Subhūti asked the World-Honored One: how should they abide, and how should they subdue their minds?

By the Buddha’s original vow, he wished only to lay bare the truth completely (to set out whole the truth of life and the universe), so that everyone might become Buddha. But living beings are thin in virtue and heavy in defilement, weak in will, unable to bear it, and hard to address plainly (just as in section fourteen of this sutra the Buddha says: “If again there is a person who, hearing this sutra, is not startled, not frightened and not afraid, know that such a person is most rare.” And as at the Lotus assembly, when Śāriputra three times begged the World-Honored One to reveal the foremost, rare and hard-to-understand Dharma, and when the World-Honored One began to expound it, five thousand bhikṣus refused to hear and withdrew from the assembly). So he had no choice but to use secret and skillful means and accommodate them; hence the word “well.”

Day after day the World-Honored One displayed thus; this is truly the most skillful protection and care and the most skillful entrusting and instructing of the bodhisattvas. As it is said: not by verbal teaching, but by turning them through his own person—the painstaking care of a good craftsman.

In the sutra text of this section, “How should they abide?” has two readings: the Qianlong Tripitaka and the popular editions adopt “How should they abide?” while another reading, based on Tang dynasty manuscripts and Ming dynasty block-printed editions, proposes that this passage should be “How should one abide?” Is it “How should they abide” or “How should one abide”? This book follows the Qianlong Tripitaka and the popular editions in adopting “How should they abide?”

The reason is this: “How should they abide” in fact means “how should one abide”; it is only that, to strengthen the tone, inverted sentence order is used, placing “should” after “how.” Inversion is very common in rhetoric, used to strengthen the tone and make the words vivid. For example, in “The Foolish Old Man Removes the Mountains” in the Liezi,

“How great is your lack of sense!” means: your lack of sense (hui, interchangeable with “wisdom”) is great! And Wei Zheng’s “Expressing My Feelings,” “On ancient trees cold birds cry; in empty mountains night apes wail,” means: on ancient trees cold birds cry, in empty mountains night apes wail. In fact, the four characters “Thus have I heard” at the very beginning of the sutra are also an inversion. If it were rendered as “I heard thus,” not only would the force of the wording and the beauty of the style be much diminished, but the poetic realm would be as different as heaven and earth.
Question: Why is “How should they abide?” explained as “how should they abide and uphold?”

Answer: Master Kumarajiva’s rendering “How should they abide” is excellent; the word “abide” fits perfectly with the sutra text before and after it. (For example, the last line of section four: “Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply abide as he is taught.”) But the meaning of “abide” here needs to be correctly interpreted. What cultivators care about most is three questions: how to abide in the mind (to gather the mind in and not let it scatter), how to practice (to correct one’s actual conduct of body, speech and mind), and how to subdue the mind. Judging from several other translations, in the Sanskrit original Subhūti raised these three questions. For example, Master Xuanzang’s translation: “World-Honored One! Those who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle—how should they abide? How should they practice? How should they subdue their minds?” Therefore some venerable ones have criticized Master Kumarajiva’s translation as “missing one of the three questions.”

In fact, combining two questions into one (merging “how to abide in the mind” and “how to practice” into “how should they abide”) was also Master Kumarajiva’s painstaking care. The World-Honored One answered the first two questions together in “Section Four: Wondrous Practice Without Abiding” (how should one abide in the mind? how should one practice?), and then in section ten he further clarified the question of how to abide in the mind and how to practice: “Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind abiding in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; they should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.” Therefore the Master merged these two questions into one, “how should they abide,” so that the wording echoes before and after, is polished and easy on the tongue, and the reader, from the sutra text before and after, can readily grasp that this “abide” contains both the sense of abiding in the mind and that of practicing—that is, how to abide and uphold.

After Master Kumarajiva first translated the Diamond Sutra, five other translations appeared one after another. By rights, each later one ought to surpass the earlier ones, ought it not? Yet history has proven that Master Kumarajiva’s translation carries the greatest power to gather and move people—that is to say, it accords most fully with the meaning of the sutra, and it has been widely transmitted without decline.

[The Buddha said: Excellent! Excellent! Subhuti, as you have said, the Tathagata protects and cares for all bodhisattvas in the best way, and instructs all bodhisattvas in the best way. Now listen attentively, and I will explain it for you. Good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide thus, and thus subdue their minds.]

The Buddha said: Excellent! Excellent! Subhuti, just as you have said, this is truly the Tathagata’s best protection and care for all bodhisattvas, and his best teaching and guidance. Listen with a focused and careful mind, and I will explain for you one by one this method of abiding in the path and subduing the mind. Good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide thus, and thus subdue their minds.

[Excellent] Wonderful! A word of praise. [Listen attentively] To listen with a focused and careful mind. [Thus] In this way. Here the two words “thus” point vaguely to what follows— “should abide thus” refers to the fourth chapter, and “thus subdue their minds” refers to the third chapter.

The Buddha said “Excellent!” twice in a row to praise Subhuti. The first “Excellent!” praises Subhuti for being able to understand the Buddha’s demonstration. The Buddha confirmed that Subhuti’s understanding was without error, saying: Subhuti, just as you have said, I demonstrate thus day after day; this is truly the Tathagata’s best protection and care for all bodhisattvas, and his best teaching and guidance. The second “Excellent!” praises Subhuti’s wisdom and compassion, his ability to request instruction on the two questions that leave practitioners so afflicted by affliction and so urgently in need of resolution—how should one abide? How should one subdue one’s mind?

Thereupon, regarding the two questions Subhuti had requested instruction on, the Buddha said: As to the two questions you have raised, listen with a focused and careful mind, and I will explain them for you in detail. Good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide thus, and should thus subdue their minds.
[Yes indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear.]
Subhuti reverently replied: Yes, World-Honored One! I long most eagerly and most joyfully to hear your teaching on these two questions.
The Mahavaipulya Buddha Avatamsaka Sutra

Chapter Thirty-Four says: “As the thirsty long for cool water, as the hungry think of fine food, as the sick recall good medicine, as bees crave fine honey; even so do we long to hear the sweet-dew Dharma!”

[Yes indeed] The word “yes” is a term of assent. For example, the Lankavatara Sutra says: “At that time the Buddha told the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati: Now I will explain for you the distinguishing marks of mind-made bodies. Listen attentively! Listen attentively! Consider it well. Mahamati said: Yes.” “Indeed” expresses an earnest wish to hear the World-Honored One’s detailed teaching on the two “thus.” [Yes indeed, World-Honored One!] Subhuti’s reverent reply expresses his profound aspiration. [We joyfully wish to hear] He gladly wishes to hear this Dharma.

Good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide thus, and thus subdue their minds”—this passage of the sutra has traditionally been given two other explanations; to understand its meaning better, let us examine them critically as follows.
1. The World-Honored One’s two “thus” already answered Subhuti’s two questions, “How should one abide? How should one subdue one’s mind?”—it is only that Subhuti did not understand.

This explanation is not sound, for even if Subhuti did not understand the two “thus,” he would hardly fail to understand the World-Honored One’s tone. If the World-Honored One’s two “thus” were answering Subhuti’s two “how,” and the elder did not understand, he would have said something like: “We only pray that the World-Honored One, in great compassion and pity, will expound it separately for the sake of all beings,” rather than joyfully going along with the World-Honored One’s tone and saying: “Yes indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear.” Compare the passage in the Lotus Sutra
Chapter Two, “Expedient Means”: “At that time the Buddha told Shariputra: … Listen well now, and I will explain it for you. Shariputra said: Yes indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear.”

2. The World-Honored One’s two “thus” already answered Subhuti’s two questions, “How should one abide? How should one subdue one’s mind?” Although Subhuti understood, the assembly had not yet understood, and so he asked the World-Honored One on their behalf to reveal it in detail.

This explanation is also not sound. At the very beginning of “Leaving Marks and Extinction, Chapter Fourteen”: “At that time, when Subhuti had heard this sutra, he understood its meaning and purport deeply, and weeping tears of sorrow he said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha has spoken a sutra of such profound depth; from ages past until now, with the wisdom eye I have attained, I have never heard such a sutra.” Judging from this passage, Subhuti had not understood before this point.

In fact, the questions Subhuti asked—“How should one abide? How should one subdue one’s mind?”—are questions of a profound level. Subhuti was already an arhat; the afflictions of views and thoughts had been cut off, and he was foremost in understanding emptiness. The questions “How should one abide? How should one subdue one’s mind?” at a shallow level he not only understood thoroughly but had long since put into practice. His question now arose from what he had realized that day from the World-Honored One’s everyday activities—putting on his robe, holding his bowl and so on—namely the World-Honored One’s profound intent and ultimate practice. This question of Subhuti’s finally brought forth the Diamond Sutra, of which it is said: “All Buddhas and the Dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra”!

Therefore the meaning of “Listen attentively now, and I will explain it for you. Good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide thus, and thus subdue their minds” is: You should listen with a focused and careful mind, and I will explain in detail the two questions you have raised. Good men and good women who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide thus, and should thus subdue their minds.

It is like one person asking another about a complicated matter and the one answering saying, “It is like this.” This is an introductory phrase, used at the beginning of a speech to draw the listener’s attention. Its meaning is: I will now explain this matter for you in detail. It is not that the words “it is like this” have already answered the question.

Of this passage of the sutra, Master Xuanzang’s translation reads: “At that time the World-Honored One told the venerable Subhuti: Excellent! Excellent! Subhuti, it is so, it is so. As you have said, even the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, can with the most excellent gathering gather all bodhisattva-mahasattvas, and even the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, can with the most excellent entrusting entrust all bodhisattva-mahasattvas. Therefore, Subhuti! You should listen attentively and attend to it most skillfully,
I will explain and expound it for you separately

—those who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle should abide thus, cultivate thus, and subdue their minds thus. The venerable Subhuti said to the Buddha: It is so, it is so. World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear.”
Please pay special attention to the eight characters “I will explain and expound it for you separately.”
[Venerable] A general designation for a bhikshu, because a bhikshu possesses not only a worldly lifespan but also the wisdom-life of the dharmakāya.

Therefore, when Subhuti responded, “Yes indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear,” his meaning was: Yes, World-Honored One! I long most eagerly and most joyfully to hear your thorough teaching on these two questions. Hence it is only in the fourteenth chapter that we find: “When Subhuti had heard this sutra, he understood its meaning and purport deeply, and weeping tears of sorrow he said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha has spoken a sutra of such profound depth; from ages past until now, with the wisdom eye I have attained, I have never heard such a sutra.”—this is precisely
the unsurpassed, profound and subtle Dharma, hard to encounter in a hundred thousand million kalpas;

In this chapter Subhuti raised two most important questions: How should one abide? How should one subdue one’s mind? This is the theme that runs through the whole sutra. To make the following passages easier to understand, the answers are set out here first.
Question: How should one abide?
Answer:
giving without dwelling in marks

. “Subhuti! A bodhisattva should give with a mind that dwells nowhere in dharmas. That is to say, give without dwelling in forms, give without dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas. Subhuti! A bodhisattva should give thus, without dwelling in marks.” “If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.” (A bodhisattva’s practice is the six paramitas; here giving, the first of the six, stands for all six, and giving without dwelling in marks encompasses the whole of the six paramitas.)
Question: How should one subdue one’s mind?

Answer: To save all living beings without clinging to the mark of saving living beings. “Thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation.” “Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.” “Leaving all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

blocks.text: The Mahayana Orthodox Teaching, Chapter Three

inline.s: The Mahayana Orthodox Teaching” means the twin functioning of compassion and emptiness—seeking the Buddha path above and transforming living beings below—which is exactly what the following passage says: saving all living beings (saving all living beings to become Buddhas), and yet in truth no living being attains salvation (in truth there is no such thing as a living being attaining salvation and becoming a Buddha). In studying the Diamond Sutra, one should again and again realize the words “saving all living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation”; this is the Mahayana Orthodox Teaching.
In this chapter the World-Honored One first says “should thus subdue their minds,” corresponding to the World-Honored One’s words in the previous chapter that one should “thus subdue their minds.”

[The Buddha told Subhuti: All bodhisattva-mahasattvas should thus subdue their minds: All kinds of living beings whatsoever—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought—I cause all of them to enter nirvāṇa without residue and attain salvation; thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation.]

The method by which a bodhisattva subdues his mind is this: universally saving living beings to become Buddhas (“saving countless, numberless, boundless living beings”), and yet not clinging to the mark of saving living beings (“in truth no living being attains salvation”). Compassion and emptiness function as a pair: compassionate saving of living beings without clinging to the mark of saving.
The Buddha told Subhuti: All bodhisattva-mahasattvas should thus subdue their minds”
—the Buddha said to Subhuti: All great bodhisattvas (bodhisattva-mahasattvas) should thus subdue their minds.

[The Buddha told Subhuti] Whenever a passage begins with “The Buddha told Subhuti,” this emphasizes that what is said is of the utmost importance. [Bodhisattva-mahasattva] Bodhisattvas have higher, middle and lower levels; to indicate bodhisattvas on the grounds, they are further called mahasattvas. The Treatise on the Stages of the Buddha Ground says: “Here we take the great bodhisattvas on the grounds, and therefore again speak of mahasattvas.” Thus “bodhisattva-mahasattva” indicates a bodhisattva on the grounds. Here “all bodhisattva-mahasattvas” refers to the good men and good women mentioned earlier who have aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; this designation expresses the World-Honored One’s boundless expectation of them, that they take the great bodhisattvas on the grounds as their model and thus subdue their minds. [Bodhisattva on the grounds] A bodhisattva, from ordinary being to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wonderful enlightenment. Bodhisattvas at the level of the ten grounds are called bodhisattvas on the grounds.

All kinds of living beings whatsoever—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought—I cause all of them to enter nirvāṇa without residue and attain salvation”

—all living beings of every kind, such as those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture or by transformation, those with form or without form, those with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought, I shall save them all to become Buddhas.

[Born from eggs] Beings that take form within an eggshell and are born only afterwards, such as birds. [Born from wombs] Beings that take form within the mother’s womb and are born only afterwards, such as humans. [Born from moisture] Beings that receive form relying on moisture, such as insects. [Born by transformation] Beings that have no support and arise suddenly through the power of karma alone, such as the gods of the heavens. [With form] Beings in the desire realm and the form realm that possess a physical body. [Without form] Such beings have no physical body, but retain the mind of consciousness and dwell in profound and subtle meditative concentration. [With thought] Among all the heavens, except the Heaven Without Thought and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, all the rest are heavens with thought. Beings in the heavens with thought possess thought and feeling, and so are called those with thought. [Without thought] The Heaven Without Thought is in the fourth dhyana heaven of the form realm; the beings of that heaven dwell without mind for five hundred great kalpas. [Neither with thought nor without thought] The Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception is the highest heaven of the three realms; its beings dwell in meditative concentration. They have no coarse thoughts, and so it is called “neither with thought”; they still have subtle thoughts, and so it is again called “nor without thought.” [The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sexual desire and the desire for food, including the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the form realm is the world inhabited by beings who are free of the two desires of sexuality and food but still possess a physical body, including the four dhyana heavens and the eighteen heavens; the formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who have no physical body but dwell with their mind-consciousness in profound and subtle meditative concentration, including the four empty heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all the domain of ordinary beings’ cycle of birth and death. [The eighteen heavens] The eighteen heavens of the form realm: the first dhyana heaven has three, namely the Heaven of the Multitude of Brahma, the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers and the Great Brahma Heaven; the second dhyana heaven also has three, namely the Heaven of Lesser Light, the Heaven of Boundless Light and the Heaven of Light-Sound; the third dhyana heaven also has three, namely the Heaven of Lesser Purity, the Heaven of Boundless Purity and the Heaven of Universal Purity; the fourth dhyana heaven has nine in all, namely the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Blessing-Birth, the Heaven of Vast Fruit, the Heaven Without Thought, the Heaven Without Affliction, the Heaven Without Heat, the Heaven of Good Seeing, the Heaven of Good Appearance and the Highest Heaven of Form.

[Attain salvation] That is, nirvāṇa. “Extinction” is the extinction of the three kinds of delusion—delusion of views and thoughts, delusion as numerous as dust and sand, and delusion of ignorance; “crossing over” is deliverance from both fragmentary birth-and-death and transformation birth-and-death. [I cause all of them to enter nirvāṇa without residue and attain salvation] I shall save them all to become Buddhas. [Nirvāṇa] The full name is parinirvāṇa, meaning not arising and not ceasing. It is rendered in Chinese as “perfect quiescence”: perfect means the perfection of all the virtues of wisdom, and quiescence means the quiescent extinction of all delusion and karma. It is also translated as “extinction and deliverance.” This is the true-such realm, neither arising nor ceasing and transcending space and time, realized by the sages; it is also the most ideal and most beautiful final home of the myriad living beings. [Nirvāṇa without residue] When a bodhisattva has exhausted the causes of transformation birth-and-death, this is called “nirvāṇa with residue” (when a follower of the Small Vehicle realizes the fruit of arhatship, this is also called nirvāṇa with residue); only when the fruit of transformation birth-and-death is exhausted, with not a hair’s breadth of delusory marks of birth and death remaining, and the Buddha’s eternal body is obtained, is it called “nirvāṇa without residue.”
Thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation”

—having thus saved countless, numberless, boundless living beings to become Buddhas, and yet in truth there is no such thing as a living being receiving salvation and becoming a Buddha. This says that when a bodhisattva saves living beings without dwelling in the mark of saving, he enters into selflessness and can thereby subdue his mind.

Saving countless, numberless, boundless living beings”—this is compassion (“compassion” being the mind that uproots the suffering of others); “and yet in truth no living being attains salvation”—this is not clinging to marks, knowing that the saving of living beings is an illusion; this is emptiness. Compassion and emptiness held equally, functioning as a pair and merging into one another, run through the Diamond Sutra from beginning to end. This is because only the twin merging of compassion and emptiness is right concentration, and only thus can the Buddha fruit be perfected. If one falls into one-sided emptiness (thinking that nothing whatsoever exists) or even into neutral indifference (still and not illuminating), one mostly plants the cause of animal rebirth, or falls into the samādhi of extinction of the shravakas, or is reborn in the formless realm. Therefore the World-Honored One in this sutra again and again speaks of giving without dwelling (non-dwelling is emptiness, giving is compassion). For a cultivator to dance according to circumstances is of course foolish; but if one becomes cold and isolated, this too is wrong—take the utmost care!

And yet in truth no living being attains salvation”—here the World-Honored One admonishes us that in saving living beings we must not cling to the mark of saving. For to save living beings is to teach them to leave marks and awaken from the dream of ignorance; if one clings to marks oneself, how can one teach others to leave marks? It is like rescuing a drowning person: one wants to save him from the water, not to sink with him to the bottom of the sea and perish together.

[Samādhi of extinction] The concentration in which both mind and mental factors (“mental factors,” short for dharmas belonging to the mind, that is, all the various mental phenomena that belong to the mind) are wholly extinguished. That is, the state of mental unification in which the mind’s activity of the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness and mind-consciousness) is entirely extinguished. Although its perception and anxiety have ceased, subtle mental activity still remains unextinguished.

Master Hanshan said: “What Buddhism values is benefiting both self and others; only then is one called a bodhisattva. The Sanskrit word bodhisattva is rendered here as ‘being of the great mind,’ because such a one can enter the realm of living beings and can cut off afflictions, and so receives this name. If a bodhisattva abandons the world, he has no practice to cultivate; if he abandons living beings, he has no tool for cutting off afflictions. Therefore a bodhisattva relies on living beings in order to cut off the afflictions of his own nature, just as a stone from another mountain can polish jade. Afflictions are the various bad habits of greed, anger, self-love, wrong views and pride (that is, self-love, self-view and self-conceit), which are the coverings that obscure the light of one’s own nature. Only the adverse conditions and circumstances of living beings in the world can grind and polish them away, as the Odes say of cutting and filing, carving and polishing.” (Dream Roam Collection
Instruction to Yuan Datu)

How should one subdue one’s mind? Even in saving all living beings, one does not cling to marks. This says: however high one’s attainment and however great one’s merit, one does not cling to marks. To cling to marks is not bodhisattva practice, for bodhisattva practice is to turn delusion into awakening, whereas clinging to marks is to enter illusion through illusion, deluded all the more.

When we arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (the mind of becoming a Buddha), we must make the vow: “All kinds of living beings whatsoever … I cause all of them to enter nirvāṇa without residue and attain salvation,” and further, “thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation.” This is a stance as lofty as a house built on high ground: we are great bodhisattvas who would save all living beings—how could we not be dignified and self-respecting? How could we harm living beings? How could we contend with them for fame and profit? How could we stand opposed to them? How could we haggle with them? In this way selfishness and self-interest, fame and gain, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and lying, greed, anger, delusion and arrogance, and all the rights and wrongs of self and others, naturally melt like ice, and the merit one creates is likewise empty of the three wheels; the mind is subdued without being subdued.

[Empty of the three wheels] With respect to giving, the giver, the receiver and the thing given are called the three wheels; if after giving, the marks of these three wheels do not remain in the mind, it is called “empty of the three wheels.”
[Why is this? Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.]

The World-Honored One said: Why is it that “thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation”? Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life, then he does not count as a bodhisattva.

Among the four marks, the mark of a self comes first. Once this mark is established, the other three marks (the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life) arise accordingly. A bodhisattva is a being of the great mind who has aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and one who has aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi must believe in and understand the true nature of all dharmas, for the true nature of all dharmas is the Buddha path. One who has the four marks gives concrete expression to the deluded clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as truly existent; this shows that he has not believed in and understood the true nature of all dharmas, and so he is not a bodhisattva. This principle is expounded in very great detail in the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury.

All living beings without exception possess the nature of awakening, numinous, luminous, empty and still, no different from the Buddha. But because from beginningless kalpas they have never awakened, they deludedly cling to body and mind (form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness) as themselves (the mark of a self), and so give rise to emotions of love and hate, acceptance and rejection. Thereupon they create karma according to their emotions, and receive retribution according to their karma, passing through birth, aging, sickness and death and cycling through kalpas without end.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All living beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversions, like a person who has lost his way and takes the four directions to be reversed (for example, taking east for west and south for north), deludedly taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadowy impressions of the six dusts as the mark of his own mind. It is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky in truth has no flowers; the diseased one deludedly clings to them. Because of deluded clinging, he is confused not only about the nature of this emptiness but also about where those real flowers arise. From this delusion there is the turning about in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.”

When one’s own nature is deluded, one deludedly takes this five-aggregate body and mind—which has a name, a form, a gender, a status and an age—as oneself, as “I,” and so turns about in birth and death.

[The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations and the aggregate of consciousness. These five arise from accumulation and so are called the “five aggregates”; they can also cover over a person’s true nature, causing him to be deluded and inverted and to create all kinds of karma, and so they are also called the “five shadows.” Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called “form dharmas”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness belong to the spiritual and are called “mind dharmas.” These are the five great elements that make up body and mind. Among them the aggregate of form is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness) are the mind. [The four great elements] Earth, water, fire and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature and wind has movement as its nature. All material things in the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth and movement, and so they are called “great.” [Shadowy impressions of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six dusts; because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy impressions of the six dusts—the phantoms of the six dusts.

[Marks] The various appearances of things as they manifest outwardly and are imagined in the mind. [The mark of a self] Deludedly clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as truly existent and taking them as “I,” thereby giving rise to thoughts, such as thoughts of gain and loss, adversity and favor, honor and disgrace, and so on. [The mark of a person] Deludedly clinging to the other, to other people, as truly existent, thereby giving rise to thoughts, such as thoughts of love and hate, right and wrong, high and low, and so on. [The mark of a living being] Here “living beings” means groups of people, for example groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and foe, age, gender, workplace, region, ethnicity, skin color, nation, and so on; the mark of a living being is deludedly clinging to these groups as truly existent and giving rise to discriminating thoughts. [The mark of a life] Deludedly clinging to lifespan as truly existent and calculating its length. What deluded living beings care about most is none other than lifespan, and so the mark of a life is separated out from the mark of a self and set up as its own item. The Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury was also translated by Master Kumarajiva; in it the Buddha says:

“After the great and majestic Buddha and his great disciples passed into extinction, there gradually came to be many people who knew that the Dharma of renunciants is peaceful and happy and who left home to study the path, but who could not know the profound and unequaled emptiness of the sutras spoken by the Buddha; most of them were deluded by evil maras, and at that time those who taught the Dharma were uncertain in mind and taught what was impure, teaching that there is self, person, living being and lifespan, and not teaching that all dharmas are empty and still.” “One who calculates a mind of self speaks of a lifespan. Because of lifespan, one is dragged about by gain and support, and is obstructed from the path.”
To leave the mark of a life is to accomplish the non-duality of early death and long life.

These four marks are the deluded clinging to self, person (the other, other people), living being (groups of people) and lifespan as truly existent, and so one stands on the standpoint of “I” to discriminate, calculate, confront and act. Once the four marks are established, one cannot know all dharmas as illusory; one is bound by them and cannot be liberated.

Among the four marks, the mark of a self comes first. Once this mark is established, the other three marks arise correspondingly. Thereupon selfish thoughts, selfish interests and selfish desires surge up, and affliction and karmic retribution follow after. To catch the bandits, first catch their leader: the first thing a student of Buddhism must break is the mark of a self, for if there is the mark of a self, there are the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life. If there is no mark of a self, then there are no marks at all; the very substance is empty and still, and all wisdom naturally appears before one.
In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury

Chapter Three, “Recollection of the Dharma,” the Buddha says: “Shariputra! If there are living beings without inversion who contemplate thus in accordance with reality, they have right view. If one gives rise to the notion of self, the notion of person or the notion of living being, you should know that such a person is entirely on a wrong path. Shariputra! The Buddha and his disciples do not speak of self, do not speak of person, do not speak of living being, do not speak of lifespan, do not speak of annihilation or permanence; therefore the Buddha and his disciples are called holders of right view. Why is this? Because their right contemplation is without inversion.” This shows that one who has the wrong views of the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life does not even qualify to be a disciple of the Buddha—how much less could he be a bodhisattva! In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury the World-Honored One expounds this principle and the true nature of all dharmas in exhaustive detail.

[The two views of annihilation and permanence] The “view of annihilation” holds that the self is limited to one lifetime and that after death everything is nothing. The “view of permanence” holds that after death the self is not extinguished but can be reborn and continues in its present state; for example, one who is born human will be human life after life, and one born a dog will be a dog life after life. Right view is: leaving annihilation and leaving permanence, and taking the Middle Way, the true nature of reality.
Question: How are the four marks to be left?

Answer: This can be done in two steps. The first step is not to mistake the five aggregates of body and mind and all circumstances for real and so give rise to clinging. In the Mahayana Lankavatara Sutra the Buddha says: “If cultivators give rise to the clinging to existence or non-existence with respect to circumstances (if with respect to circumstances they give rise to the clinging to existence and non-existence—clinging that things exist or do not exist, for example deludedly clinging that an ox has horns and a rabbit has none), then they cling to self, person, living being and lifespan.” The second step is that when you already have the power to keep a thought from continuing once it arises, leaving the four marks is leaving the four notions. The mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life are simply the thoughts of self, person, living being and lifespan that surface in your mind, and so some translations of the Diamond Sutra render the four marks as the four notions. Kumarajiva’s (350–413) translation, the Diamond Prajñā-paramita Sutra, says: “If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.” But the translation by the Tripitaka Master Paramartha (499–569), the Diamond Prajñā-paramita Sutra, says: “All bodhisattvas are without the notion of self, the notion of living being, the notion of life, the notion of receiver.” Therefore, whenever a thought about self, person, living being or lifespan surfaces, one must immediately extinguish it (this can be done once one’s skill in contemplating the mind is deep), and must never let it continue into a notion; one must be aware the moment a thought arises, and once aware, it is gone. The Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury says: “The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without notion and without thought.” The Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says: “To raise the mind and move a thought is already to deviate from the substance of the Dharma, and is precisely to cling to marks; since beginningless time there has never been a Buddha who clings to marks.”

blocks.text: Wondrous Practice Without Dwelling, Chapter Four

inline.s: Wondrous practice without dwelling—here “without dwelling” is knowing that all dharmas are empty, and therefore not grasping at conditions and not being defiled or attached, acting without clinging to action (without love and hate, acceptance and rejection); this is called wondrous practice. “Wondrous practice without dwelling” is the giving without dwelling in marks spoken of below. Not dwelling in marks is emptiness, giving is compassion; giving without dwelling in marks is the twin functioning of compassion and emptiness. This chapter answers the question “How should one abide?”—abiding (abiding and maintaining) by way of giving without dwelling in marks, which echoes from afar the World-Honored One’s words in the latter part of the second chapter, “should abide thus.”

[Non-dwelling] Not clinging to marks. That is to say, one does not dwell in or cling to the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being, the mark of a life, the mark of dharmas or the mark of non-dharmas (not deludedly clinging to them as real). The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Leaving marks, one is without marks; without marks, one does not dwell; not dwelling, one enters the Buddha’s realm—this is the unsurpassed, true and great bodhisattva path.”

[Clinging to marks] Clinging to marks is taking marks as real, whereupon desire arises and thoughts arise, and one runs after desire and thoughts. Thus one creates karma, and thus one turns about in birth and death. Therefore do not cling to marks as real and be moved by them. This sutra says:
“Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

[Furthermore, Subhuti! A bodhisattva should give with a mind that dwells nowhere in dharmas. That is to say, give without dwelling in forms, give without dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas. Subhuti! A bodhisattva should give thus, without dwelling in marks.]

This passage follows the World-Honored One’s answer to the second question, “How should one subdue one’s mind?”, and immediately answers the first question. Subhuti asked, “How should one abide?” The World-Honored One answered, “Give without dwelling in marks.” That is, a bodhisattva should give while leaving marks, should be empty of the three wheels, and should abide thus—that is to say, abide (abiding and maintaining) by way of giving without dwelling in marks.
Furthermore, Subhuti!”

—Moreover, Subhuti! This is the World-Honored One, having answered “How should one subdue one’s mind?”, immediately going on to answer the question “How should one abide?” (how should one abide and maintain).
A bodhisattva should give with a mind that dwells nowhere in dharmas.”

—A bodhisattva should give while leaving marks, and in giving should not cling to circumstances and give rise to thoughts, nor be turned about by circumstances. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When the preceding thought clings to circumstances, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves circumstances, that is bodhi.”

The word “dharmas” has several meanings: first, it refers generally to all things and matters, including thought, speech and writing, all of which are called “dharmas”; second, principle, law, regularity; third, method; fourth, the Dharma of the path, that is, the principles, methods and states of cultivating the path; fifth, the dharma-dust among the six dusts (forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects and dharmas). Which meaning is intended must be judged from the context. In the sentence “A bodhisattva should give with a mind that dwells nowhere in dharmas,” “dharmas” refers generally to all things. [Dwelling nowhere in dharmas] Knowing that all dharmas are empty, and therefore not grasping at conditions and not being defiled or attached.

Giving”: to give to others what one has. There are three kinds of giving: the giving of wealth, relieving with goods and money those who are sick, weak, poor and suffering; the giving of Dharma, guiding people out of suffering with the right Dharma; and the giving of fearlessness, freeing others from terror and fear.
That is to say, give without dwelling in forms, give without dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas.”

—This explains the preceding sentence: “A bodhisattva should give with a mind that dwells nowhere in dharmas.” Concretely, it is to give without dwelling in the dust of forms, to give without dwelling in the dust of sounds, to give without dwelling in the dust of fragrances, to give without dwelling in the dust of tastes, to give without dwelling in the dust of tangible objects, and to give without dwelling in the dust of dharmas.

Forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects and dharmas” are called the six dusts, namely: the dust of forms, the dust of sounds, the dust of fragrances, the dust of tastes, the dust of tangible objects and the dust of dharmas. “Dust” means defilement, because it can defile the human mind and prevent one’s own nature from appearing; they are also called the six objects, that is, the objects grasped at by the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind): the eye sees forms, the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue tastes flavors, the body feels tangible objects, and the mind knows dharmas. Here “not dwelling” means having no love and hate, acceptance and rejection, toward the objects of dust (forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects and dharmas).

The first five dusts (the dust of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes and tangible objects) include all material objects within the reach of the senses, while the dust of dharmas includes all spiritual objects within the reach of the mind. Therefore the six words “forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects and dharmas” refer to all objects. In the tenth chapter, “One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas,” means that one must not cling to any object. When the Buddha speaks of the six dusts, he always mentions forms first and then sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects and dharmas, because the dust of forms (what the eye sees) most easily deludes people and has the greatest influence among the six dusts, and so it is mentioned first by itself as a warning.
A bodhisattva cultivates the six paramitas and the myriad practices;
giving comes first, and giving without dwelling encompasses the other five paramitas. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter One, “The Prologue,” the Buddha says: “Shariputra! When a bodhisattva-mahasattva practices the prajñāpāramitā of giving (that is, giving without dwelling), by the power of wisdom and skillful means he can fulfill the paramita of dana (giving), the paramita of shila (precepts), the paramita of kshanti (patience), the paramita of virya (diligence), the paramita of dhyana (meditative concentration) and the paramita of prajñā (wisdom). Shariputra said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva-mahasattva, when giving, by the power of wisdom and skillful means fulfills the paramita of dana and even the paramita of prajñā? The Buddha told Shariputra: Because giver, receiver and goods are unobtainable (empty of the three wheels), he can fulfill the paramita of dana. Because offense and non-offense are unobtainable, he fulfills the paramita of shila. Because the mind does not move, he fulfills the paramita of kshanti. Because body and mind are diligent and without indolence, he fulfills the paramita of virya. Because he is neither scattered nor benighted, he fulfills the paramita of dhyana. Because he knows all dharmas are unobtainable, he fulfills the paramita of prajñā.”
In the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Two, “Learning and Contemplation,” the Buddha says: “Bodhisattva-mahasattvas who cultivate prajñāpāramitā can know in accordance with reality. If a bodhisattva-mahasattva, with non-attainment as his skillful means, cultivates the paramita of giving, he thoroughly understands that all givers, receivers and goods given are unobtainable; such giving, skillful and wise, can fulfill the paramitas of giving, pure precepts, patient acceptance, diligence, meditative stillness and prajñā.”

[The six paramitas] Also called the six paramitas: the six practices by which one can cross from this shore of birth-and-death and affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa’s peace and bliss—namely giving, observing precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration and prajñā. Giving can cross over stinginess and greed, observing precepts can cross over transgression, patience can cross over anger, diligence can overcome indolence, meditative concentration can overcome distraction, and prajñā can overcome delusion. [The six paramitas and the myriad practices] In brief they are the six paramitas, in full they are the myriad practices, and the six paramitas include all the practices cultivated by a bodhisattva.
Subhuti! A bodhisattva should give thus, without dwelling in marks.”

—The World-Honored One emphasizes once more: one should give thus, without dwelling in marks (not giving rise to discriminating thoughts about marks). For giving is meant to use illusion to leave illusion, not to use illusion to enter illusion; it is meant to dissolve the self, not to inflate the self.
