The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “To have a self is sin; to forget one’s merits, merit beyond compare.”
[Why is this? If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.]

The World-Honored One explains why “a bodhisattva should give thus, without dwelling in marks”: because “if a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable”—that is to say, the merit and virtue of giving without dwelling in marks is exceedingly great, so great that the mind cannot imagine it.

The Four Lessons of Liao-Fan says: When one does good without the mind clinging to the good, then whatever one accomplishes is perfect and complete; when the mind clings to the good, then even a lifetime of diligent effort stops at half-good and no more. For example, in relieving others with wealth, when inwardly one does not see oneself, outwardly one does not see the other, and in between one does not see the goods given, this is called being empty of the three wheels, this is called a single mind of purity; then a measure of grain can plant boundless blessings, and a single coin can dissolve the sins of a thousand kalpas. But if this mind is not forgotten (if one still clings to the good), then even ten thousand yi of gold brings no full measure of blessing. Long ago a certain woman came to a temple wishing to give but having no wealth; she had only two coins, and she donated them, and the abbot himself performed repentance for her. Later she entered the palace and became rich and noble, and she brought several thousand pieces of gold to the temple to donate, but the abbot only told his disciple to dedicate the merit. She therefore asked: Before, when I gave two coins, you yourself performed repentance for me; now that I give several thousand pieces of gold, you do not dedicate the merit. Why is this? He said: Before, the gift was small but the mind of giving was utterly sincere, and unless this old monk himself performed the repentance, the kindness could not be repaid; now the gift is large but the mind of giving is not as earnest as before, and it is enough for another to perform the repentance on my behalf.
What follows explains how inconceivable is the merit and virtue of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling in marks.

[Subhuti! What do you think—is the space in the east conceivable? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! Is the space in the south, west and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below, conceivable? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! So too is the merit and virtue of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling in marks inconceivable. Subhuti! A bodhisattva should simply abide as taught.]
Subhuti! What do you think—is the space in the east conceivable? No, World-Honored One!”
—The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think—can the vastness of space extending on and on to the east be conceived? Subhuti replied: It cannot be conceived, World-Honored One!

Is it conceivable? No.” Here both occurrences of “no” are read “fou”; “not” in ancient texts is the same as “fou.” Looking through the whole sutra, Subhuti answers “No” in more than ten places, and all of them carry a clear sense of denial, and so it is read “fou ye”; if read “fu ye” by habit, this too is acceptable.
Subhuti! Is the space in the south, west and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below, conceivable? No, World-Honored One!”

—The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think—can the vastness of space extending on and on to the south, the west, the north, the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, the northwest, as well as above and below, be conceived? Subhuti replied: It cannot be conceived, World-Honored One!
[The four intermediate directions] Southeast, northeast, southwest and northwest are called the four intermediate directions.
Subhuti! So too is the merit and virtue of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling in marks inconceivable.”

—The World-Honored One said: Subhuti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are likewise as vast and boundless as the space of the ten directions (east, south, west and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below), and cannot be conceived.
Subhuti! A bodhisattva should simply abide as taught.”
—Therefore, Subhuti! A bodhisattva should simply abide and maintain according to my teaching above (practicing the six paramitas without giving rise to discriminating thoughts about marks).

This makes clear that what was said above is answering the question “How should one abide?” The word “abide” here means abiding and maintaining, and differs in meaning from the “dwell” in the earlier “give without dwelling in forms, give without dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas.” The “dwell” in “give without dwelling in forms, give without dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas” is to dwell the mind on objects, giving rise to discrimination and clinging, arousing love and hate, acceptance and rejection, and being turned about by objects.
At this point the World-Honored One has answered Subhuti’s two great questions:
Question: How should one subdue one’s mind? Answer: To save all living beings without dwelling in marks.

Question: How should one abide? Answer: “Give without dwelling in marks.” Not dwelling in marks is emptiness, giving is compassion; the twin functioning of compassion and emptiness, with giving without dwelling in marks encompassing the whole of the six paramitas—this is the bodhisattva path.
Question: How do we know that this chapter is answering “How should one abide?”
Answer: At the end of this chapter, in summarizing this teaching, the World-Honored One says: “Subhuti! A bodhisattva should simply abide as taught (as taught above).”
Question: Why did the World-Honored One not answer the first question first?

Answer: Because the answer to the second question, “How should one subdue one’s mind?”, is the making of a great vow—saving all living beings without dwelling in marks—whereas the answer to “How should one abide?” is the great practice—giving without dwelling in marks. The great practice is built upon the foundation of the great vow, and so the World-Honored One first speaks of the great vow and then of the great practice.
Question: How can one accomplish giving without dwelling in marks?

Answer: This is what the tenth chapter says: “One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangible objects or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”

blocks.text: Seeing the Truth in Accord with Reality, Chapter Five

inline.s: Seeing the truth in accord with reality” means what the sutra text of this chapter says: “If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata.” In this chapter the World-Honored One further clarifies: Why is it that “thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation”? Why must there be no mark of a self, mark of a person, mark of a living being or mark of a life? Why is it that “a bodhisattva should give thus, without dwelling in marks”? Because: “All marks whatsoever are delusive and false.” And further: “If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata.”

[If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata] If one sees all marks and understands (not merely understands in words) that they are illusory marks, then one sees one’s own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathagata).
[Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by way of bodily form?]
The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think—can living beings, dwelling and clinging to their own physical body (bodily form), see their own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathagata)?
[Dwelling and clinging to one’s own physical body] Deludedly clinging to the physical body as real and thinking that it is oneself.

[Intrinsic nature] The intrinsic nature is also called the Buddha-nature, the original face, and true suchness. The intrinsic nature is the Buddha, and so it is called the Buddha-nature; the intrinsic nature is the original state of one’s own nature, and so it is called the original face, also shortened to “the original”; the intrinsic nature is the original state of one’s own nature, unchanging and constant, and so it is called true suchness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The intrinsic nature is the Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.”
For a detailed discussion of the intrinsic nature, see
“Mind, Intrinsic Nature and Tathagatagarbha”
. [Bodily form]
Refers to the physical body of a living being.
The older commentaries hold that

bodily form” means the Buddha’s thirty-two marks. On this point the layman Jiang Weihong’s Commentary on the Diamond Sutra points out: would not such an interpretation duplicate the later passage on the thirty-two marks? Every word and sentence of the Diamond Sutra has profound meaning; there are certainly no repetitions.
These two words “bodily form” should be taken as referring to the physical body of a living being.
In this passage, the Buddha’s meaning is: You living beings—can you see your own intrinsic nature by way of your own bodily form? [Would this not duplicate the later passage on the thirty-two marks]
In the later “Upholding the Dharma in Accord with the Dharma, Chapter Thirteen,” the sutra says:

“Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by way of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by way of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? What the Tathagata speaks of as the thirty-two marks is no marks; therefore it is called the thirty-two marks.”
Of the various principles set forth in the preceding sutra text, the most essential is the repeated clarification of not dwelling in marks. For example:

“Thus I save countless, numberless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth no living being attains salvation,” “If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva,” “A bodhisattva should give thus, without dwelling in marks”

, and so on. Why, then, should one not dwell in marks? Because only by not dwelling in marks can one realize the intrinsic nature. To realize one part is to be a bodhisattva of the first ground and to be irreversible from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; to realize it to the utmost is to become a Buddha. And among all marks, what living beings care about most and cling to most is their own physical body (bodily form); this is the root cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution and turning about in birth and death. Therefore the World-Honored One here asks suggestively: Can living beings see their intrinsic nature by clinging to the physical body? This is to break the view of the body.
[Clinging to the physical body—this is the root cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution and turning about in birth and death]
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All living beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversions, like a person who has lost his way and takes the four directions to be reversed, deludedly taking the four great elements as the mark of his own body and the shadowy impressions of the six dusts as the mark of his own mind. It is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. The sky in truth has no flowers; the diseased one deludedly clings to them, and because of deluded clinging he is confused not only about the nature of this emptiness but also about where those real flowers arise. From this delusion there is the turning about in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.”

(Translation: All living beings, from beginningless time, their own nature deluded and inverted, give rise to all kinds of inversions, taking the false as real—this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his direction, taking north for south and east for west: he deludedly takes the flesh formed by the four great elements of earth, water, fire and wind as the mark of his own body, and the deliberating mind of the six faculties as they come into contact with the six dusts (the shadowy impressions of the six dusts) as the mark of his own mind. It is like eyes clouded with disease that deludedly see flowers in the sky and a second moon. In reality the sky has no flowers; these are illusions deludedly clung to by the diseased eye. Because of deluded clinging, one not only clings to emptiness as truly existent but also thinks that real flowers truly arise from there. Because living beings, deluded and confused, deludedly take the illusory body and mind as truly existent and cling to them as self, they turn about endlessly in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.)
[View of the body] The wrong view that clings to the body as truly existent.
[No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by way of bodily form. Why is this? What the Tathagata speaks of as bodily form is no bodily form.]

Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One! One cannot see the intrinsic nature by dwelling and clinging to one’s own physical body. Why is this? Because what the Tathagata speaks of as the physical body (the mark exists) is no physical body (the substance is empty); and so the physical body is illusory, and one cannot deludedly take the illusory physical body as real and thereby see one’s own intrinsic nature.
[The Buddha told Subhuti: All marks whatsoever are delusive and false.]
The World-Honored One further taught Subhuti: Not only is the physical body (bodily form) an illusion—all marks whatsoever are likewise illusions.
[All marks whatsoever are delusive and false] All marks are illusions. In the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
this is expounded in detail.
Master Guifeng says:

“That all dharmas are like a dream, all the sages say as one. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the objects of dust are originally empty. This empty and still mind is numinously aware and not benighted. Just this empty and still awareness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not arise depending on conditions, nor does it arise because of objects. The single word ‘know’ is the gate of all wonders. Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about it, one deludedly clings to body and mind as self and gives rise to thoughts of greed, anger and so on. If one meets a good friend who reveals it, one suddenly awakens to this empty and still awareness. Awareness is itself without thought and without form—who then is the mark of a self, the mark of a person? Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, be aware at once; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here. Therefore although one cultivates the myriad practices in full, one takes no-thought alone as the essential. If one attains the knowledge and view of no-thought, then love and hate naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses are naturally cut off, and one’s practice naturally advances. Once one understands all marks as no marks, one naturally practices the practice of no practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death cease. When birth and death have ceased, quiescent illumination appears before one and its responsive function is inexhaustible; this is called a Buddha.”

(The Prolegomenon to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan) [Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, be aware at once; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here] Awakening to the fact that all marks are illusions, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must at once awaken to the fact that one is taking the illusory as real and being turned about by illusory marks. Having awakened to this, the deluded thought immediately vanishes. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here!

Here the World-Honored One tells us the most ultimate truth: all marks whatsoever are neither truly existent nor wholly nonexistent, but are illusions. (They are like things in a dream—not wholly nonexistent, because for the dreamer they truly occur and are truly felt; yet they are not truly existent either. Hence they are named with words such as illusion, delusive and false, and emptiness. People in the world all deludedly cling to marks as real, and so are seduced and driven by them, give rise to delusion and create karma, and suffer the cycle of birth and death to no purpose.)

All marks whatsoever are delusive and false”—this sentence indicates how to contemplate with wisdom; this is the point of entry for upholding the Diamond Sutra. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Knowing illusion, one is at once free, without resorting to expedients; freed from illusion, one is at once awakened, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and living beings of the final age who practice in accordance with this can thus forever leave all illusions.”

This is the crucial point in the practice of upholding the Diamond Sutra—leaving illusion! For example, when watching a 3-D movie, if a tiger suddenly leaps out, one is startled, and then smiles knowingly: it is false! Watch it a few more times and one is unmoved. But when a tiger pursues one closely in a dream, one flees in panic and suffers unbearably, because one has taken it as real. This is the difference between awakening and delusion.

Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the truth of the universe and human life: all marks are illusions. On careful reflection, this is truly astonishing. If so, which of the myriad things in the universe is not an illusion? No wonder the World-Honored One says in the fourteenth chapter:
“If again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such people are most rare.”

From beginningless kalpas living beings have taken “marks” as real, and so the mind is turned about by circumstances, karma is created and retribution received, and they cycle through the six paths. Therefore the World-Honored One tells us to leave marks. To leave marks is: seeing marks without being deluded and without giving rise to thoughts (as a mirror reflects objects), not being turned about by objects, knowing them to be illusions, without love and hate, without grasping at conditions—this is the core of upholding the Diamond Sutra. The Heart Sutra says:

“Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and far removed from inverted and dreamlike thinking, one reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”

Here “prajñāpāramitā” is the wondrous wisdom that clearly knows all marks to be illusory and leaves them—that is, the practice of leaving marks: seeing marks without being deluded and not being turned about by objects.

All marks whatsoever are delusive and false”—this is the reason for and the method of leaving the four marks (the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a living being and the mark of a life): why should one leave the four marks? Because they are all false. How does one leave the four marks? Firmly remember that “all marks whatsoever are delusive and false,” and the moment one sees illusion, leave it, without recourse to expedients.

This is just like watching a television series: if one is deeply absorbed, then along with the illusory situations one’s love and hate, acceptance and rejection, joy, anger, sorrow and happiness go on without cease. From beginningless kalpas, giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution and turning about in birth and death have been just like this. But if, while watching, we remind ourselves: this is false! this is false! and even smile faintly, we will grow more and more unmoved, until we have neither the interest nor the patience to watch the whole series of dozens of episodes. Therefore the method of leaving marks (seeing marks without being deluded and not being turned about by objects) is: constantly contemplate that “all marks whatsoever are delusive and false,” and turn it into one’s own view, into one’s own consciousness, speech and behavior—this is to be awakening. At the same time, whenever circumstances appear before one, constantly remind oneself: body, mind and world are all illusions. In whether or not one “treats them as false and is not turned about by them,” one tests one’s own awakening and skill. Contemplating and testing, testing and contemplating—this is removing habits, this is breaking ignorance, this is practice. Doing this densely and continuously, one is truly as the Sixth Patriarch said: “The disciple’s own mind constantly gives rise to wisdom; not departing from the intrinsic nature, that is the field of blessing.”

Seeing marks without being deluded, one is not harmed by them; seeing marks and falling into delusion, the harm to come is endless. One deluded by wealth dies on account of wealth; one deluded by fame dies on account of fame; one deluded by beauty dies on account of beauty.
[If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata.]
If one sees all marks and understands that they are not real (no marks) but illusory, and is not moved by them, one sees one’s own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathagata).

If one sees all marks as no marks,” deluded thoughts cease of themselves—this is illuminating the mind (clarifying one’s own mind); “then one sees the Tathagata”—this is seeing the nature. The sentence “If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata” is the essential path to illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.
In the
Buddha Treasury Sutra
, Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, the Buddha says:
"To see the true nature of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the true nature of all dharmas? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything to be found."
What is seeing the nature? To see forms and know them to be illusory, and not to be turned by them, is to see the nature. The
Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
, Chapter Two on Prajñā, says:
"But if within one's own mind one constantly gives rise to right view, so that afflictions and the dust of toil can never stain it, that is seeing the nature."

In this passage of the sutra, the World-Honored One tells Subhuti that not only the bodily form is an illusion—all forms whatsoever are illusions. If, seeing all forms, one recognizes them as illusions (rather than being muddled and taking them as real), one is not turned by circumstances, remains untroubled, and the mad mind suddenly comes to rest, so that one sees the Buddha-nature inherently present in everyone. Understanding the mind and seeing the nature is the heart of Buddhist study and practice. To see the nature is to awaken—to awaken to the fact that all dharmas are illusory. The task that follows is to cultivate in accordance with that awakening, gradually eradicating habitual tendencies, so as to be neither dragged along by thoughts nor turned by circumstances, and thus perfectly to accomplish the fruit of the path.

This teaching—"all forms whatsoever are false and unreal; if one sees all forms as not forms, one then sees the Tathagata"—is enormously important! If we now constantly train our own minds, understanding that all forms are illusions, no longer chasing after conditions, no longer craving, no longer grasping, and our minds become wholly empty and pure, then when this physical body decays and the four elements (earth, water, fire and wind) disperse, the consciousness, once it emerges, will be able to be its own master, and will not be turned by circumstances or enter a womb. In life one is free and at ease, and after death, however illusory circumstances transform themselves, there is no mind left to be stirred. If one can be like this, one can then give forth a great radiance that illuminates the ten directions, come and go freely, and respond to conditions and to the needs of beings with perfect ease—this is truly to end birth and death. The Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says:

"When an ordinary person is about to die, one need only contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty, that the four elements are without self, and that the true mind is without marks, neither coming nor going: at birth the nature does not come, at death the nature does not depart—serene and perfectly quiescent, mind and circumstances are one suchness. If one can in this way awaken directly and suddenly, not bound by the three periods of time, then one is a person who has transcended the world."

Therefore, so long as the minds of sentient beings let go of everything, they attain great freedom. "Before the eyes, each thing is divided into fair and foul; in the end, nothing whatsoever has to do with one." At every time and in every place, see through (all forms are not forms) and let go (do not be turned by circumstances)—see through and let go. The Mahasatipatthana Sutra says: "One has cultivated to the point of the state in which there is only knowing and only awareness, transcending attachment and no longer craving anything in the world of body and mind."

This section explains why one should leave forms and dwell in nothing: seeing forms without delusion, not being turned by circumstances. For in leaving forms and dwelling in nothing, besides merit and virtue beyond measure, there is a still more profound reason, namely that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal," and moreover that "if one sees all forms as not forms, one then sees the Tathagata." In the fourteenth section it is said further:
"Leaving all forms, one is then called a Buddha."

Yet it must be especially noted that so-called leaving forms means not clinging to forms, not annihilating them. To cling to forms is to fall into existence; to annihilate forms is to fall into emptiness—these are the common failings of all sentient beings. The correct way is neither to cling to forms nor to annihilate them, but to use illusion to leave illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream awakens. Thus the absence of the four marks means leaving these four marks (not clinging to them), not annihilating them: one should use forms without being used by forms.
Question: Why is it said that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal"?
Answer: In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the World-Honored One gave this teaching:
"All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes east for west and south for north
(mistaking the directions, east and west, south and north—a simile for taking the false as true and the unreal as real)

, and falsely take the four elements as the marks of their own body, and the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects as the marks of their own mind. It is like a person with a diseased eye who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon."

(The "shadowy reflections of the six sense objects" are the images that arise in dependence on the six sense objects, that is, the conceptions and deluded thoughts that arise when the six sense faculties meet the six sense objects. They exist because of the objects, and cease when the objects cease; hence they are called "shadows.")

"The sky is in fact without flowers; the sick person falsely clings to them. Because of that false clinging, he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this empty space, but also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he turns around in birth and death, and this is called ignorance
(because he revolves with circumstances and falsely undergoes birth and death, it is called ignorance)
. This ignorance has no truly existing substance
(ignorance is not truly existent; it is an illusion)

Many sutras and treatises discuss the dream of ignorance: all sentient beings are within the dream of ignorance, while the Tathagatas have exhausted the dream of ignorance and, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, freely manifest all manner of Buddha-work to deliver sentient beings. For example:

Master Hanshan says: "The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha's, originally undefiled and without any marks of birth, death, coming or going. But because of the first non-awakening, one is deluded about one's own nature, and this is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all manner of deluded thoughts arise, all manner of inversions, creating all manner of karma, and falsely grasping the suffering of birth and death within the three realms. All of this is ignorance (all of this ignorance), not understanding one's own mind, turning with deluded thoughts—like a person in deep sleep having all manner of evil dreams, with all manner of states and all manner of terror, all manner of suffering beyond endurance. And when he wakes, he seeks for the things of the dream and can find nothing at all. Thus sentient beings fall into the dream of ignorance, turn about with deluded thoughts, create all manner of karma, and bring all manner of suffering upon themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could any of these inverted states be found?" (
Dream Roam Collection,
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang)
The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Tathagata of the Great and Vast says:
"All Tathagatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish immeasurable great and mighty spiritual powers, and even penetrate to the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are illusory)

, and are able to manifest all manner of sovereign affairs throughout all Buddha-lands in the ten directions. It is like a person who in a dream sees all manner of transformations, and when he wakes, none of what he saw exists. Ordinary beings are likewise: because of the dream of ignorance, they falsely give rise to the notion of real entities in regard to all dharmas. The Buddhas, having awakened, cling to nothing at all, and so are able, throughout all worlds in the ten directions, to manifest in a single thought immeasurable Buddha-work, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing to accomplishment all sentient beings, leading them all to penetrate and enter the immeasurable, profound and wonderful gates of liberation."
The Sutra of the Secret Adornment of the Mahayana says:
"Forms in a dream
(form objects—things that can be seen)

are only falsely seen by the imagination, and when one wakes they do not exist. In the dream of ignorance one sees all manner of forms, of men and women and so on; but when one attains perfect enlightenment, none of them is seen—just as when the skin and leaves of a plantain tree are stripped away, there is nothing real within."
The
Sutra of the Divination of the Wholesome and Unwholesome Karmic Retributions says:

"If among such sentient beings there are those in whom the perfuming of the dharma-body has power, their afflictions gradually grow thin, they are able to weary of the world and seek the path of nirvāṇa, believe in and return to the one reality, and cultivate the six paramitas and all the dharmas that pertain to enlightenment; such a one is called a bodhisattva. If among such bodhisattvas one cultivates all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment and ultimately attains liberation from the sleep of ignorance, that one is instead called a Buddha."
It also says:

"Because all practices of merit are fulfilled, one becomes a Buddha. That is to say, relying on the ultimate bodhisattva ground, one is able to eliminate all obstructions, because the dream of ignorance is exhausted
(because the dream of ignorance has awakened)
The
Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
, fascicle five hundred and seventy-six, says:

"If all sentient beings could truly and thoroughly understand that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, they should originally have already realized supreme enlightenment; but because sentient beings cannot thoroughly understand that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, they turn about in birth and death within the various destinies. It is like a master illusionist who, according to whatever materials he relies on, conjures all manner of illusory transformations—namely the world, the deva Mara
(short for the son-of-heaven Mara, that is, Mara Papman, king of the sixth heaven of the realm of desire)
, Brahma and Indra
(Great Brahma Heaven King and Indra. Great Brahma Heaven King is the king of the heaven of the first dhyana; Indra is the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven),
shramanas and brahmins
(referring to renunciants of all the non-Buddhist paths)
, nagas and yakshas
(that is, yakshas)
, asuras
(that is, asuras)

and other hosts of humans and non-humans. The foolish and deluded grasp them as truly existing; the wise and the illusionist know they have no real nature, and that there are only all manner of false appearances. Thus, although all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, sentient beings are foolish and do not understand, counting the non-existent as existent and the impermanent as permanent, and making all manner of discriminations among dharmas—discriminating form or discriminating mind, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the outflows and the non-outflows, and all such kinds of discrimination. Because of these discriminations, they do not know all dharmas as they really are, as like illusions and transformations, and because they
do not know, they turn about in birth and death."
Master Hanshan's
Dream Roam Collection,
Reply to the Magistrate Yuan Cangru says:

"In the bodhisattva's cultivation, even up to the seventh ground, one has not yet shattered the dream of ignorance. All the teaching of sentient beings and the accomplishing of pure lands are Buddha-work within a dream. Thus the bodhisattva of the eighth ground, like one crossing a river in a dream, has not yet attained waking; only at Buddhahood is one called the Greatly Awakened. This is clearly stated and fully recorded in the Avatamsaka Sutra—plain and evident proof."
Question: "All forms whatsoever are false and unreal." Then if I pierce you with a needle, does it hurt or not?

Answer: Of course it hurts, because we are still within the dream of ignorance. If the dream of ignorance were awakened, there would be no body and no needle either—so where would any hurting or not hurting come from? The Song of Enlightenment says:
"In the dream, the six destinies plainly appear; after awakening, the vast thousand-world realm is empty."

In this section the World-Honored One teaches that those who give rise to true faith in this sutra are exceedingly rare, and that they obtain merit and virtue beyond measure. He also points out who is able truly to believe in and uphold the Diamond Sutra.
[Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, will there be many sentient beings who, hearing such words and phrases, give rise to true faith?]
Subhuti said to the Buddha"

—Subhuti respectfully put his question to the Buddha. Wherever this sutra has "Subhuti said to the Buddha," it is to mark a matter of grave importance and to stress that what is said is of the utmost consequence. "Said to" is what a subordinate says to a superior.
World-Honored One, will there be many sentient beings who, hearing such words and phrases, give rise to true faith?

"—World-Honored One, will there be many sentient beings who are fortunate enough to hear this true principle that you have spoken—"all forms whatsoever are false and unreal; if one sees all forms as not forms, one then sees the Tathagata"—and will they truly understand and truly believe it?

[Will there be many sentient beings] There will be many sentient beings. [Many] Very, quite—as in "quite agrees with it." [Words and phrases] The ancients, in analyzing and expounding the classics (for example, the Four Books and Five Classics and so on), mostly called their explanations "words and phrases." Here the two words "words and phrases" refer to the principle spoken of above. [True faith] True faith is not a vague, drifting sort of faith; one must be able to understand the true meaning of such words and phrases before faith can arise.

Throughout life after life, human beings have taken all things to be real. Now the World-Honored One declares that all of it is illusion. Subhuti's wisdom has already opened, so naturally he believes it; but can sentient beings believe it?

Before the sixteenth century, people believed that the planets and the sun revolved around the earth. When Copernicus, on the basis of astronomical observation, proposed that the planets and the earth all revolve around the sun, people found it hard to accept—and Bruno was even burned to death for holding to this truth! When truth conflicts with common sense and experience, truth is hard to accept. That is why, in the fourteenth section, the Buddha says: "If again there are people who, hearing this sutra, are neither alarmed, nor frightened, nor terrified, you should know that such people are exceedingly rare."
Yet if one does not know that one is within a deluded dream, how can one ever wake from that deluded dream?

The Elder Subhuti, of course, understood the World-Honored One's teaching in his heart, but for the sake of sentient beings in the age of the Dharma's decline, he put forth this question, his compassion and wisdom working as one: World-Honored One, will sentient beings who have the good fortune to hear such words and phrases be able to give rise to true faith? That is: will they believe that what the World-Honored One has said is true, and also believe that they themselves can uphold and practice it and wake from the deluded dream?

Here the Elder, with compassion and wisdom working as one, asks about this matter (what sort of people can uphold the Diamond Sutra—since the principle the World-Honored One has spoken above is so profound, must those who can give rise to true faith necessarily be of the highest faculties and keenest wisdom, or need they not be?). This is to remove the doubt of us sentient beings whose obstructions are deep and whose wisdom is shallow, so that we do not belittle ourselves and mistakenly think our faculties are insufficient, and so miss this opportunity to uphold the sutra that is hard to meet in a hundred million kalpas. Reading to this point, one feels an inexpressible gratitude!

[The Buddha told Subhuti: Do not speak thus. After the Tathagata's passing, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, and who will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases, taking them as true.]
The Buddha told Subhuti: Do not speak thus!"
The Buddha said to Subhuti: You should not speak in this way! (The World-Honored One's tone was very weighty.)

After the Tathagata's passing, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, and who will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases, taking them as true."

The teaching above means that after my parinirvāṇa, up to the fifth five-hundred-year period and the age of the Dharma's decline that follows, those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit (they need not be of the highest faculties and keenest wisdom, nor widely learned in the scriptures) will be able to give rise to faith and understand that this is true speech.

This shows that ordinary people who practice by observing the precepts and cultivating merit will surely receive the Buddha's blessing, and will then be able to give rise to faith and take this as true.

[After the Tathagata's passing, the last five hundred years] The five five-hundred-year periods after the Buddha's passing; within each period there is a certain "firmness." In the first five hundred years, liberation is firm. At that time the true Dharma flourished; practitioners did not attack other teachings but devoted themselves solely to the Mahayana, benefiting sentient beings, and many attained liberation. In the second five hundred years, meditative concentration is firm. At that time many practitioners deeply cultivated meditative concentration. In the third five hundred years, much learning is firm. At that time practitioners observed the precepts but little, were lax in cultivating meditative concentration, and prized only wide learning, understanding the teachings through words. In the fourth five hundred years, stupas and temples are firm. At that time practitioners cultivated meditative concentration but little, delighted in planting fields of merit, broadly formed good affinities, and built many stupas and temples. In the fifth five hundred years, contention is firm. At that time practitioners do not cultivate the precepts but prize only contention, increasing wrong views. "After the Tathagata's passing, in the last five hundred years" means the fifth five-hundred-year period after the Tathagata's passing and thereafter. "Cultivating merit" means cutting off evil and accumulating good. Observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the foundation for cultivating world-transcending dharmas, and so any practitioner who earnestly cultivates world-transcending dharmas can uphold the Diamond Sutra. [Taking them as true] Believing and revering this as truth.

From this we can know that the Diamond Sutra is exceedingly well suited to today's practitioners: one need only observe the precepts and cultivate merit, believe deeply and practice in person, and one can sail before the wind along the bodhi path. We are now in the age of the Dharma's decline, when sentient beings' obstructions are deep and their wisdom shallow; yet to uphold the Diamond Sutra brings merit and virtue beyond conception, and above all opens wisdom and reveals the true nature, and is the most able to shatter delusion and open awakening. What is more, the World-Honored One tells us in "Chapter Sixteen: Capable of Purifying Karmic Obstructions" that even those who, because of past offenses, should fall into the evil destinies, can uphold the Diamond Sutra, and thereby realize the fruit of Buddhahood:

"Good sons and good daughters who uphold, read and recite this sutra, if they are despised by others, do so because of offenses committed in former lives, offenses that should cause them to fall into the evil destinies. Because in this present life they are despised by others, those former offenses are thereby extinguished
, and they shall attain supreme, perfect enlightenment."

Question: As said above, one need only observe the precepts and cultivate merit to be able to uphold the Diamond Sutra. Then how should we understand the words in the fifteenth section, that this sutra "is spoken by the Tathagata for those who have set their minds on the Mahayana, and is spoken for those who have set their minds on the supreme vehicle"?

Answer: Pay special attention to the two occurrences of "set their minds on" in this sentence. "Is spoken by the Tathagata for those who have set their minds on the Mahayana, and is spoken for those who have set their minds on the supreme vehicle" means: this sutra is spoken by the Tathagata for those who have set their minds on upholding the Mahayana Buddha-Dharma, and for those who have set their minds on upholding the supreme vehicle Buddha-Dharma. So only the arousing of the mind is considered, not one's faculties. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "If one meets the Tathagata's supreme bodhi and the path of true cultivation, then whatever one's faculties, great or small, all attain the fruit of Buddhahood." The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records: "The Master (the Fifth Patriarch of Chan, Hongren) constantly urged monks and laypeople alike to simply uphold the Diamond Sutra, and thereby see their own nature and directly realize Buddhahood."

The World-Honored One's teaching also tells us that observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the foundation for upholding the Diamond Sutra. So when we feel confused in upholding the Diamond Sutra and find it hard to begin, this shows that the afflictions of our own minds are coarse and heavy, and we must make up the lesson in observing the precepts and cultivating merit. The
Vimalakirti Sutra
says: "Observing the precepts is the bodhisattva's pure land."

Merit is the practitioner's provision on the bodhi path. To walk the path without cultivating merit is to meet with obstructions and difficulties in abundance; when merit and practice support each other, there is nowhere one does not succeed. Creating evil and receiving calamity come about through body, speech and mind; cultivating good and obtaining merit likewise come about through body, speech and mind. Therefore practitioners should cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action—this is observing the precepts and cultivating merit; this is the root of studying Buddhism, the foundation. The firmer the foundation, the more secure the superstructure; if the foundation is poor, there is no way to continue building upward.

Why is it that those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit can "take this as true"? Layman Jiang Weinong's Commentary on the Diamond Sutra says: "Some say that observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the root of cultivating prajñā, first blocking off one-sided emptiness. This is certainly so, and yet there is still a doubt. The sutra plainly says 'take this as true'; after all, these two kinds of people (the two kinds who observe the precepts and cultivate merit) are deficient in wisdom and understanding—how could they understand the true essential meaning of this sutra? Here there is an important principle. Why? Because they receive the Buddha's blessing. Such people are the faculties and capacities chosen and settled upon by the Buddha; if they can practice according to the Buddha's teaching, observing the precepts and cultivating merit, they will surely receive the Buddha's blessing, and will then be able to take this as true. Students of Buddhism must, in walking, standing, sitting and lying down, at all times, seek the blessing of the Three Jewels. Whatever practice one cultivates, it is always so. Even when lecturing on the sutras one must set aside one's ordinary views and knowledge and seek the blessing of the Three Jewels. To be free of this notion is to have not yet given rise to faith. Even in Buddha-recitation: at the time of reciting, one must cast aside all one's ordinary views and knowledge, so that in the mind there is nothing at all, and one single-mindedly seeks Amitābha's blessing. ... The ancients, in writing books, mostly opened with words seeking the blessing of the Three Jewels. When great bodhisattvas composed treatises, before the treatise they too acknowledged the power of the Buddha's awe-inspiring spiritual might. This is true and not vain, and is neither dependency nor superstition. If one lacks such a notion, then a self-view remains, obstructing one's own spiritual nature—how then can a book or treatise be thoroughgoing? Therefore one must wholly set aside the self-view."

Whether one truly believes the true principle taught by the World-Honored One is reflected in our thoughts, words and actions, and so one must closely examine and test (be aware of) oneself in body, speech and mind—this is where the effort lies.

[You should know that such people have not planted wholesome roots with one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four or five Buddhas, but have already planted all wholesome roots in the presence of immeasurable thousands upon thousands of Buddhas.]

You should know that these people who "can give rise to faith and take this as true" have not planted wholesome roots with only one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four or five Buddhas, but have already planted all wholesome roots in the presence of immeasurable thousands upon thousands of Buddhas.
[Wholesome roots] The goodness of the three karmas of body, speech and mind; because it can produce wonderful fruits, it is called a wholesome root.

In fact, among students of Buddhism, those who have already planted wholesome roots in the presence of immeasurable thousands upon thousands of Buddhas are everywhere. Yet alas, in this life they fail to attain accomplishment, and in the next life there is again the delusion of passing through a womb, so that they practice life after life and transmigrate life after life, rising and sinking without end. Whenever one thinks of this, sorrow rises from within, and one feels all the more how precious is the Pure Land method by which anyone can
attain accomplishment in this very life

! Recite the Buddha's name and leave forms (see forms without delusion, do not be turned by circumstances); leave forms and recite the Buddha's name—this is the shortcut within shortcuts. (The shortcut within shortcuts indeed!)

Now, happily having heard this sutra, we too are those who have planted wholesome roots in the presence of immeasurable thousands upon thousands of Buddhas. Were it not so, this profound and wonderful prajñā could not be heard; and even if heard, one would not know what one had heard. The wholesome causes of former kalpas cannot be known, but the supreme condition of the present moment must not be lost! If one does not firmly seize this supreme condition, but willingly takes oneself to be inferior and gives rise to thoughts of difficulty and obstruction, then even though one has wholesome roots from past lives, they will be cut off; once this human body is lost, it is hard to regain in ten thousand kalpas, and one drifts ever further away. Now that one has come to the place of treasures, do not return empty-handed—be careful! Be careful! Would any wise person, knowing this to be the place of treasures, fail to seek them and go on complaining of loneliness and poverty?

The human body is hard to obtain and present circumstances are easily lost. May all who hear this never belittle themselves, but surely together arouse a deeply earnest mind, strive and advance, and never let this great opportunity fly past before their eyes and beneath their feet!
[Hearing these words and phrases, even down to a single thought of pure faith, Subhuti, the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees: such sentient beings obtain merit and virtue beyond measure.]

The World-Honored One said: Hearing these words and phrases, even down to a single thought of pure faith, Subhuti, I very clearly know and very clearly see that the merit and virtue obtained by such sentient beings is already beyond measure!

[A single thought of pure faith] In whatever place one hears, one suddenly opens and understands, and thereupon awakens and enters; one believes and understands without doubt, and there is no obstruction. Here "a single thought" means having no other thought.
[Pure faith] Believing sincerely, without the slightest doubt.
In the True Mind Direct Teaching there is a passage on faith and understanding that is very important for how to uphold the Diamond Sutra. It is excerpted as follows:

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: Faith is the mother of the source of the path and of merit; it nurtures all wholesome roots. The Consciousness-Only teaching also says: Faith is like a pearl of clear water, able to purify muddy water. From this we know that when all good qualities arise, faith is the guide; hence the Buddhist scriptures open with (that is, at the very beginning) "Thus have I heard," which is what giving rise to faith means.

Someone asks: Is the faith of the ancestral gate (the Chan school) different from the faith of the doctrinal gate (the teaching schools)? The answer: there are many differences. The doctrinal gate causes gods and humans to believe in cause and effect. Those who love blessings and happiness believe the ten wholesome actions to be the wonderful cause and gods and humans to be the happy fruit. Those who delight in emptiness and stillness believe arising-and-ceasing causes and conditions to be the right cause and the truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation and the path to be the noble fruit. Those who delight in the Buddha-fruit believe the three kalpas ("three kalpas" is short for the three great asamkhyeya kalpas, the time a bodhisattva must pass through in cultivation to attain Buddhahood) and the six paramitas to be the great cause and bodhi and nirvāṇa to be the right fruit. The true faith of the ancestral gate is not the same as these: it does not believe in any conditioned cause and effect whatsoever, but only asks one to believe that one is originally a Buddha, that the innocent and natural self-nature is complete in everyone, and that the wonderful substance of nirvāṇa is perfectly accomplished in each—not sought from another, but always and originally complete in oneself. (This is the basis of the unconditioned dharma—sentient beings are dreaming that they are poor children; one need only wake, and everything is already complete.) The Third Patriarch says: It is round and identical with great emptiness, without lack or surplus; it is only because of grasping and rejecting (being deluded by marks and chasing circumstances) that it is not so. Master Zhigong says: Within the body of marks there is the body without marks; on the road of ignorance there is no path of the unborn. Yongjia says: The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is the dharma-body. Thus we know that sentient beings are originally Buddhas.

Since true faith has arisen, one must let understanding nourish it (one must have understanding to nourish it). Yongming says: Faith without understanding increases ignorance; understanding without faith increases wrong views. Thus we know that when faith and understanding accompany each other, one enters the path swiftly. Someone asks: If one has just given rise to faith but cannot yet enter the path, is there any benefit? The answer: the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says that if a person, having heard this dharma, does not become timid or weak, you should know that such a person will surely continue the Buddha's lineage and will be prophesied by all Buddhas. Even if there were a person able to transform all the sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm so that they practice the ten wholesome actions, he would not equal one who for a single moment rightly contemplates this dharma; the merit of the latter surpasses the former beyond all comparison (the latter's merit far exceeds the former's, beyond all telling). The Prajñā Sutra also says: Even one who gives rise to a single thought of pure faith is fully known and fully seen by the Tathagata, and such sentient beings obtain merit and virtue beyond measure. From this we know: to travel a thousand li, the first step must be right; if the first step is wrong, the whole thousand li are wrong. To enter the land of the unconditioned, the first faith must be right. Once the first faith is lost, all good qualities retreat. Hence the patriarchs say: A hairsbreadth's difference, and heaven and earth are set apart. This is the principle."

[The ancestral gate and the doctrinal gate] The ancestral gate refers specifically to the Chan school, which transmits mind to mind; the doctrinal gate refers to all the theories and methods under Śākyamuni Buddha's spoken teachings. Of the eight schools, all except Chan belong to the doctrinal gate. The ancestral gate stresses understanding the mind and seeing the nature, while the doctrinal gate stresses opening wide and perfect understanding. [The eight schools] The Vinaya, Huayan, Tiantai, Sanlun, Faxiang, Zhenyan (Esoteric), Chan and Pure Land schools.

[Why is this? These sentient beings no longer have the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan; they have no mark of dharmas, and also no mark of non-dharmas.]

Why do these sentient beings obtain merit and virtue beyond measure? Because these sentient beings truly believe and understand that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal," and so they no longer cling to the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a lifespan as real; they do not falsely cling to the dharma of the path as truly existing, and still less do they negate the dharma of the path and falsely cling to it as non-existent.

[The mark of dharmas] Falsely clinging to all dharmas (including the dharma of the path) as truly existing. [The dharma of the path] The dharma of cultivation, that is, the dharma for ending birth and death and realizing nirvāṇa. [The mark of non-dharmas] Negating all dharmas (including the dharma of the path), falsely clinging to all dharmas as non-existent, and sinking into stubborn emptiness

. "Master Zhao says: 'No mark of dharmas' means clarifying that dharmas are not existent, dispelling the mind that clings to existence. 'Also no mark of non-dharmas' means clarifying that dharmas are not non-existent, dispelling the mind that clings to non-existence."

(From the Great Compendium of the Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra.) [Master Zhao] Sengzhao, one of the four philosophers among the disciples of Master Kumarajiva, the translator of this sutra. [No mark of dharmas, and also no mark of non-dharmas] This means that the two extremes of existence and non-existence are both left behind. Practicing in this way, one clings neither to dharmas nor to non-dharmas. This is not clinging to either extreme, and accords with the middle way.

This sentence says: these sentient beings will no longer cling to all marks as real. This is understanding-awakening, not yet realization-awakening. Because habitual tendencies from beginningless kalpas are deep-rooted and firmly fixed, they are hard to cut off at once; though one knows in principle that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal," when one meets adverse or favorable circumstances, anger and delight, right and wrong will still arise again. One must cultivate gradually after awakening, using prajñā's contemplation to strive to remove habits, and only then can one gradually realize awakening. As it is said: "The principle can be awakened to suddenly; the matter must be removed gradually."

Therefore, if this sentence is understood as "these sentient beings no longer have the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan, and have no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas," then these sentient beings, having left all marks, should be in the Buddha's state. (The fourteenth section says: "Leaving all forms, one is then called a Buddha.") So "these sentient beings no longer have the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan, and have no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas" means that these sentient beings have already truly believed and understood that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal," have understood that there should no longer be the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a lifespan, the mark of dharmas or the mark of non-dharmas, and accordingly, with "no mark of self, mark of a person, mark of sentient beings or mark of a lifespan, no mark of dharmas and no mark of non-dharmas" as the clear goal, actually cultivate by leaving marks.

Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have clung to marks as real, and so there are the two deaths (delimited birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death). Even in studying Buddhism, most cultivate by clinging to marks, seeking the fruit of non-attainment with a mind that seeks attainment. Now, truly to believe and understand no mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a lifespan, no mark of dharmas and no mark of non-dharmas, and further to cultivate in fact by leaving marks—this is an exceedingly great leap forward. The Song of Enlightenment says:

"Awakening is itself the end; no effort is applied. All conditioned dharmas are not the same. Giving while dwelling in marks produces heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow upward into the sky: when its force is spent, the arrow falls back, bringing an unwished-for next life. How much better the gate of the unconditioned and true reality, where one leaps straight into the Tathagata's ground."

[Why is this? These sentient beings, if their minds grasp at marks, then they cling to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan. If they grasp at the mark of dharmas, then they cling to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan. Why is this? If they grasp at the mark of non-dharmas, then they cling to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan. Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at non-dharmas.]
Why is this? These sentient beings, if their minds grasp at marks, then they cling to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan."
—Why? Because if one falsely clings to circumstances and conditions as truly existing, one clings to the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a lifespan.

Why should one not grasp and cling to the marks of circumstances and conditions? If these sentient beings' minds grasp at marks, then who is doing the grasping? It is the "I" (falsely clinging to body and mind as self) that grasps. Once the mark of self is established, the other three marks follow along (and so one clings to the four marks), and then one is deluded within the dream of ignorance, with no time of escape. This is the World-Honored One's admonition: one must not grasp at marks.
If they grasp at the mark of dharmas, then they cling to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan."
—Likewise, if one grasps at the mark of dharmas, one clings to the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a lifespan.

Likewise, then who is grasping at the mark of dharmas? It is the "I" that grasps. Once the mark of self is established, the other three marks follow along (and so one clings to the four marks), and then one is deluded within the dream of ignorance, with no time of escape. This is the World-Honored One's admonition: one must not grasp at the mark of dharmas.
Why is this? If they grasp at the mark of non-dharmas, then they cling to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan."

—Why must one not negate the dharma of the path? If these sentient beings negate the dharma of the path, they cling to the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a lifespan.

Likewise, then who is negating the dharma of the path? It is the "I" that negates. Once the mark of self is established, the other three marks follow along (and so one clings to the four marks), and then one is deluded within the dream of ignorance, with no time of escape. This is the World-Honored One's admonition: one must not grasp at the mark of non-dharmas.
Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at non-dharmas."

—From this the conclusion is drawn: "Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at non-dharmas."—So one must neither cling to the dharma of the path as real, nor still less negate the dharma of the path. This is the World-Honored One's earnest instruction to those who give rise to pure faith.

Grasping at the mark of dharmas is clinging to marks; grasping at the mark of non-dharmas is annihilating marks. Therefore one should neither cling to the dharma of the path nor negate it, but use it as a boat—and never, entering the sea, count sand and fail to take the treasure. Master Yongjia's Song of Enlightenment says: "Discriminating names and marks without knowing to stop, one vainly troubles oneself, counting sand in the sea."
[For this reason the Tathagata always says: You bhikshus, you should know that the dharma I teach is like the parable of the raft; even the dharma should be let go, how much more so non-dharmas.]

Because of this principle, I always say: Bhikshus, you know that I often use a boat as a parable for all dharmas. A boat is used to cross a river; one must use it to cross, and on reaching the far shore one should let it go—one should not, out of deluded attachment to this boat, refuse to let it go and go ashore. The dharma of the path, which has marks but no substance (like a raft), should not be clung to and held fast—how much less should one negate the dharma of the path (not using the raft at all)?

Here the World-Honored One admonishes: all dharmas are for use, and should not be clung to. It is like crossing a river: one should neither, on reaching the shore, refuse to let go of the raft, nor refuse to use the raft to cross. This is to break the two biased views of clinging to dharmas as existent and clinging to them as non-existent.

[Raft] A raft of logs bound together and used as a boat. [The dharma is like the parable of the raft] Here "dharma" means the dharma of the path. The Arittha Sutra, the fifty-fifth in the Agama, says: "In the mountains the waters were very deep, and there was no boat or bridge. A man wished to cross from this shore to the other, and bound a raft and rode it across. When he reached the far shore, he thought: 'This raft has benefited me; I cannot let it go; I should carry it on my back and go.' What do you think? Was there any benefit in the raft? The bhikshus said: No benefit. The Buddha said: If that man were to return this raft to the water, or leave it on the shore, what then? The bhikshus said: There would be benefit. The Buddha said: Just so. I have taught you the parable of the raft throughout the long night, wishing to make you let go, not wishing to make you grasp. If you know that I have taught the parable of the raft throughout the long night, then even that dharma may be let go—how much more non-dharmas?" [Non-dharmas] Negating the dharma of the path and sinking into stubborn emptiness.

Non-dharmas" has two meanings: first, negating the dharma of the path; second, dharmas that are not the right path. Which meaning is intended must be carefully discerned from the context. For this passage of the sutra, Master Xuanzang's translation (the
Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,

fascicle five hundred and seventy-seven) reads: "Why is this? Subhuti, these bodhisattvas no longer have the notion of self, the notion of sentient beings, the notion of a lifespan or the notion of a receiver. These bodhisattvas have no notion of dharmas and no notion of non-dharmas. No notion, and no non-notion. Why is this? Subhuti, if these bodhisattvas have any notion of dharmas, that is clinging to self and to sentient beings, a lifespan and a receiver. Subhuti, therefore bodhisattvas should not grasp at dharmas and should not grasp at non-dharmas. For this reason the Tathagata says that if one who contemplates the practitioner understands the sutra of the parable of the raft, even the dharma should be let go, how much more so non-dharmas?" From this we know that "non-dharmas" in this passage of the sutra means negating the dharma of the path.

The World-Honored One further explains why one "should not grasp at dharmas." Because the Tathagata's realization of the Buddha-fruit is illusory (non-attainment), and the Tathagata's teaching of the dharma is also illusory (non-teaching), it is called "non-attainment and non-teaching."

[Subhuti, what do you think? Has the Tathagata attained supreme, perfect enlightenment? Does the Tathagata teach any dharma? Subhuti said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed dharma called supreme, perfect enlightenment, and there is also no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can teach.]

Subhuti, what do you think? Has the Tathagata attained supreme, perfect enlightenment? Has the Tathagata expounded the dharma? Subhuti replied: As I understand the meaning of the World-Honored One's teaching above that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal," there is no truly existing dharma called supreme, perfect enlightenment, and there is also no truly existing dharma that the Tathagata can teach.
[Fixed dharma] Something that truly and unchangeably exists.
The World-Honored One now raises these two questions to test Subhuti: has he awakened to the true meaning of what was said above, that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal"?
In the eighth section of this sutra the Buddha says: "What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma, and so are called Buddha and Dharma." The
Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

, Chapter Eleven on the Illusory, says: "The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are themselves illusion, and illusion is itself the four foundations of mindfulness—and so on up to supreme, perfect enlightenment, which is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from supreme, perfect enlightenment; supreme, perfect enlightenment is itself illusion, and illusion is itself supreme, perfect enlightenment."

In the fifth section the World-Honored One asked: "Subhuti, what do you think? Can one see the Tathagata by means of bodily form?" Subhuti knew that bodily form is illusory, and so answered with certainty: "No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathagata by means of bodily form. Why? The bodily form spoken of by the Tathagata is not bodily form." But now the World-Honored One asks: Is the Tathagata's realization of the Buddha-fruit real? Is the Tathagata's teaching of the dharma real? Subhuti had always taken them to be real, but since the World-Honored One had just taught that "all forms whatsoever are false and unreal," then by this understanding the Tathagata's realization of the Buddha-fruit is illusory and the Tathagata's teaching of the dharma is also illusory; and so, before answering, he cautiously added a phrase: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said" (as I understand the meaning of what the World-Honored One has said above).

Question: "There is no fixed dharma" means there is no fixed dharma of the path. The World-Honored One gives medicine according to the illness; sentient beings' illnesses differ, and so the prescriptions differ too—this is what is meant by "dharmas have no fixed dharma." Why then is "fixed dharma" explained here as "a dharma that truly exists"?

Answer: Your statement that "the World-Honored One gives medicine according to the illness; sentient beings' illnesses differ, and so the prescriptions differ too—this is what is meant by 'dharmas have no fixed dharma'" is correct, but it is not appropriate to use it here and explain "there is no fixed dharma" as "there is no fixed dharma of the path." To do so not only fails to answer the question but also breaks the coherence of the meaning above and below. Compare the corresponding passage in the Tang dynasty
Yijing's translation:

"Miaosheng (that is, Subhuti)! What do you think? Has the Tathagata attained anything in regard to supreme bodhi? And is there any small dharma that has been taught? Miaosheng said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, the Tathagata has in truth attained nothing in regard to supreme bodhi, and has also taught nothing." In the
Buddha Treasury Sutra
, Chapter Four on Recollection of the Sangha, the Buddha says: "In the supreme meaning there is nothing fixed and real."
[Why is this? The dharmas taught by the Tathagata can all be neither grasped nor spoken. They are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.]

Why is it said that "there is also no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can teach"? Because all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever, ungraspable. Therefore the dharmas taught by the Tathagata can all be neither clung to nor spoken. The dharma of the path is without substance (not a dharma) and yet has marks (not a non-dharma); therefore the dharma of the path is illusory.

[All can be neither grasped] One must not falsely cling to the dharma of the path as truly existing. [Nor spoken] It cannot be put into words. That dharma spoken of by the Tathagata cannot be expressed in speech, and so it is called unspoken. The path is originally beyond words, yet without words it is not revealed; so it is spoken only as a last resort. Therefore when the Tathagata expounds the sutras and teaches the dharma he must use words and language—this is pointing at the moon with a finger; but one who hears the dharma and cultivates must leave the marks of words and language, and see the moon because of the finger; only this is the right path. That is to say, in reciting sutras and hearing the dharma one uses the guidance of words and language to realize and awaken to the dharma that words and language cannot express, and one must grasp the meaning beyond the words. Here "unspoken" means that the dharma of the path spoken of by the Tathagata is the finger pointing at the moon, and is not the dharma of ultimate liberation itself. Therefore one should not take the "finger" as the "moon," but should follow the finger and see the moon. [Not a dharma, not a non-dharma] "Dharma" means the dharma of the path. "Not a dharma" means that the dharma of the path is without substance and cannot be clung to as real; "not a non-dharma" means that the dharma of the path has marks, and one must also not cling to non-dharma (negating the dharma of the path). The dharma of the path is an illusion with marks but no substance (all of it is a matter within the dream of ignorance), and should be used well, using illusion to leave illusion—riding the raft to cross the river, and letting go of the raft on reaching the shore.

This passage says: the dharmas taught by the Tathagata are in no way truly existent, and also cannot be spoken; one should neither cling to dharmas nor cling to non-dharmas. Chan Master Huangbo's Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "Dharmas are originally non-existent; do not hold the view of non-existence. Dharmas are originally not non-existent; do not hold the view of existence. Existence (clinging to marks) and non-existence (annihilating marks) are both views of feeling, like an illusory film over the eye (the film that produces illusion)."
Because this passage of the sutra is of the utmost importance for understanding and practice, let us discuss it further in detail.

The dharmas taught by the Tathagata can all be neither grasped nor spoken" has two meanings: first, one must not falsely cling to the dharma of the path as truly existing ("the dharmas taught by the Tathagata can all be neither grasped"), for example, one must not falsely cling to supreme, perfect enlightenment and the Tathagata's teaching of the dharma as truly existing; second, the dharma of the path is a finger pointing at the moon, not the moon itself ("the dharmas taught by the Tathagata ... cannot be spoken").

The dharmas taught by the Tathagata can all be neither grasped" was already explained in detail in the previous section when it spoke of "one should not grasp at dharmas (one should not cling to dharmas)." As for understanding "the dharmas taught by the Tathagata cannot be spoken," the simile of the "finger and the moon" may be used. The "finger" is a simile for the scriptural teachings (what the Tathagata has spoken), and the "moon" is a simile for that path which the scriptural teachings are meant to speak of; practitioners should awaken to the path by relying on the words (the path can be awakened to but not spoken). The Surangama Sutra says: "It is like a person who points at the moon with his hand to show another. That person, because of the finger, should look at the moon. If instead he looks at the finger and takes it to be the substance of the moon, then not only does he fail to see the moon, he also fails to understand the finger. (Such a person not only does not see the moon, he does not understand what the finger means. This is to say that one who falsely clings to the words and language of the scriptural teachings without awakening to the path not only fails to attain the path, but also loses the meaning of the scriptural teachings.) Why is this? Because he takes the pointing finger to be the bright moon. (Because the pointing finger is used to reveal where the moon is, and one must look at the moon oneself.)" The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "The sutra teachings (the scriptural teachings spoken by the Tathagata) are like a finger pointing at the moon; if one then sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed at is after all not the moon. All the Tathagatas' various speeches and teachings to bodhisattvas are likewise so." The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: "It is like a person who points at the moon with his finger to show a confused person. The confused person looks at the finger and does not look at the moon. Someone says to him: I pointed at the moon with my finger to let you know it; why do you look at the finger and not at the moon? This is likewise so: words are the pointing finger of the meaning, and words are not the meaning." Pointing at the moon with a finger is meant to make people leave words and language and awaken solely to the purport beyond the words.

[Sutra] Translated into Chinese as "jing," the "conforming scripture." "Conforming" means that above it conforms to the wonderful principle of all Buddhas, and below it conforms to the faculties of sentient beings.

In studying the dharma, what is precious is to grasp the purport beyond words, and this must be realized in practice. Master Hanshan says: "The Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world, and with a thousand words and ten thousand phrases and all manner of skillful means, speaking of Chan and speaking of the teachings, do nothing but follow circumstances and capacities—they are tools for breaking clinging (clinging to self and clinging to dharmas), and originally there is no real dharma given to anyone." (
Dream Roam Collection,
Reply to the Censor Zheng Kunyan)

By means of words that can be spoken (the finger), one awakens to the principle that is expounded (the moon). By means of names that can be named, one attains the substance that is expounded; this is to use speech to reveal the path, and so one should understand the sutra in order to grasp its purport.

Therefore the correct attitude in studying the sutras and hearing the dharma is: neither to take the finger as the moon, nor to abandon the finger and pay it no heed, but to see the moon by means of the finger. In learning the scriptural teachings, one should practice thus, in order to understand the Tathagata's true meaning. Chan Master Huangbo sighed and said: "Those who seek knowledge and views are as many as hairs; those who awaken to the path are as few as horns. (The hairs of an ox are numberless, while its horns are but a pair.)" The Master's words are worth our vigilance! In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says: "One who is widely learned and loves the path will find the path hard to meet; one who keeps his resolve and serves the path will find that path very great."
Question: Why does the World-Honored One not directly hold out the "moon" on a tray, but instead point at the "moon"?

Answer: Because the path cannot be expressed in words, nor reasoned about or imagined by the mind; it can only be realized in practice.
