[Words that do not deceive] Words that are not deceitful. [Words that do not vary] A thousand words and ten thousand phrases, consistent from first to last, and wholly consistent with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods. [The dharma attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor void] The dharma attained by the Tathagata is neither truly existent nor annihilated into nothingness, but is an illusion. The “dharma” here means the dharma of the path, that is, the theories, states and fruitions of cultivating the path. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,

Chapter Three on Cultivating Accord, the Buddha says: “There is no Buddha and no Buddha-path either.” In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says: “Good man! When this bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the final age accomplish this mind through cultivation, in this there is neither cultivation nor accomplishment (making clear that cultivation and accomplishment are both illusions). Perfect enlightenment shines universally, quiescent and without duality; within it, hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhya, inexpressible Ganges-sand Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion. Neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor freed—only then does one know that sentient beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like last night’s dream.”

[‘Subhuti, if the mind of a bodhisattva abides in dharmas while giving, it is like a person entering darkness, seeing nothing. If the mind of a bodhisattva does not abide in dharmas while giving, it is like a person with eyes, with the sunlight shining, seeing all manner of forms.]

The mind of a bodhisattva abides in dharmas while giving”—this is the conditioned dharma; “the mind of a bodhisattva does not abide in dharmas while giving”—this is the unconditioned dharma. This passage may be compared with the earlier passage in “Wonderful Practice Without Abiding, Section Four,” “a bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that abides nowhere,” and the understanding will go deeper.
Subhuti, if the mind of a bodhisattva abides in dharmas while giving, it is like a person entering darkness, seeing nothing”

—the Buddha tells Subhuti: Subhuti, if the mind of a bodhisattva abides in dharmas and gives in the belief that there is merit, virtue or fruition to be attained, then it is like a person in the dark, who cannot see direction or road.
[The mind abides in dharmas] Clinging to the marks of dharmas, entertaining the mind that seeks to attain states, merit or fruition. [Darkness] The same as “dark.”

Cultivating the path is leaving marks; if the mind abides in dharmas, one clings to marks, and is headed in the opposite direction. It is like rowing a boat across a lake on a pitch-black night, wanting to reach the far shore, and rowing and rowing while the prow has already turned away from the destination without one even knowing. Giving while abiding in dharmas may win the praise of others and may feel quite good to oneself, but if love and hate, taking and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion and pride—this root of birth and death—are not reduced but increased, then one has entered a wrong path, and will surely stir up a round of demonic obstructions, seeking to rise but instead falling. Moreover, giving while abiding in marks is merit, not virtue; one may enjoy blessings in the next life because of it, but by doing evil in reliance on those blessings, one falls into evil destinies in the life after that. Therefore the Song of Enlightenment says: “Giving while abiding in marks brings the blessing of rebirth in heaven, like shooting an arrow upward into empty space. When the force is spent, the arrow falls back, and one attracts a next life that is not as one would wish.”

The “dharma” here, as in the sentence above, likewise means the dharma of the path, that is, the theories, methods, states and fruitions of cultivating the path. The passage above said that one should not give while abiding in form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch or dharmas; here it says that one should also not give while abiding in the marks of dharmas (merit, virtue, fruition). Giving is not inflating the self, but dissolving the self.
If the mind of a bodhisattva does not abide in dharmas while giving, it is like a person with eyes, with the sunlight shining, seeing all manner of forms”
—if the mind of a bodhisattva does not abide in dharmas while giving, it is like a person with eyes, illumined by the light of wisdom, who sees direction and road with perfect clarity.

[The mind does not abide in dharmas while giving] Giving without seeking and without clinging (the three wheels are empty). “The mind does not abide in dharmas” means not clinging to the marks of dharmas. [Seeing all manner of forms] The “form” here is form as sense object, meaning all visible states and things.

[Subhuti, in ages to come, if there are good men and good women who can receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, the Tathagata, with Buddha-wisdom, will fully know such people and fully see such people, and they will all accomplish measureless, boundless merit and virtue.]

Above it was said that the dharma the Tathagata attained within this great dream is likewise an illusion. That being so, the mind of a bodhisattva should not abide in the marks of dharmas. But the World-Honored One feared that deluded people might thereby fall into the view of annihilation and abide in the marks of non-dharmas, and so he admonished them again, saying: “Subhuti, in ages to come, if there are good men and good women who can receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, the Tathagata, with Buddha-wisdom, will fully know such people and fully see such people, and they will all accomplish measureless, boundless merit and virtue.”

blocks.text: The Merit of Upholding the Sutra, Section Fifteen

inline.s: The World-Honored One teaches that this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit and virtue.

[Subhuti, if good men and good women give in giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the first division of the day, again give in giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the middle division of the day, and also give in giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the last division of the day, thus giving bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; and if someone else hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that merit surpasses the former—how much more so if he writes it out, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it for others.]

Subhuti, if good men and good women give in giving their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the morning, again give in giving their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges at noon, and again give in giving their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the evening, and thus for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas give their bodies and lives three times each day; and if someone else hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, the merit he obtains surpasses that of the former—how much more so if he also writes out the Diamond Sutra, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it for others; the merit he obtains, surpassing the former, is then beyond all reckoning!

[The first division of the day] Ancient India divided a day and night into six divisions, each equal to four hours in our reckoning. The day divisions are: the first division, the middle division and the last division of the day; the night divisions are: the first watch, the middle watch and the last watch. [Kalpa] The extremely long time through which a world passes in its formation, duration, destruction and emptiness is called a kalpa.

[Subhuti, to speak concisely, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit and virtue. The Tathagata speaks it for those who have given rise to the Mahayana, and speaks it for those who have given rise to the supreme vehicle.]

Subhuti, to speak concisely, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit and virtue. This is what the Tathagata speaks for those who have given rise to the mind to receive and uphold the Mahayana Buddha-dharma, and speaks for those who have given rise to the mind to receive and uphold the supreme vehicle Buddha-dharma.
Here the World-Honored One clearly points out those for whom this sutra is intended.

[Mahayana] The bodhisattva’s approach, whose aim is to save the world and benefit others, and whose highest fruition is Buddhahood. Cultivating from ordinary being to Buddhahood within the Mahayana requires passing through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, the stage of equal enlightenment and the stage of wonderful enlightenment. [The supreme vehicle] The unsurpassed teaching, that is, the perfect and sudden teaching, also called the one Buddha vehicle or the one vehicle. [Speaks it for those who have given rise to the supreme vehicle] He speaks it for those who have given rise to the mind to receive and uphold the supreme vehicle Buddha-dharma.

[If someone can receive and uphold, read and recite it, and expound it widely for others, the Tathagata will fully know such a person and fully see such a person, and he will accomplish immeasurable, unweighable, boundless, inconceivable merit and virtue. Such a person is one who bears the Tathagata’s anuttara-samyak-sambodhi on his shoulders.]

If someone can receive and uphold, read and recite it, and expound it widely for others, the Tathagata fully knows such people and fully sees such people, and they all accomplish immeasurable, unweighable, boundless, inconceivable merit and virtue. Such people are bearing the household heritage of the Tathagata’s “supreme, perfect enlightenment”—they are the Buddha’s dharma-transmitting disciples.

This sutra is the road to Buddhahood; walking along it, a cultivator of the path gains true benefit and inconceivable merit and virtue. The point on which receiving, upholding, reading and reciting comes to rest is this: deep faith without doubt, and practice in accordance with the teaching.

[Why is this? Subhuti, those who delight in the small dharma cling to the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings and the view of a lifespan, and so they cannot hear, receive, read or recite this sutra, nor explain it for others.]

Why is it that “such people are bearing the Tathagata’s anuttara-samyak-sambodhi on their shoulders”? Because those who delight in the small-vehicle Buddha-dharma cling to the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings and the view of a lifespan, and so they cannot hear, receive, read or recite this sutra (the Diamond Sutra), nor explain it for others; they cannot bear the household heritage of the Tathagata’s “supreme, perfect enlightenment.”
From this we know that not clinging to the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings and the view of a lifespan is the key to receiving and upholding the Diamond Sutra.

[Small dharma] The dharma of the small vehicle. The Lotus Sutra says: “Those of dull faculties delight in the small dharma.” “People of dull faculties and small wisdom, who cling to marks and are arrogant, cannot believe this dharma.” (“This dharma” means the one-vehicle Buddha-dharma.) [View of a lifespan] The view of a lifespan. The Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury says: “Having attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, the Buddha does not teach the dharma to people of wrong views and evil, nor does he teach it to those who hold the view of self, the view of a person, the view of sentient beings or the view of a lifespan.” [View of self] Falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as self. [View of a person] Falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind of others as a person. [View of sentient beings] Falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind of sentient beings as sentient beings. [View of a lifespan] Falsely clinging to the lifespan of the physical body as one’s own lifespan.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time all sentient beings have had all manner of inversions, like a deluded person mistaking the four directions for other places, falsely taking the four great elements as the marks of their own body, and the shadow of conditions of the six sense objects as the marks of their own mind. It is like one with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky in truth has no flowers; the diseased one falsely grasps them. Because of this false grasping, he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this empty space, but is also deluded about where those real flowers arise. From this falseness there is the turning about in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.” [The shadow of conditions of the six sense objects] The images that arise in dependence on the six sense objects, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six sense faculties meet the six sense objects.

[Subhuti, wherever this sutra may be, all the devas, humans and asuras of every world should make offerings to it. You should know that such a place is a stupa. All should reverently bow, circle it in homage, and scatter flowers and incense there.]

Subhuti, wherever this sutra may be, all the devas, humans and asuras of every world should come and make offerings to it. You should know that such a place (wherever the Diamond Sutra is) is a stupa and temple of the Buddha. All should revere it, bow and walk in circumambulation around it, and scatter all manner of flowers and incense on every side.

[Bowing and circling] Bowing and walking in circumambulation (circling to the right). [Flowers and incense] Flowers and incense. “Flower” is the same as “blossom,” representing the cultivation of causes; incense represents the true incense of precepts, concentration and wisdom. Incense includes rubbed incense, powdered incense, pellet incense and so on. “Pellet incense” is various incenses blended into pellets. [The true incense of precepts, concentration and wisdom] When one’s own mind is without wrong, without evil, without jealousy, without greed or anger, without plunder or harm, it is called the incense of precepts; when, seeing all good and evil states, one’s own mind is undisturbed, it is called the incense of concentration; when one’s own mind is unobstructed and one constantly contemplates the self-nature with wisdom, doing no evil, and though cultivating all good, the mind does not cling—revering superiors and mindful of inferiors, and compassionately relieving the orphaned and poor—it is called the incense of wisdom.
The World-Honored One teaches the tremendous power of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra: it purges karmic obstructions and realizes the fruit of sagehood.

[Again, Subhuti, if good men and good women receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra and are slighted by others, this is because of evil karma from former lives, by which they should fall into evil destinies. Because in this life they are slighted by others, the evil karma of former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

Not only that, Subhuti! If good men and good women receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra and are slighted by others, this is because of evil karma created in the past (including this life before receiving and reciting this sutra, and all the lives before this one), by which they should, after death, fall at once into evil destinies. Now, because they receive and uphold, read and recite the Diamond Sutra, although in this life they are slighted by others, the evil karma created in the past is thereby extinguished, and they shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

This teaches that for those who receive and uphold, read and recite the Diamond Sutra, grave offenses become light retribution: the grave offense is falling into an evil destiny after death, and the light retribution is being slighted by others in this life—while the merit and virtue obtained is exceedingly great: they shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
[Shall attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi] Shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

On the bodhi path, obstructions caused by past karma abound everywhere, and so for a cultivator repentance of karmic obstructions is of the utmost importance. Yet there is karma that can be repented and karma that cannot. If the offense is extremely grave and has become fixed karma, repentance is especially difficult. In the sutra text, “evil destinies” shows that these are grave offenses; “should fall” shows that this is fixed karma. A good man or good woman who has grave offenses that have become fixed karma, now receiving and upholding, reading and reciting this sutra, is merely slighted by others (grave offense, light retribution; fixed karma already transformed), and yet will certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. This shows the tremendous power of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra: it purges karmic obstructions and realizes the fruit of sagehood.

From this passage of the sutra one can also see that those for whom the Diamond Sutra is intended include good men and good women who, because of evil karma from former lives, should fall into evil destinies.

For whom, after all, was the Diamond Sutra spoken? This is an extremely important question. In “Subhuti’s Request, Section Two,” we saw that this sutra was spoken by the World-Honored One in response to the request of the Venerable Subhuti, for good men and good women who have newly given rise to the great mind. Moreover, in “True Faith Is Rare, Section Six,” it says: “After the Tathagata’s passing, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, and who will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases, taking them as true.” In “The Merit of Upholding the Sutra, Section Fifteen,” it says: this is what the Tathagata speaks for those who have given rise to the mind to cultivate the Mahayana, and speaks for those who have given rise to the mind to cultivate the supreme vehicle. (The sutra text: “The Tathagata speaks it for those who have given rise to the Mahayana, and speaks it for those who have given rise to the supreme vehicle.”) Here the World-Honored One also says: good men and good women who, because of past karma, should fall into evil destinies can likewise receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, and “because in this life they are slighted by others, the evil karma of former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.” Thus we know that the Diamond Sutra was spoken for good men and good women who have newly given rise to the great mind, and for sentient beings above them. The basic conditions for receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra are: observing the precepts and cultivating merit. Even those good men and good women who, because of evil karma from former lives, should fall into evil destinies can also receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, and thereby realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Subhuti, I recall that in the past, throughout measureless asamkhya kalpas, before the coming of Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred and forty million billion nayutas of Buddhas, and honored and served them all without ever passing one by. If someone in the final age can receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains, compared with the merit I gained by honoring all those Buddhas, is such that mine does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his—indeed, it cannot be reached by any number or simile.]

Subhuti, I recall that throughout countless kalpas in the past, before I met Dipankara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty million billion billion Buddhas, and I honored and served them all without passing one by. If someone in the final age can receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, then the merit he obtains: compared with the merit of my honoring all those Buddhas, my merit does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his—indeed, it does not come to one part of the vast number that his merit reaches, a number beyond reckoning or simile.
[Asamkhya] Translated into Chinese as “countless,” meaning so many that no number can calculate them. [Nayuta] A numeral, equal to the “billion” of today.

This passage shows that the merit of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting this sutra surpasses the merit of making offerings to Buddhas by far, far more. It tells us that the merit of making offerings to Buddhas cannot even be compared with the merit of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting this sutra—how much less can other merits compare with it.

[Subhuti, if good men and good women in the final age receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, and I were to describe in full the merit they obtain, some who heard it would become frantic and confused, doubtful and unbelieving. Subhuti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable.]

The World-Honored One said to Subhuti: Subhuti, if good men and good women in the future age of the final dharma receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, and I were to set forth in full the merit they obtain, some people, hearing it, would go mad and confused, doubt and disbelieve, and even give rise to slander and thereby create great evil karma; and so I have truly not yet set forth in full the merit of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra! Subhuti, you should know that the grandeur and profundity of the meaning of this sutra cannot be imagined with the mind, nor expressed or spoken of in words; and the exceedingly great karmic reward of receiving and upholding this sutra likewise cannot be imagined with the mind, nor expressed or spoken of in words.

[If I were to describe in full] If I were to set it all forth. [Doubtful as a fox] Extremely doubtful. The fox is by nature full of suspicion, and so the fox is used as a simile. [Inconceivable] That which cannot be thought or imagined with the mind, nor expressed or spoken of in words.

Above, the World-Honored One said that he had not yet set forth in full the merit of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra! Then how much, after all, is the merit and virtue that the World-Honored One has already set forth in the Diamond Sutra? The World-Honored One uses similes to explain:
1. Compared with Giving the Seven Treasures

Subhuti, what do you think? If a person filled a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away in giving, ... and if again there are people who receive and uphold even so much as a four-line verse from this sutra and expound it for others, that merit surpasses the former.”
(Dharma Born of Thusness, Section Eight)

“Subhuti, if there were as many Ganges rivers as the sands of the Ganges, and if there were as many Ganges rivers as that, what do you think—would the sands of those Ganges rivers be many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Even the Ganges rivers alone would be countless in number, how much more so their sands. Subhuti, I will now truly tell you. If good men and good women filled with the seven treasures as many trichiliocosms as all those Ganges-sand Ganges rivers and gave them away in giving, would the merit they obtain be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: If good men and good women receive and uphold even so much as a four-line verse from this sutra and expound it for others, this merit surpasses the former merit.”
(The Unconditioned Merit Surpasses, Section Eleven)

“Subhuti, if a person took the seven treasures equal in measure to all the Sumeru, king of mountains, in a trichiliocosm and gave them away in giving; and if a person received and upheld, read and recited even so much as a four-line verse of this Prajñāpāramitā Sutra and expounded it for others—as for the former merit, it does not come to one hundredth of it, nor to one hundred thousand ten-thousand millionth of it, and indeed cannot be reached by any number or simile.”
(Merit and Wisdom Beyond Compare, Section Twenty-Four)

“Subhuti, if someone with the seven treasures filling measureless asamkhya worlds gave them away in giving; and if a good man or good woman who has given rise to the bodhi mind took up this sutra, even so much as a four-line verse, received and upheld it, read and recited it, and expounded it for others, that merit surpasses the former.”
(The Transformation Body Is Not Real, Section Thirty-Two)
2. Compared with Making Offerings to All Buddhas

“Subhuti, I recall that in the past, throughout measureless asamkhya kalpas, before the coming of Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred and forty million billion nayutas of Buddhas, and honored and served them all without ever passing one by; and if someone in the final age can receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains, compared with the merit I gained by honoring all those Buddhas, is such that mine does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his—indeed, it cannot be reached by any number or simile.”
(Purging Karmic Obstructions, Section Sixteen)
3. Compared with Giving Body and Life

“Subhuti, if good men and good women give in giving bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and if again there are people who receive and uphold even so much as a four-line verse from this sutra and expound it for others, their merit is very great.”
(Receiving and Upholding in Accord with the Dharma, Section Thirteen)

“Subhuti, if good men and good women give in giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the first division of the day, again give in giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the middle division of the day, and also give in giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the last division of the day, thus giving bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; and if someone else hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that merit surpasses the former—how much more so if he writes it out, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it for others.”
(The Merit of Upholding the Sutra, Section Fifteen)
Not only that: the Diamond Sutra can also dissolve karmic obstructions. In this section, the World-Honored One says:

“If good men and good women receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra and are slighted by others, this is because of evil karma from former lives, by which they should fall into evil destinies. Because in this life they are slighted by others, the evil karma of former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”

This means: receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra can dissolve even karma that should bring a fall into evil destinies, and one shall realize the fruit of Buddhahood; then the lighter offenses that obstruct our cultivation and obstruct our daily life can certainly be dissolved as well. The merit and power of receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra are truly immense beyond words!

Therefore, to receive and uphold, read and recite, and expound the Diamond Sutra for others is not only to cultivate wisdom but also to cultivate merit and dissolve karmic obstructions—it is the double cultivation of merit and wisdom!
The first half of this sutra ends here.
The second half of this sutra begins with this section.

Non-self is the heart of this sutra: breaking the two selves—the self of persons (clinging to self) and the self of dharmas (clinging to dharmas). The first half of this sutra breaks the self of persons; the second half breaks the self of dharmas. The sutra text of this section says: “there is in truth no dharma by which one gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi,” “there is in truth no dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi,” and “there is in truth no dharma called a bodhisattva”; hence this section is titled “Ultimate Non-Self.”
[Then Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, when good men and good women give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?]

At this time Subhuti once more respectfully asked the Buddha: World-Honored One, when good men and good women have given rise to the great mind of attaining Buddhahood and saving sentient beings, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

By the end of the preceding section, the questions seemed already to have been answered, and the name of the sutra and the merit of receiving, upholding and transmitting it had also been given; generally speaking, the sutra text might well have ended here. But what the World-Honored One speaks is the great dharma of attaining Buddhahood, of the utmost importance. The Venerable Subhuti, though he had deeply understood the purport (Section Fourteen: “Then Subhuti, hearing this sutra spoken, deeply understood the purport, and wept tears of sorrow”), and was able to believe, understand, receive and uphold it (Section Fourteen: “World-Honored One, that I now hear such a sutra, believe, understand, receive and uphold it, is not difficult”), nevertheless, considering that this instruction’s purport is deep and wonderful (in Section Fourteen Subhuti said to the Buddha: “Rare indeed, World-Honored One! When the Buddha speaks such a profound sutra, I, from of old, having obtained the wisdom eye, have never heard such a sutra”), hoped that the World-Honored One would further clarify: how, through this sutra, does one ultimately reach the other shore? Therefore he once more, with the same question (how should one abide, how should one subdue the mind), requested the World-Honored One to instruct him.

[The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who have given rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should give rise to this mind: I should bring all sentient beings to nirvāṇa, and when all sentient beings have been brought to nirvāṇa, in truth not one sentient being has been brought to nirvāṇa.]

The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who have given rise to the great mind of attaining Buddhahood and saving sentient beings should give rise to this mind: I should bring all sentient beings to Buddhahood; and having thus brought all sentient beings to Buddhahood, in truth there is no such thing as a sentient being who has been brought to Buddhahood.

Cultivation is cultivating the mind, which is to say, how one should give rise to mind. The substance of the two questions “How should one abide? How should one subdue the mind?” is: how should a cultivator of the path give rise to mind? Therefore the World-Honored One here uses “should give rise to this mind” to answer both questions together: to vow to save all sentient beings while not abiding in dharmas—that is, even when all sentient beings have been brought to Buddhahood, one does not cling to the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan, does not cling to the marks of dharmas, and does not cling to the marks of non-dharmas.

Thus should one abide, thus should one subdue the mind: even when all sentient beings have been brought to Buddhahood, one clings not in the least to marks (“in truth not one sentient being has been brought to nirvāṇa”), how much less in other matters.
This instruction has several layers of meaning:

1. Since one is to bring all sentient beings to Buddhahood, one will no longer stand opposed to sentient beings. One will not harm them, will not envy them, will not slight them, will not contend with them for fame and profit. When sentient beings intrude upon one, or even harm one, one will not be angry either. In bringing all sentient beings to Buddhahood, this stubborn “I” is dissolved, and the afflictions are naturally subdued.

2. To bring all sentient beings to Buddhahood is far from being the work of one lifetime (the whole of this present life); so long as even one moment remains within the dream of ignorance, one must do this work with all one’s strength—and then one naturally abides in it.

3. To bring all sentient beings to Buddhahood is a matter within the dream of ignorance, and of course no sentient being is in truth brought to nirvāṇa. Yet whether one can give rise to such a mind depends on one’s skill in leaving marks. If the skill of leaving marks has reached the point where “when all sentient beings have been brought to nirvāṇa, in truth not one sentient being has been brought to nirvāṇa,” what worry is there that the work of the path will not be accomplished! As it is said, when you are in the Hanyuan Hall, why ask about Chang’an?

[When you are in the Hanyuan Hall, why ask about Chang’an] The Hanyuan Hall was the name of a palace hall of the Tang dynasty, made famous by the “Rhapsody on the Hanyuan Hall” written by Li Hua of the Tang. Chang’an was the capital of the Tang; being in the Hanyuan Hall, one is naturally within the capital.

[Why is this? Subhuti, if a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan, he is not a bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhuti, there is in truth no dharma by which one gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

Subhuti, if a bodhisattva falsely clings to all dharmas as truly existing (having the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings and the mark of a lifespan), he is not a bodhisattva. (This sentence repeats the instruction of Section Three.) Why is this said? Because even the very giving rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is itself an illusion. (Here the “dharma” in “there is in truth no dharma” means the dharma of things and phenomena.)
Question: Why is it said that the very giving rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is itself an illusion?

Answer: Because the “I” that gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is an illusion, and anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is also an illusion (see Section Seven: “There is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi”).

The question Subhuti raised was: “When good men and good women give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” The World-Honored One answered “how should they abide? how should they subdue their minds?” in the passage above. To put it further: the very giving rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is itself an illusion.

[Subhuti, what do you think? Did the Tathagata, in the presence of Dipankara Buddha, attain any dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, the Buddha, in the presence of Dipankara Buddha, had no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti, what do you think—was there, for the Tathagata in the presence of Dipankara Buddha, such a thing as attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, for the Buddha in the presence of Dipankara Buddha there was no such thing as attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Here it is taught that the matter of attaining Buddhahood is not existent, but is an illusion. Because Subhuti himself had not yet had the experience of “attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi,” he answered on the basis of the Buddha’s instruction.

[The Buddha, in the presence of Dipankara Buddha, had no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi] The Buddha, while in the causal stage, though he ascended to the Buddha-path, in truth attained nothing—it was attaining by not attaining.

Compare “Adorning the Pure Land, Section Ten”: “The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Did the Tathagata, in former times in the presence of Dipankara Buddha, attain anything with regard to dharmas? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata, in the presence of Dipankara Buddha, in truth attained nothing with regard to dharmas.”

The Tathagata saves sentient beings—in truth nothing is saved; yet though in truth nothing is saved, it is saving by not saving. The Tathagata attains Buddhahood—in truth nothing is attained; yet though in truth nothing is attained, it is attaining by not attaining.

The two passages above say: one does not see (does not entertain the thought) that there are sentient beings to be saved, and does not see (does not entertain the thought) that there is a Buddhahood to be attained, because saving sentient beings and attaining Buddhahood are both matters within the dream of ignorance; using illusion to leave illusion, one must not cling to them as real.

[The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti, there is in truth no dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prediction: “In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.” Because there is in truth no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara Buddha gave me the prediction, saying: “In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.”]
The Buddha said: So it is, so it is.”
—the World-Honored One greatly affirmed and praised Subhuti’s answer.

Subhuti, there is in truth no dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prediction: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’”

—Subhuti, there truly is no such thing as “the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.” Subhuti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prediction: “In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.”

[If there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prediction.] The Tathagata’s attainment of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is not truly existent; therefore I should not entertain the thought: I have attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. If I entertained the thought that I had attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, I would still be clinging to the mark of “attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi”; this is practicing the conditioned dharma, and one has already strayed from the Buddha-path—and Dipankara Buddha certainly would not have given me the prediction: “In a future age you shall become a Buddha.”
Because there is in truth no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara Buddha gave me the prediction, saying: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’”

—because the attainment of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is an illusion, and because I do not entertain the thought that there truly is a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, therefore Dipankara Buddha gave me the prediction.
[Why is this? The Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas.]
Why is it said this way? Because “Tathagata” means realizing that all dharmas are originally thus (originally such).

[If someone says that the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—Subhuti, there is in truth no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti, the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor void within it.]

If someone says that the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—Subhuti, I tell you truly, there is in truth no such thing as “the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.” The Tathagata’s attaining Buddhahood is neither existent nor non-existent, but is an illusion.

[Neither real nor void] Neither existent nor non-existent. [The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor void within it.] The matter of attaining Buddhahood is neither existent nor non-existent, but is an illusion.
[Therefore the Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma.]
Therefore, all the dharmas spoken by the Tathagata are the dharma of the path to Buddhahood.

[Therefore] The tone of this connects with the passage above, “the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor void within it.” [The Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma] Although the Tathagata’s attaining Buddhahood is an illusion, within the dream of ignorance the Tathagata truly did attain Buddhahood; therefore the dharmas spoken by the Tathagata within the dream of ignorance are all the dharma of the path to Buddhahood.

Regarding the sutra passage “therefore the Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma,” there have traditionally been two interpretations. From the context, the “Buddha-dharma” here means the dharma of attaining Buddhahood. On this point there is no disagreement. But as to the meaning of this sentence, because of differences in punctuation there are two views:
1. “Therefore, the Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma.” (The meaning is: therefore, all the dharmas spoken by the Tathagata are the dharma of attaining Buddhahood.)
2. “Therefore, the Tathagata says: all dharmas are Buddha-dharma.” (The meaning is: therefore, the Tathagata says: all dharmas are the dharma of attaining Buddhahood.)

Those who hold the first view, for example the Great Compendium of the Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra, under the sutra passage “therefore the Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharma,” quote Wang Rixiu’s commentary: “For this reason the Buddha says that all dharmas are what one uses to cultivate, and are the dharma of attaining Buddhahood.”
Wang Rixiu

He was the Layman Longshu of the Song dynasty, author of the Pure Land Text, who collated and edited the Larger Amitābha Sutra. When the layman was about to pass away, he took leave of all his relatives and old friends, and urged them on in Pure Land practice. Before the end he still recited and lectured with his disciples and paid homage to the Buddha as always, and at death he passed away standing upright.

This book adopts the first view. The reason is that, judged by the essential purport and the thread of meaning of the sutra, it should read: "Therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathagata are dharmas of becoming Buddha." Second, the Buddha-dharma spoken of here means the dharma of becoming Buddha. If it were interpreted as "Therefore, the Tathagata says: all dharmas are dharmas of becoming Buddha," then the false teachings of other paths, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and lying, and so on, would also be dharmas of becoming Buddha; and above all, this assertion (that all dharmas are dharmas of becoming Buddha) risks being abused. Should one not be careful? If, for the sake of greedily enjoying worldly pleasures, one makes the excuse that one "eats yet does not eat" or "acts yet does not act," that is exceedingly dangerous. The Song of Realizing the Way says: "Emptiness unhindered, denying cause and effect, vast and boundless, it invites calamity; the sickness of discarding existence and clinging to emptiness is the same—it is like fleeing drowning only to leap into fire."

Yet, to return to the point: the assertion that "all dharmas are dharmas of becoming Buddha" is, spoken from a deeper level, correct. As the Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "Every form is the Buddha's form; every sound is the Buddha's sound." But one must have awakened to the corresponding ground before one may speak in this way. It is like the general rule that water extinguishes fire: yet if the fire is a raging blaze, the water poured on it is broken down by the high heat into hydrogen and oxygen; hydrogen burns of itself and oxygen feeds the flame, so that the fire blazes even more fiercely. For one who has reached this stage, "the yellow flowers beyond the window are none other than prajñā; the green bamboo in the courtyard is all true suchness." If one sees things thus, then every matter can be polished and tempered, every time is practice, everywhere one receives the benefit, and every place is the Buddha-dharma.
[Subhuti! What are called all dharmas are not all dharmas; therefore they are called all dharmas.]

Subhuti! What are called all dharmas (their marks exist), are not all dharmas (their essence is void); therefore they are called all dharmas (they are illusory). This says that all dharmas have marks but no essence; they are illusory.

Considering that there would again be sentient beings who cling to the Buddha-dharma, the World-Honored One admonished further: what the Buddha speaks of as all dharmas is illusory. Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have clung either to existence or to nonexistence; this is a habitual tendency formed over life after life, extremely stubborn. That is why the World-Honored One says again and again in this sutra: it is not existence, not nonexistence, but illusion.
Compare Section Eight: "Subhuti! What are called Buddha and dharma are not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma."
[Subhuti! Suppose a person's body is great and tall. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! When the Tathagata speaks of a body great and tall, it is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body.]

Subhuti! Suppose a person's body is great and tall. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! When the Tathagata speaks of a body great and tall (its marks exist), it is not a great body (its essence is void); therefore it is called a great body (it is illusory).

In Section Ten there is this passage: "Subhuti! Suppose there were a person whose body were like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains. What do you think—would that body be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? The Buddha says it is not a body; therefore it is called a great body." Here the World-Honored One had taught the principle of the purified mind ("one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on form, nor give rise to the mind dwelling on sound, fragrance, taste, touch or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that dwells on nothing whatsoever"), and then tossed out this topic of the wondrous reward body, in which cultivators take such keen interest, to see how well Subhuti had grasped and mastered this principle of the purified mind. Subhuti's first sentence, "Very great," was like a mirror reflecting an object—that was right; his second sentence said at once that this body is an illusion, tightly guarding the original mind and not being dragged along by circumstances. This shows that the Venerable Subhuti had not only grasped the principle of the purified mind but applied it very well, setting us an example: every thought abides in the Way. Now the World-Honored One said again: "Subhuti! Suppose a person's body is great and tall." And so Subhuti said at once: "World-Honored One! When the Tathagata speaks of a body great and tall, it is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body." This is the example of tightly guarding the original mind and not being dragged along by circumstances.

[Subhuti! Bodhisattvas are likewise. If one should say, I shall liberate countless sentient beings, then one is not called a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma called bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life span.]

Subhuti! The great body is an illusion, and the bodhisattva is likewise an illusion. If a bodhisattva thinks, I shall liberate countless sentient beings, then he is not a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! In truth, there is no such thing as a bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says there is no such dharma as self, person, sentient being or life span.

[If one should say, I shall liberate countless sentient beings, then one is not called a bodhisattva] In liberating sentient beings a bodhisattva must not cling to marks. "If one should say, I shall liberate countless sentient beings"—this is clinging to marks. Cultivation means turning delusion into awakening, and clinging to marks is delusion; hence cultivation that clings to marks cannot succeed—as the saying goes, boiling sand will not make rice. Therefore one who practices the six paramitas while clinging to marks is not called a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva should say: I shall liberate countless sentient beings, and yet in truth no sentient being attains liberation. [In truth there is no dharma called bodhisattva] In truth there is no such thing as "called bodhisattva." This says that the bodhisattva is an illusion and not truly existent; it echoes the passage above, "in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi." [The Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life span] This says that there is no such thing at all as self, person, sentient being or life span; they are all illusions.

[Subhuti! If a bodhisattva should say, I shall adorn the Buddha lands, then he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as adorning the Buddha lands is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self, the Tathagata calls him a true bodhisattva.]

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva thinks, I shall adorn the Buddha lands, then he is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this said? Because adorning the Buddha lands is an illusion, and to take an illusion as real (I shall adorn the Buddha lands) is therefore not a bodhisattva. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self (no self of person, no self of dharmas), such a bodhisattva the Tathagata calls a true bodhisattva. (See Section Ten, Adorning the Pure Land: "Subhuti! What do you think—does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha lands? No, World-Honored One! Why? What is called adorning the Buddha lands is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning.")

Since there is no such thing as self, person, sentient being or life span, a bodhisattva practicing the six paramitas and all practices to adorn the Buddha lands must likewise not cling to marks. Only one who comprehends the dharma of no-self is truly a bodhisattva.

Above it was said that body and mind are illusory; now it is said that becoming Buddha is illusory, that self, person, sentient being and life span are illusory, and that a bodhisattva's cultivation and adorning of the Buddha lands is likewise illusory. Then who is it that cultivates? And how does one cultivate?
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, Bodhisattva Samantabhadra raised precisely this question:

"World-Honored One, if those sentient beings know that all is like an illusion, and that body and mind are likewise illusory, how can they use illusion to cultivate what is illusory? If all illusory natures are utterly extinguished, there is then no mind—who is it that cultivates? And why further speak of cultivation as illusory? If those sentient beings do not cultivate at all, they will forever dwell in illusory transformation within birth and death, never understanding the realm that is like an illusion; how then can their deluded minds be liberated? We pray you to tell us, for the sake of all sentient beings of the final age, what skillful means and gradual stages of practice will enable all sentient beings forever to leave behind all illusions."
The World-Honored One gave this teaching in reply:

"Good man! The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathagata's wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just as flowers in the sky come into being from the sky: though the illusory flowers perish, the nature of the sky is not destroyed. The illusory minds of sentient beings are still extinguished in dependence on illusion; when all illusions are utterly extinguished, the mind of enlightenment does not move. To speak of enlightenment in dependence on illusion is also called illusion; if one says there is enlightenment, one has not yet left illusion, and to say there is no enlightenment is likewise so. Therefore the extinction of illusion is called unmoving.

"Good man, all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should keep far away from all illusory and false realms; because of firmly holding to the mind that keeps far away, the mind that is like an illusion is likewise kept far away; the keeping far away is itself illusion and is likewise kept far away; the illusion of keeping far away from keeping far away is likewise kept far away; when one reaches having nothing left to keep away from, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks rub against each other, fire comes forth and the wood is consumed, and the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished; cultivating the illusory with the illusory is likewise so: when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation
(it is not that everything becomes nothing, but that the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment shines forth clearly).

"Good man! Knowing illusion, one at once leaves it, without resorting to skillful means; leaving illusion is itself enlightenment, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who cultivate in accordance with this will thus be able forever to leave behind all illusions.

"At that time the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again, spoke in verse: Samantabhadra, you should know, all sentient beings without exception, their beginningless illusory ignorance, all is established from the Tathagata's mind of perfect enlightenment; like flowers in empty space, which depend on space and have marks. If the sky flowers perish again, empty space itself does not move. Illusion is born from the various enlightenments; when illusion is extinguished, enlightenment is complete, because the mind of enlightenment does not move. If those bodhisattvas, and sentient beings of the final age, always keep far from illusion, all illusions are wholly left behind. As fire is born from wood, and when the wood is consumed the fire is extinguished, so enlightenment admits no gradual stages, and skillful means are likewise so."
(For detailed annotations, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

blocks.text: One Essence, Equally Contemplated, Chapter Eighteen

inline.s: This section uses the five eyes to show the perfection and harmony of the Buddha's vision, which contemplates all equally and, amid apparent birth and death, sees only the unborn. Hence its title, One Essence, Equally Contemplated.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the physical eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the physical eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.
[Physical eye] The physical eye is the eye of an ordinary being in a physical body; when it meets darkness or an obstruction, it cannot see.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the heavenly eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the heavenly eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the heavenly eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the heavenly eye.
[Heavenly eye] The heavenly eye is the eye of heavenly beings; near and far, by day and by night, it can see all.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.

[Wisdom eye] The wisdom eye is the eye of the sravaka; it can see through false marks and recognize true emptiness. [True emptiness] The state beyond all marks of form and consciousness, that is, the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the dharma eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the dharma eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the dharma eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the dharma eye.
[Dharma eye] The dharma eye is the eye of the bodhisattva; it can thoroughly understand all dharma gates both worldly and world-transcending.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.

[Buddha eye] The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathagata; having the Buddha eye, one also possesses the four eyes that precede it, and can know all things and see all things. Amid all dharmas the Buddha eye constantly illumines.

The next passage says that the Tathagata has these five eyes (physical, heavenly, wisdom, dharma and Buddha eye), knows all and sees all; therefore what the Tathagata speaks is all true words seen with his own eyes.

[Subhuti, what do you think—are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River spoken of by the Buddha as sand? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata speaks of them as sand. Subhuti! What do you think—if there were as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and as many Buddha worlds as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be many? Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: in all those lands, the various minds of all the sentient beings therein are all known to the Tathagata.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River spoken of by the Buddha as sand? Subhuti replied: so it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata speaks of them as sand. The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—if each grain of sand in the Ganges River were one Ganges River, and there were as many Buddha worlds as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be very many? Subhuti replied: exceedingly many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: in all those lands of yours (that is, in the trichiliocosm multiplied by the grains of sand of the Ganges, and multiplied again), the various minds (thoughts) of all the sentient beings therein are fully known to the Tathagata.

[Mind] The "mind" here means the deluded mind, that is, thoughts. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes east for west and south for north, falsely taking the four elements as the marks of their own body, and the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects as the marks of their own mind." [Shadowy reflections of the six sense objects] These are the images that arise in dependence on the six sense objects, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six sense faculties meet the six sense objects. [In all those lands of yours] This refers to "as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and as many Buddha worlds as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers"; that is, the trichiliocosm multiplied by the grains of sand of the Ganges, and multiplied again.
[Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as all minds are all not minds; therefore they are called minds.]

Why does the Tathagata fully know all these countless minds? Because what the Tathagata speaks of as all minds (their marks exist) are all not minds (their essence is void); therefore they are called minds (they are illusory).

[All minds] That is, what the passage above calls "the various minds of all sentient beings." [What the Tathagata speaks of as all minds are all not minds; therefore they are called minds] This says that the minds of all sentient beings are illusory. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter Eleven on the Illusory Learning says: "Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, perception, formations and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One." Thus we know that body and mind are illusory.

This passage says: why does the Tathagata know all these countless minds? Because they are deluded minds in which thoughts flow on and change; they are illusions, and illusions have marks (modern science and technology can already measure and record the brain waves produced by the activity of thought), and therefore the Tathagata knows them all.

When ordinary people give rise to a thought, even ghosts and spirits know it, how much more the Tathagata. In the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang, a bhikshu came from the West whom people called Great-Ear Tripitaka; he claimed to have the penetration of knowing others' minds (the spiritual power to know the thoughts of other people). Suzong asked National Master Huizhong of Nanyang to test him. The master sat for a while and then asked: where is this old monk's mind? He answered: at Western Sichuan, watching a boat race. After a while the master asked again: where is this old monk's mind? He answered: on the Tianjin Bridge, watching a monkey show. The master then became utterly still, and after a while asked again: where is this old monk's mind? Great-Ear Tripitaka could not answer even after a long time, because the master's thoughts had come to rest, quiescent and without marks.
[What is the reason? Subhuti! The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped.]

Why are they said to be illusions? Because the past mind, the present mind and the future mind are all shadowy reflections of the six sense objects, arising from the objects and ceasing when the objects cease (cannot be grasped); therefore they have no essence to speak of.

The Sutra of the Great Vehicle's Contemplation of the Mind Ground of Original Birth says: "All mind-dharmas of the three periods have emptiness as their intrinsic nature." The three minds are what dwells and the six sense objects are that on which they dwell; both what dwells and that on which it dwells are illusions, all ungraspable. Therefore one must certainly see through and let go: see through that all marks whatsoever are false and unreal, and let go of clinging, discrimination and deluded thinking.
[Three periods] Past, present and future.

blocks.text: Pervading Transformation Throughout the Dharma Realm, Chapter Nineteen

inline.s: Above it was said that the three minds are illusory; this section says that merit and virtue are illusory. "Pervading transformation throughout the dharma realm" means: if one realizes that merit and virtue are illusory and thereupon practices markless giving, one's giving and transformation pervade the dharma realm. This is what Section Four, Wondrous Practice Without Dwelling, says: "Subhuti! What do you think—can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! Can the space in the south, west and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling on marks, the merit and virtue are likewise so, beyond measure."

[Subhuti! What do you think—if someone filled the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away, would that person, by this cause and condition, obtain much merit? So it is, World-Honored One! That person, by this cause and condition, would obtain very much merit.]

Subhuti! What do you think—if someone took the seven treasures filling the trichiliocosm and gave them away, would that person, by this cause and condition, obtain much merit? Subhuti replied: so it is, World-Honored One! That person, by this cause and condition, obtains very much merit.

[Subhuti! If merit and virtue were real, the Tathagata would not say that the merit and virtue obtained are much; because merit and virtue are not [real], the Tathagata says that the merit and virtue obtained are much.]

Subhuti! If merit and virtue were real (truly existing), the Tathagata would not say that the merit and virtue obtained are much; because merit and virtue are not real (not truly existing), the Tathagata says that the merit and virtue obtained are much.

The World-Honored One explains again: only because merit and virtue are illusory is there any "much" to speak of. Compare Section Eight: "Subhuti! What do you think—if a person filled the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away, would the merit and virtue that person obtains be much? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? This merit and virtue is not the nature of merit and virtue; therefore the Tathagata says the merit and virtue is much." In Section Eight it is Subhuti who says that only because merit and virtue are illusory is there any "much" to speak of; here it is the World-Honored One who says that only because merit and virtue are illusory is there any "much" to speak of.

blocks.text: Leaving Form, Leaving Marks, Chapter Twenty

inline.s: This section says that the Buddha's perfect form body is an illusion, and that the Buddha's thirty-two marks of a great being and eighty subsidiary marks are likewise illusions. "Leaving form, leaving marks" means that the Buddha's perfect form body and the thirty-two marks of a great being with the eighty subsidiary marks can all alike not be clung to as real.

[Subhuti! What do you think—can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect form body? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect form body. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the perfect form body is not the perfect form body; therefore it is called the perfect form body.]

Subhuti! What do you think—can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect form body? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect form body. Why? Because the perfect form body is an illusion—what the Tathagata speaks of as the perfect form body (its marks exist) is not the perfect form body (its essence is void); therefore it is called the perfect form body (it is illusory).
[Perfect form body] The perfected form body.

The perfected form body has marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and unreal; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of it. The sutra says: "If one sees all marks as not marks, one then sees the Tathagata."

[Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by means of the perfect marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the marks being perfect is not perfection; therefore it is called the marks being perfect.]

Subhuti! What do you think—can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect marks? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect marks. Why? Because perfection itself is likewise an illusion—what the Tathagata speaks of as the perfection of marks (their marks exist) is not perfection (its essence is void); therefore it is called the perfection of marks (it is illusory).

[Perfect marks] The thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty subsidiary marks that the Buddha's form body possesses. Among the surpassing features and shapes possessed by the Buddha's form body, those that are conspicuous and easily seen are thirty-two in number and are called the thirty-two marks of a great being (the thirty-two marks for short); those that are subtle, hidden and hard to see are eighty in number and are called the eighty subsidiary marks. A wheel-turning sage king likewise possesses the thirty-two marks, but does not possess the eighty subsidiary marks.

The thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty subsidiary marks" have marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and unreal; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of them. The sutra says: "If one sees all marks as not marks, one then sees the Tathagata."

Compare: Section Five, Seeing the Truth in Accord with Reality: "Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by means of bodily marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of bodily marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as bodily marks is not bodily marks." Section Thirteen, Upholding the Dharma in Accord with the Dharma: "Subhuti, what do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the thirty-two marks is not marks; therefore it is called the thirty-two marks."

blocks.text: Non-Teaching and What Is Taught, Chapter Twenty-One

inline.s: Non-teaching and what is taught—one who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma.

[Subhuti! Do not say that the Tathagata thinks, I should teach a dharma. Do not think so! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata teaches a dharma, he slanders the Buddha, because he cannot understand what I teach.]

Subhuti! Do not think that the Tathagata has such a thought: I should teach some dharma. Do not think so! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata has the thought that he is teaching the dharma, that person slanders the Buddha, because he cannot understand what my teaching of the dharma really is. (The Buddha teaches while leaving marks: he teaches yet does not teach.)

The Tathagata does not teach by forming a thought (the Tathagata has no thought that he should teach the dharma, nor any thought that he is now teaching the dharma or has already taught it); rather, he responds to conditions and brings forth function, flowing forth naturally from the intrinsic nature. The Tathagata does not cling to the mark of teaching the dharma: he teaches yet does not teach. As it is said, "How does one expound it for others? Not grasping marks, thusness unmoving." (See Section Thirty-Two, Response and Transformation Are Not Real.) Moreover, this very matter of the Tathagata's teaching the dharma is not truly existent; in truth there is no dharma called teaching the dharma. (For "the Tathagata has not taught anything," see Section Thirteen, Upholding the Dharma in Accord with the Dharma: "Subhuti! What do you think—has the Tathagata taught a dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has not taught anything.")
[Subhuti! One who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma.]
Subhuti! One who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught—this is truly teaching the dharma.

The meaning is that one who teaches while clinging to the mark of teaching the dharma (conditioned dharmas) cannot speak of the path of liberation (unconditioned dharma), because he himself has not realized it and does not uphold it. Therefore at the close of this sutra the World-Honored One admonishes: "How does one expound it for others? Not grasping marks, thusness unmoving." (Section Thirty-Two, Response and Transformation Are Not Real.) At the same time, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is itself already perfect and no different from that of the Buddhas; in this respect there is truly no dharma that can be taught, no practice that can be cultivated, no fruit that can be realized. The problem is that the Buddhas have awakened and have verified their intrinsic nature, while we are still in a dream of delusion and must cultivate and realize before we can awaken. In this respect there is a dharma that must be taught, a practice that must be cultivated, a fruit that must be realized. Yet these dharmas, practices and fruits all proceed within the dream of ignorance; though it is using illusion to leave illusion, it is after all illusion, and illusion is not real. A cultivator must certainly not cling to marks. Hence it is said: no dharma can be taught, no practice can be cultivated, no fruit can be realized.

Master Hanshan says: sentient beings "merely because of beginningless ignorance, which obscures for them the wondrous brightness, give rise to all manner of inversions, deluded thinking and discrimination, and create all manner of karma. It is like a waking person who has nothing to do, yet suddenly in sleep dreams all kinds of dreams, and in the dream the affairs of suffering and joy appear vividly before him; when he wakes and seeks for them, they cannot be found at all. This is called producing something out of nothing—how could it be a real dharma? But deluded people, being inverted, cling to it as truly existent; this is because their seeing is not thorough. When the Buddha appeared in the world and taught all manner of dharmas, these were merely tools for shattering the dream, and had no root either. Yet students of the Buddha-dharma cling to them as dharmas that they themselves truly possess—this is adding dream upon dream." (Dream Roam Collection
Instructions to the Chan Monk Tanyan Zong)

The Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "The Buddha has three bodies: the dharma body teaches the dharma of the intrinsically empty and penetrating nature, the reward body teaches all pure dharmas, and the transformation body teaches the dharma of the six paramitas and all practices. When the dharma body teaches the dharma, it cannot be sought through words, sounds, forms or letters; there is nothing taught and nothing realized—the intrinsic nature is simply empty and penetrating. Hence it is said: 'No dharma can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma.' The reward body and the transformation body both appear in response to the perceptions of beings, and the dharmas they teach likewise follow the matter and respond to the faculties in order to gather and transform; none of them is the true dharma. Hence it is said: the reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they teachers of the dharma."

Master Baojing says: "Now, the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words; the ground of actual principle is originally without anything taught. As it is said, the Way is originally without words, the dharma is originally without teaching. As the Diamond Sutra says: if one says the Tathagata teaches a dharma, that is to slander the Buddha. Why then does the Buddha have a dharma that can be taught? You should know that the Way is originally without words, and words are borrowed to reveal the Way; the dharma is originally without teaching, and teaching is used to reveal the dharma. If one clings to its being inexpressible, one falls into the other paths' view of cutting off speech; if one clings to its being expressible, one incurs the reproach of slandering the Buddha. If one understands that teaching is no teaching, then there is no harm in teaching without teaching. That is why the World-Honored One, teaching the dharma for forty-nine years, never spoke a single word; and though he never spoke a single word, he spoke sideways and upright, blazing forth in unbroken teaching without end. The wonder of the Buddha-dharma lies precisely in this." (Record of Personal Hearing on the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra)
[At that time the wise-life Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Are there many sentient beings in future ages who, hearing this dharma, will give rise to faith?]
At that time the wise-life Subhuti reverently said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Will the many sentient beings in future ages who hear you speak in this way believe it?
[Wise life] To take wisdom as one's life. Subhuti was foremost in understanding emptiness; taking wisdom as his life, he is called wise-life Subhuti.

The passage above says: "If a person says that the Tathagata teaches a dharma, he slanders the Buddha... one who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma." Subhuti was afraid that sentient beings would find this hard to understand, and so asked: in future ages, when they hear you speak in this way, will there be sentient beings who believe it?

[The Buddha said: Subhuti! They are not sentient beings, and yet not non-sentient beings. Why? Subhuti! Sentient beings, sentient beings—the Tathagata says they are not sentient beings; therefore they are called sentient beings.]

The Buddha told Subhuti: Subhuti! They are not sentient beings, and yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why? Subhuti! Because sentient beings are merely illusions (sentient beings, sentient beings—the Tathagata says they are not sentient beings; therefore they are called sentient beings), and yet their intrinsic nature is equal to the Buddha's: they are all-knowing and all-capable, and so are fully able to give rise to faith in this.
[Sentient beings, sentient beings] By the emphatic tone of repetition, this carries on the passage above, "they are not sentient beings, and yet not non-sentient beings."

blocks.text: No Dharma Can Be Attained, Chapter Twenty-Two

inline.s: The preceding section said that the Tathagata has no dharma that can be taught; this section says that the Tathagata has no dharma that can be attained.
[Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Is it that the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and yet there was nothing attained?]
Subhuti reverently said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Is it that the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and yet there was nothing attained?
[The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! As to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, there is not even a single dharma that can be attained; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

The Buddha replied: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! Not only is there nothing to be attained with respect to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—there is not even the slightest dharma that I attain; it is by leaving behind all marks that it is called supreme perfect enlightenment.

Compare Section Seven, No Attainment and No Teaching: "Subhuti! What do you think—has the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Has the Tathagata taught any dharma? Subhuti said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha teaches, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathagata can teach." Section Seventeen, Utterly Without Self: "Subhuti! What do you think—when the Tathagata was with the Buddha Dipankara, did he attain any dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha teaches, when the Buddha was with Dipankara, he had no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara would not have given me the prediction: in a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara gave me the prediction, saying: in a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Why?
