The Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. If someone says that the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor unreal therein."

Cultivation without cultivation, realization without realization—this has two meanings. First, why cultivate and why realize? The purpose is to wake from the dream of ignorance. Therefore one must cultivate while leaving marks and realize while leaving marks in order to leave illusion; hence to cultivate without cultivating and to realize without realizing is the true path. Second, fundamentally speaking, cultivation and realization are both matters within the dream of ignorance; there is no truly existing cultivation or realization, and so it is said to be no cultivation and no realization. Even so, one still must cultivate and realize in order to wake from the dream of ignorance—but one must certainly cultivate while leaving marks and realize while leaving marks.
That the World-Honored One taught no dharma and attained no anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is truly hard to believe, and so the sutra speaks of these two matters again and again.

Speaking of how all dharmas are like the realm of illusion and dream, Master Hanshan says: "All Buddhas appear by the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate by the power of illusion; all followers of the Two Vehicles hasten to quiescence by the power of illusion; all followers of other paths are stupefied by the power of illusion; all sentient beings are born and die by the power of illusion; and as for the heavenly palaces and Pure Lands, they are established by the power of illusion; the jewel groves and precious trees flourish by the power of illusion; the iron bed and copper pillar are set up by the power of illusion; the cauldron of boiling water and the brazier of coals seethe by the power of illusion; the scaled, the shelled, the feathered and the furred fly and dive by the power of illusion; the wriggling worms and the creeping things move and rest by the power of illusion—so that all that the Buddhas of the three periods have realized and all that the patriarchs of the six generations have transmitted never goes beyond this net of illusion." (See Dream Roam Collection
Instructions to the Chan Monk Zhenyu)

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Good man, when bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who cultivate and master this mind reach the state in which there is no cultivation and no attainment, perfect enlightenment illumines everywhere, quiescent and without duality; within it, the hundreds of thousands of millions of asankhyeyas of inexpressible Ganges-sand Buddha worlds are like flowers in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion, neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor freed. Only then does one know that sentient beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth and death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of yesterday."

Master Hanshan comments: this explains again the mark of perfect enlightenment illumining everywhere, quiescent and without duality, in order to reveal the ultimate realization of the one mind in its entirety. For in the tathagata-garbha there is originally no mark of delusion or awakening, of birth or death, of coming or going. Yet birth and death and nirvāṇa are all matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is shattered, looking back on past affairs, they are like a dream of yesterday.

blocks.text: Purified Mind, Practicing Good, Chapter Twenty-Three

inline.s: Purified mind means the pure mind free of discrimination and clinging. The sutra text of this section says: "With no self, no person, no sentient being and no life span, cultivate all good dharmas, and you will attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi." Hence the title of this section: Purified Mind, Practicing Good.

[Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. With no self, no person, no sentient being and no life span, cultivate all good dharmas, and you will attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]
Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

—Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma (referring to the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi spoken of above) regards all things with equality, because one truly understands that they are all illusions; therefore there is no discrimination of high and low, noble and base, right and wrong, defiled and pure, and so on. That is why it is called supreme perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-sambodhi).
Tang
Xuanzang's translation: "Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma is equal; within it there is nothing unequal. Therefore it is called supreme perfect bodhi."

This sentence says: what is supreme perfect enlightenment? Supreme perfect enlightenment is the total relinquishing of all discrimination and clinging—this is the Buddha, and this is the dharma attained by the Buddha.
This dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi" has several meanings as follows:
1. Any sentient being whatsoever can realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

2. Whichever path one takes, and whether the time is short or long, so long as one awakens completely, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. For the one who realizes it, there is no high or low, no new or old, no shallow or deep.
3. The dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi regards all things with equality.
Why is there discrimination and clinging? Because one takes illusions as real! Thus one clings to marks and grasps at objects, and so there is turning about.

The Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "Students of the Way today do not awaken within their own minds, but outside the mind cling to marks and grasp at objects, all of which is contrary to the Way. As for the Ganges sand: the Buddha says it is sand (the Buddha speaks of this sand); when all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, Shakra, Brahma and the heavenly hosts walk across it, the sand is not pleased; when oxen, sheep, insects and ants trample over it, the sand is not angry; with precious gems and fragrant perfumes, the sand is not greedy; with filth, urine and stench, the sand is not averse. This mind is the mind of no-mind (not grasping marks, regarding all with equality). Leaving all marks, there is no further difference between sentient beings and Buddhas; if one can simply be without mind (free of discrimination and clinging), that is the ultimate. If a student of the Way does not directly become mindless, then even kalpas of cultivation will in the end not accomplish the Way; bound by the practices of the Three Vehicles, one will not attain liberation."

[Three Vehicles] "Vehicle" means a conveyance; here it is a metaphor for the dharma gates that carry sentient beings across birth and death to the other shore of nirvāṇa. In accordance with the dull, middling and keen faculties of sentient beings, the Buddha correspondingly taught the three teachings of the sravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle and the bodhisattva vehicle. The Three Vehicles are the Lesser Vehicle, the Middle Vehicle and the Great Vehicle. The Lesser Vehicle is the sravaka vehicle, the Middle Vehicle the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Great Vehicle the bodhisattva vehicle.

The World-Honored One teaches again and again with earnest instructions throughout this sutra, precisely so that we may awaken from the dream of delusion and no longer discriminate or cling. Love and hate, taking and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion and arrogance are the root of birth and death; they must be removed before birth and death can be ended. Therefore one must put great effort into removing discrimination and clinging from the mind.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, in its Verse on No Direction, says:
Those who truly walk the Way discern no fault in the world;
If you see others' faults, your own fault is the worse;
Their fault is not my fault, but my fault is truly mine;
Only cast off the fault-finding mind and shatter your afflictions;
With hate and love unminded, stretch out both legs and lie at ease.

[With hate and love unminded] means that the feelings of hate and love do not arise in the mind. Sentient beings are deluded, and their delusion lies in clinging to marks and grasping at objects, in false reckoning and discrimination.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Good man, because enlightenment is accomplished, you should know that the bodhisattva is not bound by dharmas and does not seek liberation from dharmas; he does not loathe birth and death and does not love nirvāṇa; he does not revere the keeping of precepts and does not hate the breaking of precepts; he does not value long practice and does not slight the beginner. Why? Because all is enlightenment. It is like the eye's light clearly knowing the objects before it: that light is perfect and complete, and so attains freedom from hate and love. Why? Because the essence of the light is without duality, and is therefore without hate and love."

Master Hanshan comments: here is shown the one mind of still extinction, equal and non-dual, which precisely reveals the mark of pure enlightenment. Bondage and liberation, hate and love, and the rest are all dual marks; it is because of deluded seeing that there are dual marks. Now, by perfect illumination, all is enlightenment, and therefore there is no duality. The eye's light is the present-moment perfect illumination of the eighth consciousness; among the faculties it is most manifest in the eye, and so it is taken as the simile for the substance of perfect enlightenment, which shines universally and is without duality.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Good man, all hindrances are precisely ultimate enlightenment. Attaining a thought and losing a thought are both liberation. Accomplishing dharmas and destroying dharmas are both called nirvāṇa. Wisdom and folly are alike prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and by those of other paths are alike bodhi. Ignorance and true suchness are not different realms. The precepts, concentration and wisdom, and lust, anger and delusion, are all the pure conduct of the holy life. Sentient beings and their lands are one dharma-nature. Hell and the heavenly palaces are both the Pure Land. Those with nature and those without nature alike accomplish the Buddha Way. All afflictions are ultimately liberation. The wisdom-sea of the dharma realm illumines all marks as being like empty space. This is called the Tathagata's accord with the nature of enlightenment."

Master Hanshan comments: this "ultimate" is precisely meant to show the equal Buddha-wisdom. As for attaining a thought and losing a thought and the rest, these ten pairs of dharmas are all matters on the side of delusion and awakening, for the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment does not belong to the causes and effects of delusion and awakening, or of opposition. All is still and extinct, equal and one suchness. Seen with deluded vision, there are dual marks; illumined with the sea-wisdom of the dharma realm, all is like empty space, and all marks whatsoever are utterly unobtainable. (See Master Hanshan's Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment.)
The Song of Realizing the Way says: "In the dream there plainly are the six destinies; after awakening, all is empty and the great thousand worlds are gone."
By no self, no person, no sentient being and no life-span, cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one then attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

—So then how is anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained? The World-Honored One says: by no self, no person, no sentient being and no life-span, cultivating any wholesome dharma whatsoever, one can attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
"By no self, no person, no sentient being and no life-span"
means realizing that all marks are illusory, and so seeking nothing and clinging to nothing.

This says that the key to attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is freedom from the four marks, and not the kind of wholesome dharmas one cultivates. The wholesome dharmas cultivated when there are no four marks are precisely the unconditioned dharma. Here the World-Honored One reveals for us the universal principle for attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; from this we also know how crucial, how very important, it is to be free of the four marks!
[Wholesome dharmas] The Mahaprajna Paramita Sutra

Chapter Three on the Practice of Correspondence says: "What are wholesome dharmas? They are the ten wholesome paths, the five precepts, the eight-fold accomplished fast (that is, the eight-fold fasting precepts), the four dhyanas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless concentrations, the four bases of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of supernatural power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path." Because bodhisattvas originally cultivate the six perfections and thereby attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, the six perfections are not listed among the wholesome dharmas above.
[Subhuti! What are called wholesome dharmas, the Tathagata says are not wholesome dharmas; therefore they are called wholesome dharmas.]
Subhuti! What are called wholesome dharmas (their marks exist), the Tathagata says are not wholesome dharmas (their essence is void); therefore they are called wholesome dharmas (they are illusory).

This says that wholesome dharmas are illusory. To keep sentient beings from again clinging to marks where wholesome dharmas are concerned, the World-Honored One admonishes: wholesome dharmas are illusory, and so one must be free of marks and practice wholesome dharmas with a pure mind.

blocks.text: Blessings and Wisdom Without Compare, Chapter Twenty-Four

inline.s: One who receives, holds, reads and recites this sutra and speaks it for others has blessings without compare, and wisdom without compare; hence "blessings and wisdom without compare."

[Subhuti! Suppose in the three thousand great thousand worlds there were as many Sumeru, king of mountains, as all the mountains there are, and a person gathered together such a mass of the seven treasures and gave it away in charity; and suppose another person received, held, read and recited this Prajñā Paramita Sutra, even a four-line verse of it, and spoke it for others: the former's merit would not come to one hundredth part of the latter's, nor to a hundred thousand ten-millionth part, nor to any part that numbers or similes could reach.]

Subhuti! If someone gave in charity a mass of the seven treasures filling a volume as great as all the Sumeru, king of mountains, in the three thousand great thousand worlds; and if someone else received, held, read and recited this Diamond Prajñā Paramita Sutra, even a four-line verse of it, and spoke it for others: the former's merit does not come to one hundredth part of the latter's, nor to a hundred thousand ten-millionth part of it, nor to any part of the enormous number that the latter's numbers and similes cannot describe.

After saying that wholesome dharmas are illusory ("Subhuti! What are called wholesome dharmas, the Tathagata says are not wholesome dharmas; therefore they are called wholesome dharmas"), the World-Honored One went on to speak of one who receives, holds, reads and recites this sutra and speaks it for others, whose blessings are without compare—lest some people go to the opposite extreme of the mark of non-dharma.

blocks.text: Transformation Without a Transformer, Chapter Twenty-Five

inline.s: Transformation without a transformer" means that the Tathagata transforms and liberates sentient beings while free of marks.

[Subhuti! What do you think? You should not say that the Tathagata has this thought: I should liberate sentient beings. Subhuti! Do not have this thought. Why? Truly there is no sentient being whom the Tathagata liberates. If there were a sentient being whom the Tathagata liberates, the Tathagata would then have self, person, sentient being and life-span.]

Subhuti! What do you think? You should not suppose that the Tathagata gives rise to such a thought: I should liberate sentient beings. Subhuti! Do not think so. Why? Because truly there is no such thing as the Tathagata liberating sentient beings. If the Tathagata held that there were such a thing as the Tathagata liberating sentient beings, then the Tathagata would have the marks of self, person, sentient being and life-span.

[Truly there is no sentient being whom the Tathagata liberates] Truly there is no such thing as the Tathagata liberating sentient beings. This says that the Tathagata's liberating sentient beings is likewise illusory, because "all marks whatsoever are false and unreal." In reading the Diamond Sutra one must take note: in many places it is expounding "all marks whatsoever are false and unreal."

[Subhuti! When the Tathagata speaks of a self, it is not a self; yet ordinary people take it to be a self. Subhuti! As for ordinary people, the Tathagata says they are not ordinary people; therefore they are called ordinary people.]

Subhuti! The Tathagata, in order to transform and liberate sentient beings, speaks of a self; but this "self" of which the Tathagata speaks is an illusion. Yet ordinary people take the "self" to be truly existent. Subhuti! The "self" is an illusion; and moreover, these ordinary people who take "the self is truly existent" are also illusions—ordinary people (their marks exist), the Tathagata says are not ordinary people (their essence is void); therefore they are called ordinary people (they are illusory).
[Ordinary people] Sentient beings within the three realms.

blocks.text: The Dharma Body Is Not Marks, Chapter Twenty-Six

inline.s: The dharma body is not marks" means that the dharma body is without marks and cannot be seen by means of marks. The Sutra on the Identity of the Great Vehicle says: "The Tathagata's true dharma body is: without form, without manifestation, without clinging, invisible, without speech, without dwelling place, without marks, without retribution, without birth, without extinction, without simile."
[Dharma body] One of the Buddha's three bodies (the dharma body, the reward body and the responsive body); that is, the body of true suchness realized by all Buddhas.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathagata be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhuti said: So it is! So it is! The Tathagata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks.]
Subhuti! What do you think? Is one who has the thirty-two marks the Tathagata? Subhuti answered: So it is, so it is. The Tathagata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks.
[Contemplate] The Jingying Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: "To contemplate means to fix the thought and ponder; this is called contemplation."

In Chapter Thirteen the question was whether the Tathagata could be "seen": "Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the thirty-two marks are not marks; therefore they are called the thirty-two marks." Subhuti answered: "The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks." (Because the thirty-two marks are illusory.)

Here the World-Honored One asks: can the Tathagata be "contemplated" by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhuti answers: So it is, so it is. The Tathagata may be contemplated by means of the thirty-two marks.
This answer is wrong, and so the World-Honored One corrects it below.

[The Buddha said: Subhuti! If one contemplates the Tathagata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king would be the Tathagata. Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, one should not contemplate the Tathagata by means of the thirty-two marks.]

Subhuti! If one held that one who has the thirty-two marks is the Tathagata, then a wheel-turning sage king would be the Tathagata, for a wheel-turning sage king has the thirty-two marks. Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, one should not hold that one who has the thirty-two marks is the Tathagata.

[Wheel-turning sage king] Abbreviated as wheel-turning king, or wheel king: the most blessed person in the world, who appears when human life-span is eighty-four thousand years and rules the four continents. He has four kinds of reward: first, great wealth—treasures, goods and property, fields and dwellings, and so on, in abundance, the foremost in the world; second, a majestic and dignified appearance, possessing the thirty-two marks; third, a healthy body free of illness, peaceful and happy; fourth, long life, the foremost in the world. When a wheel-turning king appears, the world is at peace, the people are happy and secure, and there are no natural calamities or man-made disasters. This comes from having cultivated many blessed deeds in past lives; but alas, he did not cultivate the wisdom that transcends the world, and so he becomes only a greatly blessed king who rules the world, and cannot practice and awaken to the Way or realize its fruit.
[Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Who seeks me by a form, or pursues me by a sound,
walks a path that is perverse, and shall not see the Tathagata.]
At that time the World-Honored One spoke in verse, saying: if anyone vainly seeks to see me by a form or to seek me by a sound, that person walks a perverse path and cannot see the Tathagata.

The form body and the sound are both illusions; the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of them. If anyone would see the Tathagata by means of the form body and sound, his road is wrong and he cannot see the Tathagata. How then can the Tathagata be seen? This is what Chapter Five says: "If one sees all marks as not marks, one then sees the Tathagata."

blocks.text: No Annihilation, No Extinction, Chapter Twenty-Seven

inline.s: No annihilation, no extinction" means that one must not cling to the view of annihilation. Above, the World-Honored One all along broke clinging, repeatedly making clear that all dharmas are not truly existent; and he feared that sentient beings would fall into the other extreme—thinking that all dharmas are utterly nonexistent, so that even existing marks are denied. Therefore in this chapter he admonishes: "One who has generated the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi does not speak of marks of annihilation where dharmas are concerned."

[Subhuti! If you have this thought: the Tathagata, because he does not have the complete marks, attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! Do not have this thought: the Tathagata, because he does not have the complete marks, attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

Subhuti! If you think thus: the Tathagata, without needing to have the complete marks, attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (supreme perfect enlightenment). Subhuti! Do not think thus: the Tathagata, without needing to have the complete marks, attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

[Complete marks] That is, what was earlier called "the complete marks." The Tathagata has the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty subsidiary characteristics, and so is said to have the complete marks.

The previous chapter said that the thirty-two marks are illusory and that the Tathagata cannot be contemplated by means of them. To keep his hearers from falling into annihilation, the World-Honored One went on to admonish: "Do not have this thought: the Tathagata, because he does not have the complete marks, attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

In Chapter Twenty there is this passage: "Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by means of the complete marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the complete marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the marks being complete are not completeness; therefore they are called the marks being complete."
Now the World-Honored One tells Subhuti: do not deny the fact that "the Tathagata must have the complete marks in order to attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

[Subhuti! If you have this thought, one who has generated the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi speaks of all dharmas as annihilated. Do not have this thought! Why? One who has generated the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi does not speak of marks of annihilation where dharmas are concerned.]

Subhuti! If you think thus: the Tathagata, without needing to have the complete marks, attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—that is, if you deny the fact that "the Tathagata must have the complete marks in order to attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi"—then you deny existing marks, and that is to cling falsely to the view of annihilation. One who has generated the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should not harbor this wrong view.

[Annihilation] The denial of everything. The view of annihilation, also called the nihilistic view, belongs to the most evil of wrong views and is exceedingly harmful. [Speaks of all dharmas as annihilated] To say that all dharmas are utterly nonexistent, so that even existing marks are denied—such a statement is a wrong view. The correct view is this: all dharmas have marks but no essence.

To cling to dharmas (all things and phenomena) as truly existent is one wrong extreme; to cling to dharmas as utterly nonexistent is the other wrong extreme. What is correct is the middle way: all dharmas have marks but no essence; they are illusions.

[Middle way] Neither clinging to marks nor annihilating marks. That is, as is commonly said: not leaning to existence nor to nonexistence; neither existent (essence void) nor nonexistent (marks present); both existent (marks present) and nonexistent (essence void); falling into neither extreme, perfect and unobstructed—this is called the middle way.

Again and again in this sutra the World-Honored One gives examples to make clear this fundamental view: it is not thus (that is, it is not existence), it is not so (that is, it is not nonexistence); all dharmas are illusions that have marks but no essence.

The previous chapter said that existing marks must not be denied; this chapter turns back to say: one must not cling to marks. Where the merit and virtue he creates are concerned, the bodhisattva should not accept and should not covet them.

[Subhuti! If a bodhisattva filled worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and gave them away in charity; and if another person knew that all dharmas are without self and accomplished the patience thereby, this bodhisattva would surpass the former bodhisattva in the merit obtained. Why? Subhuti! Because all bodhisattvas do not accept merit and virtue.]

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva filled worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and gave them away in charity; and if another person knew that all dharmas are without self and accomplished the patience thereby, this bodhisattva would surpass the former bodhisattva in the merit obtained."

—Subhuti! If a bodhisattva took the seven treasures filling three thousand great thousand worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and gave them away in charity; and if another bodhisattva knew that all dharmas are illusions and thereby accomplished the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, the merit the latter obtains surpasses the former's.

[Worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges] Three thousand great thousand worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. [Knew that all dharmas are without self] Knew that all dharmas have no substantial essence and are all illusions. [Accomplished the patience thereby] Accomplished the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. "Patience" here means calm acceptance: to abide calmly in the principle without the mind stirring. The Northern Wei translation by

Bodhiruci reads: "If a bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are without self and attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, this merit surpasses the merit formerly obtained." [Patience of the non-arising of dharmas] Abbreviated as the patience of non-arising. To awaken to the fact that all dharmas are illusions, never having arisen and therefore never ceasing (neither arising nor ceasing), and to abide calmly in this principle without moving: "patience" means to abide, that is, the mind abides in the principle without wavering. In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, Chapter Forty
the Chapter on Kaundinya, the Buddha says: "All dharmas are false." The Mahaprajna Paramita Sutra

Chapter Fifty says: "The patience of the non-arising of dharmas means: in the true suchness of dharmas that neither arise nor cease, to believe, accept and comprehend without obstruction or regression—this is called the patience of non-arising."

Non-arising is the essence of the Buddha-dharma and the very core of practice. A verse of the Pure Land school says: "When the flower opens one sees the Buddha and awakens to non-arising; bodhisattvas who never regress are one's companions." The Mahaprajna Paramita Sutra

Chapter Seventy-Three says: "As for the patience of non-arising: not even the subtlest dharma can be obtained, how much less a great one? This is called non-arising. Having attained this non-arising dharma, one does not create and does not arise in any karmic action; this is called attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. A bodhisattva who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is called a non-regressing bodhisattva." The Mahaprajna Paramita Sutra

Chapter Six on the Marks of the Tongue says: "At that time the Buddha knew that the good man had brought his mind to the utmost in regard to all dharmas: neither arising nor ceasing, neither emerging nor acting, and had attained this patience of dharma. The Buddha then smiled, and lights of various colors came forth from his mouth. Ānanda said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile? The Buddha told Ānanda: Among this assembly a hundred thousand million people have attained the patience of non-arising in regard to all dharmas. These people, in future ages, after sixty-eight hundred million kalpas, shall become Buddhas; the kalpa shall be named Flower Heap, and all these Buddhas shall bear the name Enlightenment Flower."

To accomplish the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, one must cut off not only the self of the person but also the self of dharmas. If there is a self of dharmas by which one practices, that is itself a mind of birth and death, and it is impossible to accomplish the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. To better grasp the principle of non-arising, a passage from A Direct Explanation of the True Mind that discusses birth and death is quoted below:

Someone asks: I have heard that one who sees the nature leaves birth and death behind. Yet the patriarchs of old were men who saw the nature, and they all had birth and death; and today we plainly see that those who cultivate the Way in the world also have the matter of birth and death. How then can one speak of leaving birth and death behind?

The answer: birth and death are fundamentally nonexistent; it is deluded reckoning that makes them exist. It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in empty space. One who is not ill (or one whose eyes are not diseased) says: there are no flowers in space. The sick person (the one with diseased eyes) does not believe it. If the eye disease is cured, the flowers in space vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe that the flowers do not exist. Even before the flowers vanish, those flowers are still empty; it is only that the sick person, through deluded clinging, takes them for flowers, and they are not truly existent in essence. So too, a person deludedly takes birth and death to exist; but one who has no birth and death tells him: birth and death are fundamentally nonexistent. One day, when his delusion subsides, birth and death are removed of themselves, and only then does he know that birth and death were fundamentally nonexistent. Even while birth and death have not subsided, they are not truly existent, because he deludedly takes birth and death to exist. The sutra (the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment) says: 'Good man, all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of inversions, like a confused man who mistakes the four directions for other places, deludedly taking the four elements as the mark of his own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects as the mark of his own mind; it is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in empty space. And even when those flowers in space are extinguished in empty space, one cannot say there is a fixed place of extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, within non-arising, deludedly see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death.' According to this sutra passage, we may believe and know that one who has penetrated and awakened to the true mind of perfect enlightenment is fundamentally without birth and death. If one now knows that there is no birth and death, yet cannot escape birth and death, it is because one's practice has not reached the mark. Hence the teaching says: the woman Amba asked Manjushri: 'Knowing clearly that birth is the dharma of non-birth, why is one still swept along by birth and death?' Manjushri said: 'Because one's power is not yet full.' Later there was Master Jinshan, who asked Master Xiushan: 'Knowing clearly that birth is the dharma of non-birth, why is one still swept along by birth and death?' Xiu said: 'A bamboo shoot will after all become bamboo; can you use it as a bamboo strip right now?' Therefore, to know that there is no birth and death is not as good as to realize that there is no birth and death; to realize that there is no birth and death is not as good as to be united with no birth and death; to be united with no birth and death is not as good as to function with no birth and death. People today do not even know that there is no birth and death—how much less do they realize, are united with, or function with no birth and death? So it is only fitting that those who take birth and death to exist do not believe in the dharma of no birth and death!"
Why? Subhuti! Because all bodhisattvas do not accept merit and virtue."

—Why does the bodhisattva who "knows that all dharmas are without self and accomplishes the patience thereby" have such great merit? Subhuti! Because they do not accept merit and virtue. (This is to say: not accepting merit and virtue, being free of marks, is precisely what enables the accomplishment of merit and virtue.)
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Chapter Three on Resolving Doubts there is a passage that makes clear the difference between merit and virtue; the translation follows:

Prefect Wei said: Your disciple has heard that when Master Bodhidharma first transformed Emperor Wu of Liang, the emperor asked him: All my life I have built temples, ordained monks, given in charity and established vegetarian feasts—how much merit is there in this? Master Bodhidharma answered: There is truly not a bit of merit. Your disciple does not understand this principle and begs the Master to explain it for me.

The Sixth Patriarch said: Emperor Wu of Liang's building of temples, ordaining of monks, giving in charity and establishing of vegetarian feasts were indeed many, yet there was truly not a bit of merit! Do not doubt the word of the former sage and think that Master Bodhidharma spoke wrongly. Emperor Wu of Liang harbored wrong views and did not know the right dharma. Building temples, ordaining monks, giving in charity and establishing vegetarian feasts—these are the cultivation of blessings; one must not take blessings for merit. Merit lies within the dharma body, not in the cultivation of blessings. ... Merit must be seen within one's own nature; it cannot be obtained by outward giving and offering. Therefore blessings and merit are different. Emperor Wu of Liang did not understand the true principle of how merit is made, and so although his good deeds were many, he truly had no merit; it is not that our Patriarch spoke wrongly.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Chapter Seven on Conditions says: "When there is a self, transgression is born; forgetting merit, one's blessings are without compare."

[Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! How is it that a bodhisattva does not accept merit and virtue? Subhuti! The merit and virtue created by a bodhisattva should not be coveted and clung to; therefore it is said that he does not accept merit and virtue.]

Subhuti reverently asked the Buddha: World-Honored One! Why does a bodhisattva not accept merit and virtue? The Buddha answered: Subhuti! The merit and virtue created by a bodhisattva should not be coveted and clung to; therefore it is said that he does not accept merit and virtue.

[The merit and virtue created by a bodhisattva should not be coveted and clung to] Because all dharmas are in the end empty, without anything whatsoever, unobtainable. If one covets merit and virtue as obtainable, one clings falsely to merit and virtue as truly existent, and then there are the marks of self, person, sentient being and life-span; such a one is not a bodhisattva.

The Song of Realizing the Way says: "Giving while clinging to marks brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow up into empty space. When its force is spent the arrow falls back, and brings a future life of unsatisfactoriness. How much better the gate of unconditioned true suchness: one leap straight into the Tathagata's ground." If a bodhisattva covets the merit and virtue he creates, he is turned by marks. Master Huiyuan's Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra says: "To relinquish marks and enter reality is called right mindfulness." So long as one does not lose right mindfulness, carrying firewood and fetching water is practice; if right mindfulness is lost, even sitting with eyes closed in meditation is not practice. Hold fast to right mindfulness!

blocks.text: Majestic Bearing, Still and Quiet, Chapter Twenty-Nine

inline.s: The World-Honored One feared that people would seek a Buddha with form and marks amid the four majestic bearings (walking, standing, sitting and lying down), not knowing that the Buddha of true nature is without marks, and has no coming or going, no sitting or lying—majestic bearing, still and quiet.
[Subhuti! If anyone says that the Tathagata comes, goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have said.]
Subhuti! If anyone says that the Tathagata has coming and going, sitting and lying down, that person does not understand the meaning of the Tathagata of which I speak.

Master Yinshun writes in his Study of the Tathagata-garbha: "In the India of Śākyamuni's time, it was already the common faith of the great majority that the life of sentient beings continues—from a former life into this life, and from this life into a later one. As for the continuation of sentient beings from one life to the next, coming to birth and passing away in death, people always felt that there was something coming and going, and this they called 'thus coming' or 'thus going.'" So the World-Honored One here points out that the Tathagata is not, as people imagine, one who comes and goes, sits and lies down.
[Why? The Tathagata means one who comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathagata.]
Why? Because the Tathagata (the dharma body) is utterly still and without marks, and so has neither coming nor going; this is what is meant by Tathagata.
In the Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra

Chapter Four Hundred, the Buddha says: "Good man! All Tathagatas, worthy ones and perfectly enlightened ones cannot be seen by the form body. The Tathagata is the dharma body. Good man! The Tathagata's dharma body is precisely the true suchness and dharma realm of all dharmas; and since true suchness and the dharma realm cannot be said to have coming or going, the Tathagata's dharma body is likewise so, without coming and without going."

[Dharma body] One of the Buddha's three bodies; the true body of the Buddha. It is also called the body of self-nature, or the body of dharma-nature: the body of true suchness and dharma-nature realized by all Buddhas. Again: the dharma body is the inherently possessed body of dharma-nature, which, whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, abides forever without moving and without change. Again: the dharma body means that the Tathagata's dharma-nature is true and permanent, utterly pure, and pervades the dharma realm. The sutra says: the Buddha takes dharma as his body, pure as empty space; this is called the dharma body. Again: the dharma body refers to the right dharma spoken by the Buddha, the undefiled dharmas attained by the Buddha, and the Buddha's own-nature true suchness and Tathagata-garbha.
[One combined mark] "One combined" means joined into one, like the modern phrase "a whole." "One combined mark" is the single combined mark spoken of in this chapter.

[Subhuti! If a good man or good woman ground the three thousand great thousand worlds into dust, what do you think? Would the mass of that dust be much? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? If that mass of dust were truly existent, the Buddha would not speak of a mass of dust. Why is that? What the Buddha speaks of as a mass of dust is not a mass of dust; therefore it is called a mass of dust.]
Subhuti! If a good man or good woman ground the three thousand great thousand worlds into dust, what do you think? Would the mass of that dust be much?"
—The World-Honored One asks: Subhuti! If a good man or good woman ground the three thousand great thousand worlds into dust, what do you think? Would all that dust not be very much?

[Grinding the three thousand great thousand worlds into dust] In modern terms: breaking the three thousand great thousand worlds down into elementary particles. [That mass of dust] All those specks of dust. [Elementary particles] Elementary particles are the smallest and most basic units composing matter. But because human understanding of the composition of matter has deepened gradually, the connotation of "elementary particle" has also changed over time.

Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? If that mass of dust were truly existent, the Buddha would not speak of a mass of dust. Why is that? What the Buddha speaks of as a mass of dust is not a mass of dust; therefore it is called a mass of dust."

—Subhuti answered: There are very many, World-Honored One! Why? If the mass of dust were truly existent, the Buddha would not speak of a mass of dust. Why? What the Buddha speaks of as a mass of dust (marks exist) is not a mass of dust (essence void); therefore it is called a mass of dust (it is illusory).

[If the mass of dust were truly existent, the Buddha would not speak of a mass of dust. Why is that? What the Buddha speaks of as a mass of dust is not a mass of dust; therefore it is called a mass of dust.] If elementary particles were truly existent, the Buddha would not say that these elementary particles are many. Why does he say so? Because what the Buddha speaks of as elementary particles being many is not elementary particles being many; therefore it is called elementary particles being many. This says that elementary particles are illusory.

This says: not only are all material things illusory, but the elementary particles composing these things are illusory too. Judged by the traditional notions of the world, a tall building is real and a mirage is illusory; yet in fact the dust, vapor and light that compose the mirage are of the same nature of existence as the tall building of steel and cement. If the tall building is said to be real, then the dust, vapor and light that compose the mirage should also be real. Therefore the World-Honored One analyzes it in depth and says: not only are the three thousand great thousand worlds illusory, but the basic units composing those illusions of the three thousand great thousand worlds are illusory too.

[Mirage] A false image formed when light reflected by objects on earth is refracted by the atmosphere; the so-called mirage is an optical illusion. The shen is a giant clam; legend says that the shen can breathe out vapor that forms the shape of towers and terraces.

[World-Honored One! The three thousand great thousand worlds spoken of by the Tathagata are not the world; therefore they are called the world. Why? If the world were truly existent, it would be a single combined mark. What the Tathagata speaks of as a single combined mark is not a single combined mark; therefore it is called a single combined mark.]

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! The three thousand great thousand worlds spoken of by the Tathagata (marks exist) are not the world (essence void); therefore they are called the world (they are illusory). (This says that the three thousand great thousand worlds are an illusory mark.) Why? If the three thousand great thousand worlds were truly existent, then they would be a single combined mark. What the Tathagata speaks of as a single combined mark is not a single combined mark; therefore it is called a single combined mark.

In Chapter Thirteen, on receiving and holding the sutra in accordance with the dharma, the World-Honored One plainly told Subhuti that the world is illusory: "What the Tathagata speaks of as the world is not the world; therefore it is called the world." Why then does he still speak of "if the world were truly existent"? Because although Subhuti had already awakened to the fact that "all marks whatsoever are false and unreal," he still wished to probe further into "what is truly existent," that is, where the dream of ignorance ends; and so he said, "If the world were truly existent, it would be a single combined mark," deliberately following the formula "the Tathagata speaks of ... it is not ... therefore it is called ..." and adding, "What the Tathagata speaks of as a single combined mark is not a single combined mark; therefore it is called a single combined mark," to see how the World-Honored One would comment on and reveal this "truly existent."
[Subhuti! A single combined mark is precisely indescribable; yet ordinary people covet and cling to the matter.]

The World-Honored One told Subhuti: this "single combined mark" of which you speak is far beyond thought and imagination and verbal discussion; it is indescribable. Yet ordinary people covet and cling to the matter, always wanting to make it out clearly.

On this ultimate question the World-Honored One reveals in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment: "Good man! The realm perfected by the hearers—body, mind and speech are all cut off there—can never reach the nirvāṇa manifested by that which is personally realized; how much less can one use a thinking mind to fathom the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment! That would be like taking a firefly's flame to burn Mount Sumeru: it can never take hold. With a mind of birth and death, giving rise to views of birth and death, to enter the Tathagata's great sea of still extinction—one can never arrive. Therefore I say: all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings of the final age must first cut off the root of beginningless birth and death."
Therefore, to understand the truly existent single combined mark, one must first cut off the root of beginningless birth and death—ignorance.

[A single combined mark is precisely indescribable.] The truly existent single combined mark cannot be expressed in words or imagined by the mind. [Yet ordinary people covet and cling to the matter.] Yet ordinary people recklessly conjecture and discuss it. Since the thinking of ordinary people is illusory, how can an illusory thinking be used to know what is truly existent? Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Thought is itself illusion; how much more so disputing about the false! If one can understand this mind, one may then seek perfect enlightenment."

Question: a single combined mark should be understood as "a collection of dust." The Great Floriation Sutra, Subcommentary on the Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra says: "A single combined mark is so called because many conditions are combined. Gathering many dust motes to form form, and combining the five aggregates and so on to form a person—this is called a single combined mark."

Answer: a single combined mark should not be understood as "a collection of dust." Master Xuanzang's translation of the passage in this chapter (Great Prajñā Paramita Sutra, Chapter Five Hundred Seventy-Seven) reads thus: "Furthermore, Subhuti. If a good man or good woman ground worlds as numerous as the ultimate particles of dust in the great earth of three thousand great thousand worlds, and made ink of the material forms of those countless worlds, as a mass of ultimate particles—Subhuti, what do you think? Would that mass of ultimate particles be much? Subhuti answered: That mass of ultimate particles is very much, World-Honored One; very much, Sugata. Why? World-Honored One, if that mass of ultimate particles were truly existent, the Buddha should not speak of it as a mass of ultimate particles. Why is that? What the Tathagata speaks of as a mass of ultimate particles is precisely not a mass; therefore it is called a mass of ultimate particles. What the Tathagata speaks of as the three thousand great thousand worlds is not the world; therefore it is called the three thousand great thousand worlds. Why? World-Honored One, if the world were truly existent, it would be a single combined clinging; what the Tathagata speaks of as a single combined clinging is precisely not clinging; therefore it is called a single combined clinging. The Buddha said: Subhuti, this single combined clinging cannot be spoken of and cannot be debated; yet all those foolish ordinary beings and heterogeneous beings stubbornly cling to this dharma." In this translation, "a collection of dust" is called "a mass of ultimate particles," while "single combined clinging" is precisely what Master Kumarajiva translated as "single combined mark." From this we know that a single combined mark should not be understood as "a collection of dust."

[Sugata] One of the ten epithets of the Tathagata. Su means good, gata means gone: the Buddha practiced the right path, entered nirvāṇa, and departed toward a good destination; therefore he is titled "Sugata." [Heterogeneous being] Another name for the ordinary person, because the ordinary person revolves through the six destinies and is born receiving all manner of different and varied retributions.

blocks.text: Knowledge and Views Do Not Arise, Chapter Thirty-One

inline.s: Knowledge and views do not arise" means not to cling falsely to the dharma of the Way as real, and to go further in breaking the self of dharmas. The Surangama Sutra
Chapter Five says: "When knowledge and views set up a knowledge, that is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and views are without views, that is precisely nirvāṇa."

[Subhuti! If anyone says: the Buddha speaks of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span. Subhuti! What do you think? Does that person understand the meaning of what I have said? No, World-Honored One! That person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathagata has said. Why? The World-Honored One speaks of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span as not the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span; therefore they are called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span.]

The World-Honored One said: Subhuti! If someone says that the Buddha speaks of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span, so that there really are such views of self, person, sentient being and life-span—Subhuti! What do you think? Does this person understand the meaning of what I have said? Subhuti answered: World-Honored One! This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathagata has said. Why? The view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span spoken of by the World-Honored One refer to the illusion of the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being and the view of a life-span, and do not say that such things truly exist.
In the Sutra of the Buddha Treasury

Chapter Three on the Recollection of Dharma, the Buddha says: "The noble and holy do not have this thought: this is right view, this is wrong view. Why? All views arise from false conditions. Shariputra! If one has the thought 'this is right view,' that person is then of wrong view. Shariputra, in the holy dharma one uproots the root of all views and cuts off all paths of language, as in empty space, where the hand meets no obstruction; all the dharmas of the shramana should be likewise."
[As in empty space, where the hand meets no obstruction] As in empty space, where nothing at all can be touched. [Obstruction] Chu means to touch; he means to block or impede.

The Buddha says: "Shariputra! The Tathagatas' anuttara-samyak-sambodhi has only one meaning, namely detachment. What is detachment? Detachment from all desires and all views. Desire is ignorance, and view is recollection. Why? All dharmas have recollection as their root; whatever is thought and conceived is a view, and a view is wrong. Shariputra! Even a view within wholesome dharmas I likewise call a wrong view. Why? Shariputra! In detachment and still extinction there is no dharma and no non-dharma, no good and no evil; all these matters are empty, far removed from all knots and all recollection; therefore it is called detachment." (Sutra of the Buddha Treasury
Chapter Seven on Former Ages)

The layman Jiang Weinong says in his Lectures on the Diamond Sutra: "One should know that the marks of the four marks are in fact nothing but the one mark of self; and the root of the mark of self in fact arises from the view of self." This says that the view of self is the root of ignorance. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha says: "What is ignorance? Good man! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all manner of inversions, like a confused man who mistakes the four directions for other places, deludedly taking the four elements as the mark of his own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects as the mark of his own mind. It is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in empty space and a second moon. Good man! In empty space there are truly no flowers; the sick person deludedly clings to them, and through that deluded clinging he is not only confused about the nature of empty space, but further deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance."
[Subhuti! One who has generated the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should, in regard to all dharmas, thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand, and not give rise to the marks of dharmas.]

Subhuti! One who has generated the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should, in regard to all dharmas of the Way, thus (that is, in the light of the four views above being illusory) know, regard, believe and understand them: not nonexistent, not existent, but illusory.
[Not give rise to the marks of dharmas] Not to cling to the marks of the dharmas of the Way and take them for real.

Of this passage the Lectures on the Diamond Sutra comments: "That is to say, the bodhisattva who has generated the great mind should thus know, see, believe and understand. From the opening of the sutra onward, all that has been said of generating the vast mind, undertaking vast practice, not grasping the marks of dharmas and non-dharmas, and further of not abiding even in the generation of the mind, not abiding in speaking the dharma, not abiding in the fruit obtained, and not abiding even in non-abiding—all of it is nothing but causing them to know, see, believe and understand thus and thus. For only by knowing, seeing, believing and understanding thus can one penetrate the dharma of no-self. Therefore it says: one should thus know, see, believe and understand."
Question: "Dharma" refers to all things and phenomena; why is "dharma" here interpreted as "the dharma of the Way"?

Answer: the word "dharma" has several meanings: first, all things and phenomena; second, the dharma of the Way (the dharma of becoming Buddha); third, mental objects. The core of this sutra is to break clinging to the four marks (self, person, sentient being and life-span) and to the marks of dharmas—what is called "cutting off ordinary sentiment and doing away with holy understanding (even awakening is spat out)." The content of this chapter is to do away with holy understanding and thoroughly break the self of dharmas (one must not falsely cling to the dharma of the Way as real, thinking that there is a dharma to cultivate, a Way to accomplish, a fruit to realize); in Chapters Six and Seven, "no marks of dharmas, and no marks of non-dharmas," "one should not grasp dharmas, and should not grasp non-dharmas," "non-dharmas, non-non-dharmas"—the "dharma" spoken of there also always means the dharma of the Way. Therefore, according to the purport of the sutra and the context, "dharma" here means the dharma of the Way. Master Jiazang's Commentary on the Humane King Sutra

Chapter Two says: "Emptiness breaks the five aggregates, and emptiness of emptiness breaks emptiness. It is like taking medicine that can cure a disease: once the disease is cured, the medicine too should be expelled. If the medicine is not expelled, it is itself the disease. One uses emptiness to break the disease of the afflictions, but one fears that emptiness will in turn become a calamity. Therefore one uses emptiness to relinquish emptiness; this is called the emptiness of emptiness." The meaning is: use medicine to cure disease, and once the disease is healed one should stop taking the medicine; if one goes on taking it, it is still harmful. This makes clear: use holy understanding to cut off ordinary sentiment, and once ordinary sentiment is cut off, one should do away with holy understanding. Concretely: use the principle of emptiness (the medicine) to break clinging to the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness) (the disease)—this is cutting off ordinary sentiment; once clinging to the five aggregates is broken, if one still clings to the principle of emptiness and will not let it go, that is failing to abandon the raft after crossing the river and lingering on the shore, and one cannot then reach the treasure isle (cannot wake from the dream of ignorance). Therefore one must empty out even the principle of emptiness (awaken to the fact that the principle of emptiness is also empty—is illusory and not to be clung to, that is, the emptiness of emptiness). Cut off ordinary sentiment (break the clinging to a person), do away with holy understanding (break the clinging to dharmas).

All dharmas are false, fundamentally empty and still; when no views arise, there are no marks of self, person, sentient being and life-span. Master Dixian says: "What is known is not in itself a hindrance; the Way lies simply in not clinging. Deluded thoughts need not be eliminated; the Way lies simply in not being turned by them." All Buddhas, amid what plainly seems to be arising and ceasing, see only non-arising; sentient beings, amid the utterly still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing. Awakened, arising and ceasing are all non-arising; deluded, non-arising is all arising and ceasing. When one has seen through all dharmas as illusory, objects no longer drag the mind along, love and hate have no way to arise, and one will no longer be deluded and create karma.

All dharmas are illusory, and the dharma of the Way that one holds to is illusory too. When practice goes on in this way, breaking through illusion layer by layer like peeling a banana tree, and one breaks through to the utmost point—the great dream is awakened!

Marks arise from thought, and thought arises from views. Hence an ancient worthy said: “You need not seek the real; you need only put an end to views.” If knowing and views dissolve, what need is there to wait for the real? Departing from views is precisely the ultimate principle for escaping birth and death and realizing the dharmakāya. Master Ashvaghosha showed people that freedom from thought is true cultivation and true realization, because views exist owing to thought (for thoughts come from views); once views fall away, thought departs of itself, and the deluded is extinguished of itself. Therefore the departing from views is of the utmost importance. Let the mind be left empty and bare, holding back not the slightest knowing or view to act as master. When knowing and views no longer exist, the true view sends forth its light. (See Master Hanshan, Dream Roam Collection
Instructions to the Master of the Six Ease Pass)
Free from marks, free from thought, free from views. Of these, freedom from views is the most ultimate and most fundamental.
[Subhuti, what are called dharma-marks, the Tathagata says, are precisely not dharma-marks; therefore they are called dharma-marks.]
Subhuti, what are called dharma-marks, the Tathagata says, are not real—they are illusion.

In the fourteenth chapter, “the Tathagata says that all marks are precisely non-marks” means that all things and phenomena are illusions. The dharma-marks spoken of here refer to the dharma of the path, which, as was said at the end of the eighth chapter, is likewise an illusion (an affair within the dream of ignorance)—so that clinging to dharmas is thoroughly shattered.
Here the main part of the sutra comes to an end.

blocks.text: Manifestation and Transformation Are Not Real, Chapter Thirty-Two

inline.s: To expound this sutra for others is to save and transform beings in response to their capacities and conditions; this work too is illusory, and one must not cling to marks. Hence it is called “manifestation and transformation are not real.” This chapter is the circulation part.

[Subhuti, if someone were to fill measureless asamkhya worlds with the seven treasures and give them away in giving; and if a good man or good woman who has given rise to the bodhi mind were to take up this sutra, even so much as a four-line verse, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and expound it for others, that merit would surpass the former.]

Subhuti, if someone were to give in charity as many seven treasures as would fill measureless asamkhya (incalculable) worlds; and if a good man or good woman who has given rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi were to take up this sutra, even so much as a four-line verse, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and expound it for others, that merit would surpass the former.
[Bringing forth the bodhi mind] The abbreviation of “bringing forth the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”

The giving of the seven treasures has been spoken of in the earlier sutra text. In “Dharma Born of Thusness, Chapter Eight” it is said: if a person were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them away. In “The Unconditioned Merit Surpasses, Chapter Eleven” it is said: to give as many seven treasures as would fill trichiliocosms equal in number to the Ganges sands multiplied by the Ganges sands. Here it is to give as many seven treasures as would fill measureless asamkhya trichiliocosms—a number far greater still.

The text of this sutra must be awakened to in practice (receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, and expounding for others) and practiced in awakening. This is what it means to receive and uphold the Diamond Sutra, and its karmic fruit is inconceivable.
What does the Diamond Sutra teach? It teaches:

“All marks whatsoever are delusive and false. If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathagata.” “No mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a lifespan.” “No dharma-mark, and no non-dharma-mark either.” “Bodhisattva-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind abiding in sound, fragrance, flavor, touch or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.” “Departing from all marks—this is called the Buddhas.” “I should liberate all sentient beings, and when all sentient beings have been liberated, yet not one sentient being has in fact been liberated.” “Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness.” “All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated.”

Keep these few lines of the sutra firmly in mind, and at all times contemplate and examine them, so as not to be turned about by circumstances—this is what it means to receive and uphold the Diamond Sutra. (The reason one is turned about by circumstances is that one takes the marks that are all delusive and false as real.)
[Contemplation] To observe the principles of things and all dharmas with wisdom, and to illuminate and see them clearly.
Question: The World-Honored One says:

“If someone were to fill measureless asamkhya worlds with the seven treasures and give them away in giving; and if a good man or good woman who has given rise to the bodhi mind were to take up this sutra, even so much as a four-line verse, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and expound it for others, that merit would surpass the former.”
And earlier it was also said:
“If a good man or good woman were, in the first watch of the day, to give away bodies equal in number to the Ganges sands
(a single grain of sand standing for one life)
, and in the middle watch of the day again to give away bodies equal in number to the Ganges sands, and in the last watch of the day likewise to give away bodies equal in number to the Ganges sands
(three times in a single day)

, and thus for measureless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas to give away bodies in giving; yet if someone else hears this sutra and his faith does not waver, his merit surpasses that—how much more so if he writes it out, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it for others.” “I recall that in past measureless asamkhya kalpas, before the Buddha Burning Lamp, I met eight hundred and forty million billion nayutas of Buddhas, and honored and served them all without ever passing one by; yet if someone in the final age can receive and uphold, read and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my honoring all those Buddhas—mine does not come to a hundredth part of his, nor to a thousand-myriad-billionth part, nor can it be reached even by reckoning or simile.”
Why is the merit and virtue obtained from receiving and upholding, reading and reciting the Diamond Sutra and expounding it for others so very great?

Answer: The self-nature of sentient beings is no different from the Buddha’s; its merit and virtue are originally perfect and beyond all measure. Yet sentient beings are deluded—like a millionaire who has lost his memory in a foreign land and, forgetting the countless gold and silver treasures in his own house, goes out to work for a living. How could the few small coins earned by such labor compare with the countless treasures at home? Therefore the Sixth Patriarch Huineng said:
“Not departing from the self-nature—this is the field of merit.”
To receive and uphold, read and recite the Diamond Sutra and expound it for others is to unfold the merit and virtue inherent in our own self-nature; of course it is as great as this! The Lotus Sutra
Chapter Eight: The Prediction to Five Hundred Disciples, says:
“Suppose a man goes to the house of a close friend and, drunk with wine, lies down. At that time the friend must go out on official business
(his friend must set out at once on a distant journey because of official business)

. He ties a priceless pearl into the lining of his garment, gives it to him, and departs. The man, drunk and asleep, is wholly unaware of it. When he rises he wanders on and reaches another country. For the sake of food and clothing he toils and searches with great difficulty, and if he gains but little he thinks it enough. Later the close friend happens to meet him and speaks thus: ‘Fie, sir! Why should you go so far for the sake of food and clothing? I once wished to give you ease and happiness and the free enjoyment of the five desires, and on such-and-such a day I tied a priceless pearl into the lining of your garment. It is still there now, yet you do not know it, and you labor and grieve to keep yourself alive—how foolish! You may now take this treasure and trade for whatever you need, and you will always have your wish and lack nothing.’”
[How should one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness.]
(Question:) How should one expound it for others? (Answer:) Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness.

How should one expound it for others?” This is a question, and it carries two meanings. One asks how the expounder himself should expound it; the other asks what, for the hearers, should be expounded to them. Hence the answer, “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness,” likewise carries two meanings. First, the expounder should be “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness”—that is, when expounding for others he himself must not cling to marks, teaching by his own example, for example in conduct outweighs instruction in words. At the very beginning of this sutra the World-Honored One was expounding it in precisely this way, and Subhuti saw through it and praised it as rare. Second, as for the hearers, he must tell them that all marks whatsoever are delusive and false, that they should not grasp at marks and should be unmoved in suchness—that is, he must tell them to leave marks.

[Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness] Not holding marks to be real (the sutra says, “all marks whatsoever are delusive and false”) and being entangled by them; that is, not clinging to marks and not stirring the mind. [Unmoved in suchness] To be such as true suchness. This is the realm of the self-nature, equal and non-dual, in which inverted discrimination does not arise. [True suchness] “True” is the true state, and “such” is thus: the true state is thus, and so it is called “true suchness,” that is, the true reality of all dharmas.
Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness”

(within, not turned about by thoughts; without, not drawn along by circumstances)—this is the stroke that puts the pupil in the dragon’s eye for the whole text! This is what the World-Honored One demonstrated for us at the very beginning of this sutra, from putting on his robe and taking up his bowl to spreading his seat and sitting down; and this is what the Elder Subhuti praised as rare. Now we understand the essential purport of the Diamond Sutra: leaving illusion—not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness.
Not grasping at marks”

—if, on meeting circumstances (outer circumstances or inner circumstances), the mind is moved, and there arise feelings of love and hate, of liking and disliking, this is “grasping at marks.” When the Buddha awakened to the Way on the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month, seeing the morning star, he said:
“How wondrous! All sentient beings are endowed with the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue, with all his marks. It is only because of deluded thinking, inversion and clinging that they cannot realize it.”

Yet deluded thinking, inversion and clinging all come from “grasping at marks” (taking illusions as real). Therefore, when meeting circumstances, one must not grasp, not be defiled, not dwell in thought; in every matter and every place, diligently examine and test—and then one’s effort is applied exactly at the vital point.
Unmoved in suchness”

—that is, to dwell securely in the principle of true suchness, and amid seeming birth and death to see only the unborn, inwardly perfuming ignorance. Here the World-Honored One has set forth the unconditioned dharma: not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness.
Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness”
—this is to leave marks and turn the light back to shine upon the pure self-nature—what is called “dismissing marks and contemplating the nature.” In the Surangama Sutra the Buddha says:

“You should know that all sentient beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous substance of the nature, but employ various deluded thoughts; these thoughts are not true, and so there is turning about in rebirth.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous substance of the nature
(that is, because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, this pure and luminous substance of the nature)
, but employ deluded thoughts
(and so go on employing deluded thoughts)
; these thoughts are not true, and so there is turning about in rebirth.”

[The permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous substance of the nature] The pure and luminous substance of the nature—the wondrous luminous substance whose nature is originally pure. Grammatically, “the pure and luminous substance of the nature” is an appositive, qualifying the noun “true mind.” [Turning about in rebirth] Delimited birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death. [Delimited birth-and-death] Beings within the three realms and the six paths, whose lifespans are all limited and whose bodies are all of distinct kinds, because of the good and evil karma they have attracted—their birth-and-death is therefore called “delimited birth-and-death.” One who has ended delimited birth-and-death escapes the wheel of rebirth. [Transformational birth-and-death] The sages of the Three Vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended delimited birth-and-death, gradually extinguish deluded thought and gradually increase their realization as they cultivate the path. This migration of delusion and awakening differs in every period; the passage from the earlier period into the later is exactly like one round of birth-and-death, and its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable—hence it is called “transformational birth-and-death.” One who has ended transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha fruit.
Question: How is one to accomplish “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness”?

Answer: On this point Mr. Jiang Weihong’s Diamond Sutra Commentary has a most penetrating discussion. The Commentary says: “Taking together the sutra passages quoted above (‘not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness’), one may clearly understand (see plainly) that to be aware and illuminate directly at the place where nothing is ever born is the wondrous method for removing ignorance. What is the place where nothing is ever born? It is at the time before a thought has arisen. When a thought has not yet arisen, what can be called a mark? Still less can there be any grasping. If one can be thus fine and continuous without interval, then in not grasping one will naturally have a firm hold. In sum: on the one hand, toward the unmoving place, gather the mind in aware illumination, so as to accomplish one’s not grasping; on the other hand, when meeting conditions, firmly hold to not grasping (at marks), so as to perfect one’s unmoving. Thus may one find an entry into the substance of suchness.”

It also says: “To sum up: ‘unmoved in suchness’ is the meaning of non-arising; ‘not grasping at marks’ is the meaning of non-abiding. One must first be aware and illuminate the originally unborn, and only then can one be non-abiding. When one abides nowhere at all, one realizes non-arising. Working alternately at the two is the essential gate. Moreover, working in this way is to carry through to the very end. From the first entry, on through the stages of abiding, practice and dedication, the grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment (the fifty-two stages through which one passes from ordinary being to Buddhahood, namely: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment), none goes beyond this. Hence it is said: ‘Departing from all marks—this is called the Buddhas.’”

It also says: “However, the method of practice must be taken up by being aware and illuminating from the place where no thought has moved, that is, to contemplate the intrinsically unmoving nature. This is the meaning of the Surangama in taking the unborn and undying as the fundamental cause of cultivation; it is also the meaning of cultivating cessation through the inherently still nature and thereby attaining concentration, and of cultivating contemplation through the inherently luminous nature and thereby attaining wisdom. If one does not know to begin from here, one’s practice is confused and disordered, a blind cultivation and a reckless refining—as though boiling sand to make rice, which can never succeed. Though a beginner is wholly in ignorance and cannot see it by contemplation, one should still understand this principle deeply and diligently contemplate it roundly. As said before, when the earlier thought has already ceased and the later thought has not yet arisen, at just that very moment the single mind is wholly still and clearly luminous—this is what is called contemplation. ‘Round’ means neither exerting effort nor not exerting effort, neither sinking nor floating. This is a single thread of the light of wisdom, the very first expedient of knowing illusion and being freed of it. At the same time, following this verse, one contemplates all dharmas as like dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew and lightning, empty in their very arising from conditions. This method is an even greater expedient—the so-called knowing of illusion. The two are best cultivated together, for these two methods aid each other. To be aware and illuminate the intrinsic nature is to work at the very source; to contemplate all dharmas is to work upon circumstances and conditions. Moreover, the former contemplation is more concerned with cultivating concentration, whereas the latter is more concerned with cultivating wisdom. Concentration can indeed give rise to wisdom, but unless wisdom is first opened, that concentration can never be achieved either. Hence, in their mutual assistance the contemplation of arising from conditions is especially important, because by contemplating arising from conditions one can be led directly into the unmoving suchness. This meaning has been spoken of in detail before. Consider the phrase ‘thus should they be contemplated’: it carries strongly the sense that nothing else will do. How earnest it is! The word ‘contemplate’ is the crucial one—it means that one should contemplate with the utmost intentness.”
