[Why is this? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated.]

Why must one be “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness”? Because clinging to marks and abiding is a conditioned dharma, and all conditioned dharmas are delusive and unreal like a dream, burst and vanish in an instant like a bubble or a shadow, appear and are gone like morning dew or a lightning flash; and one should contemplate them in this way (thus observe, realize and examine them upon all circumstances and conditions).
The Diamond Sutra Commentary says:

“‘All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated’—this is precisely pointing out that ‘unmoved in suchness’ must be entered through contemplating all dharmas as dreamlike and illusory. To make such contemplations as of dream and illusion is to banish the clinging of feeling. These are all crucial keys in the sutra, not to be neglected.”

[Conditioned dharmas] Generally, dharmas produced by causes and conditions are called “conditioned dharmas”; dharmas not produced by causes and conditions are called “unconditioned dharmas.” Among the five positions and hundred dharmas, the first ninety-four dharmas are all conditioned dharmas with arising, ceasing and change; only the last six dharmas are the pure, still and extinct unconditioned dharmas. But in this sutra, judging from the context, clinging to marks as real is a conditioned dharma, and not clinging to marks as real is the unconditioned dharma.
The conditioned dharmas spoken of here are relative to the seventh chapter’s
“all sages and saints are distinguished from one another through the unconditioned dharma”
, and are likewise relative to the unconditioned dharma in the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections. The Sutra of Forty-Two Sections says:
“The Buddha says: To take leave of kin and go forth from home, to know the mind and reach the root, to understand the unconditioned dharma—this is called a shramana.”
Mr. Jiang Weihong’s Diamond Sutra Commentary says:

“What this sutra teaches is all unconditioned dharma. And it plainly says: ‘All sages and saints are distinguished from one another through the unconditioned dharma.’ Yet now, when instructing on expounding and upholding it, it has one contemplate the conditioned dharmas
(like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning)
. This is a matter of the greatest moment for the purport of the whole sutra, and likewise a crucial point for students of the Buddha-dharma.”

Therefore, judging by the way the sutra text echoes back and forth, the “conditioned dharmas” of this chapter (seeking and clinging) are relative to the “unconditioned dharma” in “Non-Attainment and Non-Teaching, Chapter Seven,” and to the passage above, “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness” (the unconditioned dharma). This is the World-Honored One answering why one should be “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness” (the unconditioned dharma), saying: because “all conditioned dharmas (seeking and clinging) are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated.” (Sutra text:

“How should one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness. Why is this? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated.”
) This is the World-Honored One, before concluding his instruction, earnestly admonishing once more: leave marks!

In the seventh chapter, where it says “all sages and saints are distinguished from one another through the unconditioned dharma,” it has been explained that the unconditioned dharma is cultivation by leaving marks. To give without abiding in marks, with no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, no mark of a lifespan, no dharma-mark and no non-dharma-mark either—this is the unconditioned dharma. For example, in the third chapter the Buddha says, “Thus I liberate measureless, countless, boundless sentient beings, yet in truth not one sentient being attains liberation,” and in the fourth chapter the Buddha says, “give without abiding in marks”—these are the unconditioned dharma. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections Spoken by the Buddha,

“the Buddha says: A renunciant shramana cuts off desire and does away with love, recognizes the source of his own mind, penetrates the Buddha’s profound principle, and understands the unconditioned dharma. Within, there is nothing attained; without, there is nothing sought. The mind is not tied to the path, and does not bind up karma; without thought and without action, neither cultivating nor realizing. Not passing through the various stages, one is of himself most honored—this is called the path.”
Whereas
the conditioned dharma is cultivation by clinging to marks. The Buddha says:
“If a bodhisattva’s mind abides in dharmas while giving
(the conditioned dharma)
, he is like a person entering darkness, who sees nothing. If a bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in dharmas while giving
(the unconditioned dharma)
, he is like a person with eyes, in the bright sunlight, who sees all manner of forms.”

(Chapter Fourteen) The giving spoken of here stands for the six paramitas and all practices. The six paramitas and all practices performed with clinging to marks are the conditioned dharma; those performed while leaving marks are the unconditioned dharma.

[All conditioned dharmas] In cultivating the path one must above all avoid seeking and clinging. To cultivate while clinging to marks is to enter illusion through illusion: the wish to awake only deepens the delusion. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Birth and death and nirvāṇa are like last night’s dream. Good man! Because they are like last night’s dream, you should know that birth and death and nirvāṇa neither arise nor cease, neither come nor go; as for that which is realized, there is no gain and no loss, no grasping and no rejecting; as for that which realizes, there is no doing and no stopping, no keeping and no extinguishing. In this realization there is neither a realizer nor an object; ultimately there is no realization and no one who realizes—the nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.”

[Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow] This speaks of clinging to marks and abiding: delusive and unreal like the illusion of a dream, like the shadow of a bubble; though at times it shows all the colors of the rainbow, it is soon destroyed. The reason is that cultivating while clinging to marks and abiding gains only the blessings of gods and humans; and having gained such blessings, one again does evil on the strength of them, and falls even deeper. Therefore the Song of Realizing the Way by Yongjia says:
“Giving while clinging to marks brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow up into empty space. When its force is spent the arrow falls back, and brings a future life of unsatisfactoriness.”
The Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of the Original Nature says:
“The thoughtless heavens live eighty thousand years; when blessings end they return to the evil paths, like a dream, an illusion, and a bubble, and like morning dew and lightning.”

[The thoughtless heavens live eighty thousand years] Master Taixu’s Lectures on the Sutra of the Great Vehicle’s Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: “This is the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception in the formless realm. Eighty thousand years should be eighty thousand great kalpas.”

Therefore, on the path of bodhi, one must leave marks not only in circumstances and conditions—“all marks whatsoever are delusive and false”—but also in the dharma of the path: “all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow.” Only when the two clingings, to person and to dharma, are shattered and both person and dharma are extinguished does one realize the great Way.

Why must one be “not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness”—leaving marks and abiding nowhere (the unconditioned dharma)? Because if, in “receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, and expounding for others,” one grasps at marks, that is clinging to marks and abiding, and clinging to marks and abiding is the conditioned dharma. All conditioned dharmas (clinging to marks and abiding) are like a dream, like an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; though at times they show all the colors of the rainbow, they are soon destroyed—like morning dew or lightning, appearing and gone in an instant.

At the end of the text the World-Honored One once again, with deep earnestness, charges us: by no means, by no means cultivate while clinging to marks; cultivation that clings to marks is the conditioned dharma, and “one is like a person entering darkness, who sees nothing.” The conditioned dharma gains only the blessings of gods and humans; one cannot even escape the three realms, much less realize the fruit of Buddhahood and wake from the great dream!
In “Non-Attainment and Non-Teaching, Chapter Seven,” it says:
“All sages and saints are distinguished from one another through the unconditioned dharma.”
Master Yongjia drew a striking contrast between the conditioned and the unconditioned dharma. The Song of Realizing the Way says:
Awake, and it is at once done, with no effort applied; all conditioned dharmas are not like this.
Giving while clinging to marks
(the conditioned dharma)
brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow up into empty space.
When its force is spent the arrow falls back, and brings a future life of unsatisfactoriness.
How much better the gate of unconditioned true suchness
(the unconditioned dharma)
: one leap straight into the Tathagata’s ground.
The Diamond Sutra is precisely the perfectly round, perfectly sudden gate of the unconditioned true reality, in which one springs straight into the Tathagata’s ground!

Therefore the key to liberation is to shatter all clinging and realize non-discriminating wisdom (also called realizing emptiness): not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness. As for how to take up the work, how to contemplate, and how to leave marks, Mr. Jiang Weihong’s Diamond Sutra Commentary speaks of it very well:
“The Buddha spoke this sutra fundamentally for ordinary beings who have brought forth the great mind. These two lines
(‘not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness’)
and this one verse
(‘all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated’)

precisely point out where the ordinary being of great mind should take up the work. Therefore the two contemplations, before and after, must be practiced with fine and unbroken continuity, alternating the one with the other. Practiced long, one will surely come to a place of attainment.
This unworthy one
(the humble way of saying ‘I’)

— in the twenty years since I began studying the Buddha-dharma, though I practiced various methods and made various contemplations, I made no progress at all. One day, at these four lines of verse, I suddenly seemed to awaken, and cultivated contemplation accordingly. At first it was as though near and as though far, as though clear and as though dim, not yet forming a piece, and it had no great effect.
Then I understood that one should, upon all circumstances and conditions, apply the utmost intentness in observing them

. Whether in the smallest matter, or at times when all goes smoothly or when nothing goes smoothly, one seals it all with such principles as dream and illusion; even in practicing and upholding the Buddha-dharma one takes such principles as dream and illusion
to seal it

, and in walking, standing, sitting and lying down, never depart from this. Thus, after a long time, though one’s skill in ‘not grasping at marks, and unmoved in suchness’ is still shallow, yet it truly begins from making this contemplation. The mind gradually feels hollow and empty, and toward all circumstances and marks one gradually becomes unmoved within. When reading the sutras one’s eyes feel a little brighter, and when reciting the Buddha’s name one feels a little more solid. Now I ask you all to try it; you will surely find it useful. You should know that for the ordinary being of this lowly ground, who wishes to turn the light back and shine inward, apart from this there is no place to take up the work. Take care! Take care!”

[The Two Contemplations] To contemplate the unmoving intrinsic nature (the contemplation of intrinsic nature) and to contemplate all dharmas as illusory (the contemplation of illusion). The Diamond Sutra Commentary says:
However, the method of practice must be taken up by being aware at the very point where no thought has yet arisen, that is, to contemplate the intrinsically unmoving nature
(the contemplation of intrinsic nature)

. This is the meaning of the Surangama Sutra in taking the unborn and undying as the fundamental cause of cultivation; it is also the meaning of cultivating cessation through the inherently still nature and thereby attaining concentration, and of cultivating contemplation through the inherently luminous nature and thereby attaining wisdom. If one does not know to begin from here, one’s practice is confused and disordered, a blind and reckless cultivation—as though boiling sand to make rice, which can never succeed. Though a beginner is wholly in ignorance and cannot see it by contemplation, one should still understand this principle deeply and contemplate it diligently and roundly. As said before, when the earlier thought has already ceased and the later thought has not yet arisen, at just that very moment the mind is wholly still and clearly luminous—this is what is called contemplation. ‘Round’ means neither exerting effort nor not exerting effort, neither sinking nor floating. This is a single thread of the light of wisdom, the very first expedient of knowing illusion and being freed of it. At the same time, following this verse, one contemplates all dharmas as like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew and lightning, empty in their very substance
(the contemplation of illusion)

. This method is an even greater expedient—the so-called knowing of illusion. The two are best cultivated together, for these two methods aid each other. To contemplate the intrinsic nature is to work at the very source; to contemplate all dharmas is to work upon circumstances and conditions. Moreover, the former contemplation is more concerned with cultivating concentration, whereas the latter is more concerned with cultivating wisdom. Concentration can indeed give rise to wisdom, but unless wisdom is first opened, that concentration can never be achieved either. Hence, in their mutual assistance the contemplation of illusion is especially important, because by contemplating dharmas as dreamlike and illusory one can be led directly into the unmoving nature.

[Dream, illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, lightning] Illusory and unreal like a dream; vanishing in an instant like a bubble or a shadow; appearing and gone in a moment like morning dew or a lightning flash. [Empty in their very substance] Without waiting for analysis, directly realizing that their substance is originally empty and non-existent. [Common ground (thin ground)] The lowly and inferior position; refers to the position of the lowly, ordinary person.

Question: In the verse, does ‘conditioned dharmas’ refer to the conditioned dharmas in Bodhisattva Vasubandhu’s (also translated as Tianqin Bodhisattva) Treatise on the Gate of the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahayana—all things that arise from the union of causes and conditions—so why not explain it that way?

Answer: Taken on its own, the common explanation that the conditioned dharmas in this verse are all things arising from the union of causes and conditions is not mistaken. But the Diamond Sutra speaks of the real nature of all dharmas, and so not only are conditioned dharmas like dreams and illusions—unconditioned dharmas (all things that do not arise from causes and conditions) are likewise like dreams and illusions. Therefore the conditioned dharmas spoken of here are relative to
“all sages and saints are distinguished from one another through the unconditioned dharma”
the unconditioned dharma in the seventh chapter, and are likewise relative to the unconditioned dharma in the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections.

In the Treatise on the Gate of the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahayana, all dharmas are gathered into one hundred kinds; the first ninety-four are conditioned dharmas and the last six are unconditioned dharmas. If the conditioned dharmas in ‘all conditioned dharmas, like dreams, illusions, bubbles and shadows’ refer to the conditioned dharmas in that treatise, then a question arises: are the unconditioned dharmas in the Treatise on the Gate of the Hundred Dharmas also like dreams and illusions?

The answer is: unconditioned dharmas are also like dreams and illusions. That is to say, all dharmas are like dreams and illusions. The basis for saying this is that at the very beginning of the Treatise on the Gate of the Hundred Dharmas, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu says:
“As the World-Honored One said,
all dharmas
are without a self.”
That is to say, all dharmas are empty, and all dharmas are like dreams and illusions—not only conditioned dharmas are like dreams and illusions. In the Smaller Prajñā-paramita Sutra, the Buddha says:
all dharmas
are like illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame.”
In the Mahayana Lankavatara Sutra, the Buddha says:
“A bodhisattva-mahasattva should say that
all dharmas
are like illusion, like a dream.”
[All dharmas are without a self] All things whatsoever are illusory and have no fixed, intrinsic nature to speak of; this is called dharma-selflessness, also called dharma-emptiness.

Since all dharmas are like dreams and illusions, why does the Buddha here say only ‘all conditioned dharmas, like dreams, illusions, bubbles and shadows, like dew and lightning, should be viewed in this way’ rather than ‘all dharmas, like dreams, illusions, bubbles and shadows, like dew and lightning, should be viewed in this way’? Hence the conditioned dharmas spoken of here mean: clinging to forms as real is a conditioned dharma.

[When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Elder Subhuti, together with the bhikshus, bhikshunis, upasakas and upasikas, and all the gods, humans and asuras throughout the world, having heard what the Buddha said, were filled with great joy, and believing, receiving and practicing it, carried out his teaching.]

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhuti, together with the bhikshus, bhikshunis, upasakas and upasikas, and all the gods, humans and asuras throughout the world, having heard what the Buddha said, were filled with great joy, and believing, receiving and practicing it, carried out his teaching.

[Upasaka] Translated into Chinese as a ‘pure and faithful layman’, that is, a male lay practitioner who in the home draws near to and serves the Three Jewels and observes the five precepts. [Upasika] Translated into Chinese as a ‘pure and faithful laywoman’, that is, a female lay practitioner who in the home draws near to and serves the Three Jewels and observes the five precepts. [Believe, receive, practice] To believe, to accept, and to cultivate as it is taught.

The wisdom of the assembly suddenly opened and they were filled with the joy of the Dharma—dispelling my inverted thoughts of countless kalpas, obtaining the Dharma-body without passing through the asamkhyeya kalpas.
[Samkhyeya] An asamkhyeya kalpa.
What the whole Diamond Sutra teaches can be summed up in four questions: For what purpose? Relying on what meaning? Awakening to what dharma? Practicing what conduct?
1. For what purpose? To end the two deaths—to put an end to delimited birth-and-death and to transformational birth-and-death.
2. Relying on what meaning? All dharmas are empty. Constantly and intimately applying the effort of contemplation and examination, truly realize that ‘all forms whatever are false and illusory’.

3. Awakening to what dharma? The unborn dharma. Dharmas are originally unborn (all dharmas have never arisen—all dharmas have never existed), so one contemplates the principle of non-arising in order to destroy the afflictions of arising and ceasing, until the great awakening emerges from the dream. The sutra says:
“This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not true.”
(from the Lotus Sutra, the
Expedient Means
chapter).
4. Practicing what conduct? The practice of leaving forms—seeing illusion and immediately being free of it, leaving illusion and immediately awakening. This sutra says:
“Not grasping at forms, forever still and unmoving” and “leaving all forms, one is then called a Buddha.”
The main theme of the Diamond Sutra:
Ultimately empty, ungraspable, leaving all forms, waking from the great dream.
The central idea of the Diamond Sutra:
The ten realms are a single dream of ignorance, and so one must awaken from this deluded dream to attain the eternal, great freedom.

[The ten realms] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, sravakas (voice-hearers), pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary beings; the last four are the four sages.
How can one awaken? By leaving forms—realizing the unborn dharma, seeing forms without being deluded, and not being turned by circumstances. How does one set about it?

“One should not give rise to a mind that dwells in forms; one should not give rise to a mind that dwells in sounds, scents, tastes, sensations and objects; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”
The core of practice in the Diamond Sutra is leaving forms (seeing forms without delusion, not being turned by circumstances). Why leave forms? Because
“all forms whatever are false and unreal”
, and furthermore
“if one sees all forms as not forms, one then sees the Tathagata”
“leaving all forms, one is then called a Buddha”
. How does one leave forms?
“One should not give rise to a mind that dwells in forms, nor in sounds, scents, tastes, sensations and objects; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”
“knowing that all dharmas are without a self, one is accomplished in patience”
“not grasping at forms, forever still and unmoving”

Not being turned by circumstances—this is the genuine skill of ending birth and death (delimited birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death). In fact, when originally a single thought of ignorance arose and one fell into being an ordinary person, that too was being turned by circumstances. Now, to return home along the very same path is to cultivate not being turned by circumstances. So what does one cultivate in practice? Simply not being turned by circumstances—‘not grasping at forms, forever still and unmoving’; this is the unconditioned dharma.
The purpose of studying the Diamond Sutra:
to end birth and death. Master Hanshan (Hanshan Deqing) says:

From antiquity people have left home (renounced the world) for this great matter of birth and death. Even the Buddhas and patriarchs appearing in the world came only to reveal and explain this one matter. There is no Buddha-Dharma apart from birth and death, and no birth and death apart from Buddha-Dharma. As it is said: in delusion, birth and death begin; in awakening, the wheel of transmigration ceases. From this one knows that the ancient seekers, in their questioning and striving, sought only to settle the truth and pursue the ultimate along the road of birth and death—and that apart from this, set down in ink and paper, in words and letters, in the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teaching, there is no separate, rare and wonderful matter to be made of it.

So Bodhidharma came to the West and did not establish words and letters, but only awakened to his own mind, because this mind is the root of the proper and dependent retributions of all sages and ordinary beings in the ten realms. To awaken fully to this mind is the supreme and holy Mahayana; to awaken a little is the two vehicles; not to awaken at all is the ordinary person. If one awakens yet does not hold to it, and realizes yet gains nothing, that is the upward path that transcends sages and ordinary beings and passes beyond birth and death.
Students of recent times are ever further removed from the sages; they do not see the true way of conducting oneself of the ancients,
(namely)

in passing one by one through the present everyday states and the shore of birth and death. In this very everyday life, not apart from a single dharma, not dwelling on a single dharma, and never letting a single thing slip by lightly—that is genuine, earnest effort. In whatever one passes through one by one among the present sounds and forms, the favorable and adverse, and the states of love and hatred, that is the true gate of awakening. In that very place of awakening, every head and every dharma is the genuine Buddha-Dharma.

“…If one can, at the places where thoughts arise in daily use, where the emotional roots are firmly knotted, where love and hatred are intertwined and hard to unravel, where the manifold habits of greed, anger, delusion and pride are hard to wear away, there drive the awl into the very root of the pain (the same as ‘pierce’), investigating each one and passing through each one, then this is true and real knowledge, and one at once ascends the supreme gate of unobstructed, self-mastering great liberation. Apart from this, what knowledge (good and wise knowledge) is there to consult? What other rare and wonderful gate is there to enter?”

Praise of the Diamond
Severing doubt, giving birth to faith; transcending forms, going beyond the schools; in a single instant forgetting self and dharma, and realizing the true emptiness.
The flavor of prajñā, layer upon layer; the four-line verses fused and understood; the merit and virtue praised without end.
[The Diamond Praise] It is the verse of praise for the Diamond Sutra.
Sever doubt and give birth to faith”:

dispelling doubt and deeply believing the wonderful principle that ‘all dharmas are illusory, and when the illusion is exhausted the dream awakes’—this is the supreme function of the Diamond Sutra. Layman Pang says:
“The world prizes precious treasures; I value the stillness of a single instant. Much gold disturbs the mind
(entering illusion)
, in stillness one sees the true suchness nature
(leaving illusion)

[Layman Pang] Pang Yun, a famous lay Chan practitioner of the Tang dynasty. He studied Chan under Mazu and attained awakening; he was known as Layman Pang and was praised as the Vimalakirti of the East. In the Yuanhe era he traveled north to Xiangyang, and loving its local customs, he sank his wealth into the river with his boat, and together with his wife and son farmed at the foot of Mount Lumen, often making bamboo articles to support themselves. At the moment of his passing he bade his daughter Lingzhao go out to see whether the day was yet early or late; Lingzhao reported: ‘The sun is already at its height, and there is an eclipse.’ Pang Yun then went out of doors to look, whereupon Lingzhao climbed onto her father’s seat, and with palms joined passed away sitting. Pang Yun laughed and said: ‘My daughter is sharp and quick indeed!’ So he lingered on for another seven days before passing away. Mrs. Pang then went to tell her son in the fields, and the son too, leaning on his hoe, passed away. Before long, having gone about to all the neighboring villages to say farewell and retire into seclusion, no one knew where she ended.
Transcend forms and go beyond the schools”:

to transcend forms is to have no mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a lifespan; to have no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas. To go beyond the schools is to transcend all the schools.

[The schools] When the World-Honored One appeared in the world he taught the various teachings of great and small, complete and partial, to gather in and transform all the conditions of beings. After the World-Honored One’s passing, sages each divided into schools according to the teachings, in order to bring benefit to those with affinities. The rise of the schools of Chinese Buddhism dates from about the Sui and Tang dynasties; there is a doctrine of thirteen schools, namely: Vaibhashika, Satyasiddhi, Vinaya, Sanlun (Three Treatises), Nirvāṇa, Dilun, Shelun, Pure Land, Chan, Tiantai, Huayan, Faxiang (Dharma Nature), and Esoteric (Mijiao) schools. The Chan school has the doctrine of the Five Houses and Seven Schools; the five houses are: Linji, Weiyang, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. The seven schools are these five houses, besides the Yangqi and Huanglong branches that were split off from the Linji house. [Great and small] The Mahayana and the Hinayana. [Complete and partial] The definitive Mahayana is the complete-word teaching; the non-definitive Hinayana is the partial-word teaching.
In an instant forget self and dharma, and realize the true emptiness”:

in an instant forgetting self and dharma means at once doing away with self and dharma; here ‘forget’ is used in the sense of ‘do away with’. That is, there is no longer a self of a person (pudgala) or a self of dharmas (dharma-self).
[True emptiness] Not the emptiness of emptiness—empty yet not empty; that is, having the appearance of existence while its substance is non-existent.
The flavor of prajñā, layer upon layer”:
The meaning and interest of prajñā are profound, vast and without end.
The four-line verses fused and understood; the merit and virtue praised without end”:

The sutra speaks again and again of the immeasurable merit of ‘receiving and upholding even a four-line verse and speaking it for others’. Therefore, as long as one fuses together and fully understands any four lines of the sutra (meaning a small portion), one’s merit and virtue will be without end.

As for the Diamond Sutra, it takes formlessness as its fundamental principle, non-abiding as its essence, and wonderful function as its use, leading people to awaken to principle and see their nature, and to still forever the deluded mind. What I hope for those who study it is that together they may see the nature of gold within the ore, and smelt it with the fire of wisdom; when the ore is gone and the gold remains, this is what is called a Buddha.
The great master Hanshan (Cold Mountain) has a verse:
I see people turning the sutra, understanding it through another’s words.
The mouth turns but the mind does not turn; mind and mouth go against each other.
When the mind is true there is no crookedness, and one commits none of the entanglements and coverings.
But just examine your own self; do not seek another to stand in for you.
When one is master within the mind, one knows there is no inside and no outside.

[Entanglements and coverings] ‘Entanglement’ and ‘covering’. Both entanglement and covering are another name for afflictions; entanglement has ten kinds, and covering has five kinds. [The ten entanglements] The ten kinds of affliction. ‘Entanglement’ is another name for affliction, because affliction entangles the body and mind of sentient beings, so that they cannot escape birth and death and realize nirvāṇa. The ten entanglements are: shamelessness, lack of shame, envy, miserliness, remorse, drowsiness, restlessness, torpor, anger, and concealment. [Concealment] ‘Concealment’ means hiding. It refers to hiding the evil one has committed, fearful only that others know of it, so that one cannot repent one’s faults and turn toward the good. [The five coverings] The five kinds of affliction. ‘Covering’ is another name for affliction, because affliction covers over people’s mind-nature so that wholesome dharmas do not arise. The five coverings are: greed, anger, drowsiness, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt about the Dharma.
